pages.description: What Data Hub does, what it doesn't do, where your data shows up, and which page to read next.
pages.markdown:
# Overview (/docs/overview)



**For:** Everyone

Instrument data tends to stay where it was made. Files sit on the PC wired to the plate reader, named by whoever was at the bench, backed up if someone remembers. Finding a result from three months ago means knowing which machine made it and who was running it.

Data Hub moves that data off the instrument PC automatically. A small program called a watcher runs on each instrument PC, watches the folder the instrument saves to, uploads new files as they appear, and groups them into runs. From then on the data is searchable in a browser and reachable from a script or an AI assistant, without anyone copying files to a shared drive. Whoever ran a run can claim it, so their name stays on it.

## What Data Hub isn’t [#what-data-hub-isnt]

Data Hub stores and shows instrument data. It doesn’t do these four things:

* **Change raw files**: uploads are exact copies, and processing only adds new files next to them
* **Replace your lab notebook**: each run has a comment thread for notes and can link to the notebook pages where the experiment is written up
* **Analyze data**: Data Hub reads vendor formats into something you can view and download, and the analysis is still yours
* **Run on the instrument**: processing happens on the server after upload, so nothing competes with the acquisition software for the PC’s resources

## How a file becomes a run [#how-a-file-becomes-a-run]

1. A [watcher](/docs/concepts#watcher) on the instrument PC notices a new file in the folder it’s watching, waits for the file to stop changing, and groups it with the other files from the same acquisition into a [run](/docs/concepts#run).
2. The watcher uploads those files to cloud storage. For [supported instrument types](/docs/instrument-preprocessing), server-side code then reads the vendor’s format, pulls out settings like wavelength or imaging mode, and builds viewable versions such as plate maps or contrast-adjusted images.
3. The run appears in the web app, the REST API, and the Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoint at the same time, because all three read the same record.

The full picture, including where each piece runs, is in [Architecture](/docs/architecture).

## Where your data shows up [#where-your-data-shows-up]

These are the web app’s main pages:

* **Home**: every instrument’s recent runs together, with counts for today and this week, and today’s comments
* **Instruments**: one instrument’s runs, with columns matching what that instrument records, and a status badge that says whether its new files can arrive. Each instrument also has a watcher page for the people who maintain it
* **My runs**: runs you’ve claimed, so you can find your own work without filtering
* **Lab Notebooks**: each lab notebook’s runs from every instrument, gathered on one page. See [Lab notebooks](/docs/lab-notebooks)
* **Comments**: every run comment by day, which you can filter to your runs or to one instrument. Open it from **View all comments** on Home

To see what has changed in Data Hub recently, open **Changelog** from the account menu.

If a term on those pages is unfamiliar, [Concepts](/docs/concepts) defines it. Start with run, watcher, run status, and instrument type.

## Get at the same data from code [#get-at-the-same-data-from-code]

The runs, files, and comments you see in the web app are also available from a REST API that you can call yourself, and from an MCP endpoint that AI clients call on your behalf. Both read the same records as the web app, so a script sees the same runs you do.

* **REST**: at `/api/v1/` on your deployment’s host. Each deployment publishes an OpenAPI 3.1 document at `/api/v1/openapi.json`, so you can generate a client instead of writing one. See the [API overview](/docs/api)
* **MCP**: at `/mcp/v1`. Add it to Claude Code, Claude Desktop, or Cursor by pasting the URL, and the assistant can search runs, read metadata, and fetch files during a conversation. Clients that support MCP Apps also show the same interactive run reports as the web app. See the [MCP overview](/docs/mcp)

The two sign in differently:

* **REST**: a script sends a [personal access token](/docs/concepts#personal-access-token) that an admin creates in the web app, limited to the scopes it needs. The token acts under its own name, so anything the script does is labeled with the token, not a person
* **MCP**: the AI client opens a browser sign-in and a consent screen, then acts as you with your own permissions. Nobody pastes a credential into the AI client

For example, you can pull every run from an instrument for a batch reanalysis, save the latest run’s archive to disk from a script, or ask an assistant which plates from last week failed processing.

## What’s supported today [#whats-supported-today]

Nine instrument types have a processor, covering plate readers, gel docs, qPCR, TapeStation, FPLC, flatbed plate scanners, ND2 microscopy, DishCam time-lapse photos, and the Unchained Labs Aunty for protein melting temperature and particle size. [Instrument data preprocessing](/docs/instrument-preprocessing) lists what each one extracts.

An instrument without a matching processor still works. Its files upload, and you can search, claim, comment on, and download them, but you get no extracted metadata, badges, or previews. Adding a new instrument type takes code changes, so an engineer has to do it.

## Self-hosted by design [#self-hosted-by-design]

Your team runs Data Hub on its own infrastructure, so raw instrument data and everything made from it stay on systems you control. The source code is open under the MIT license.

An engineer deploys these pieces once:

* The web app, which also serves the API and the MCP endpoint, on Vercel
* A PostgreSQL database for instruments, runs, files, and comments
* Three AWS S3 buckets for raw files, processed files, and download archives
* An AWS Lambda that processes each instrument’s files and builds download archives
* A Google OAuth client, which decides who can sign in

The Google OAuth client allows either only your Google Workspace organization or any Google account. Nothing inside Data Hub can override it, so the engineer makes that choice when deploying, and an admin can’t change it later.

Until those pieces exist, nobody can sign in and no watcher can upload. [Deploy Data Hub](/docs/self-hosting) explains the deployment and links to the step-by-step guides in the repository.

## Getting access [#getting-access]

Sign in with a Google account that your deployment allows. Everyone who signs in can browse instruments, runs, and files, comment on runs, and [send feedback](/docs/send-feedback) about Data Hub. Admins can also confirm instruments, create tokens, make other people admins, and connect Linear and Slack. Only an existing admin can make you an admin. See [Security and permissions](/docs/security#roles) for what each role can do.

## Start here [#start-here]

<Cards>
  <Card title="Deploy Data Hub" href="/docs/self-hosting" description="Engineers: the database, web app, and AWS stack." />

  <Card title="Set up an instrument" href="/docs/set-up-an-instrument" description="Operators and admins: go from a new PC to an uploading instrument." />

  <Card title="Browse runs" href="/docs/browse-runs" description="Everyone: find runs, claim your work, download files, and leave lab notes." />

  <Card title="Administration overview" href="/docs/administration" description="Admins: instruments, watchers, tokens, and members." />
</Cards>

## Reading these docs with AI [#reading-these-docs-with-ai]

Every page has a **Copy Markdown** button and a **View Options** menu. Use them to do either of these:

* Copy a page as Markdown into an assistant
* Open a page’s raw Markdown at `/docs/<path>.md`, the list of every page at [`/docs/llms.txt`](/docs/llms.txt), or every page in one file at [`/docs/llms-full.txt`](/docs/llms-full.txt)

pages.markdown:
# Deploy Data Hub (/docs/self-hosting)



**For:** Engineers

Data Hub is self-hosted, so nobody can sign in or install a watcher until your team has deployed it. This page explains what gets deployed, what access you need, and in what order. The commands are in the repository.

<Callout type="warn">
  For the step-by-step deploy, open [First-time deployment](https://github.com/Arcadia-Science/data-hub/blob/production/docs/developer/first-time-deployment.md) in the data-hub repository. That guide has every command, environment variable, and checklist. Read this page first for the overall order.
</Callout>

## What you’ll deploy [#what-youll-deploy]

You deploy three pieces:

| Piece                  | What it does                                                                              | Where it runs                            |
| ---------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- |
| PostgreSQL database    | Stores instruments, runs, files, watchers, and tokens                                     | Any PostgreSQL host, managed or self-run |
| Web app                | Serves the web pages, the REST API, and the MCP endpoint                                  | Vercel                                   |
| Storage and processing | S3 buckets for raw, processed, and archived files, plus the Lambda that processes uploads | AWS, deployed with AWS SAM               |

You’ll also create a Google OAuth client, which decides who can sign in to your deployment. Data Hub has no invitations and no email allowlist of its own, so that client’s setting is the whole access policy. Read [Who can sign in](/docs/security#who-can-sign-in) before you create it.

Give `staging` and `production` separate databases and separate AWS stacks. They’re independent deployments holding independent data.

## Access you need before you start [#access-you-need-before-you-start]

The deploy stops partway without any one of these, so confirm all four first:

* **Admin-level AWS credentials**: the first deploy creates the stack, which the automated deploy role can’t do. That role can only update a stack that already exists
* **Vercel project access**, including permission to set environment variables for the environment
* **Google Cloud Console access**, to create the OAuth client
* **GitHub repository settings access**, to store the secrets that let continuous integration run every later deploy

You’ll also need the AWS CLI and the AWS SAM CLI installed locally.

## How the deploy is sequenced [#how-the-deploy-is-sequenced]

The web app and the AWS stack each need something the other creates, so the order matters. [First-time deployment](https://github.com/Arcadia-Science/data-hub/blob/production/docs/developer/first-time-deployment.md) has the commands for each step:

<Steps>
  <Step>
    **Create the database** and keep its connection string. Make sure the host accepts connections from Vercel and from your continuous integration runners.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    **Deploy the web app**, set its environment variables, apply the database migrations, then sign in and create the access token the Lambda will use.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    **Deploy the AWS bootstrap stack**, once per AWS account, not once per environment. It creates the shared resources both environments use.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    **Deploy the AWS stack** for this environment, using the web app’s URL and that token.
  </Step>

  <Step>
    **Copy the AWS stack’s outputs into the web app’s environment variables**, then redeploy so it picks them up.
  </Step>
</Steps>

The web app deploys at step 2 but doesn’t fully work yet. Files, uploads, reprocessing, and run archives stay broken until step 5 connects it to AWS.

## Common first-deploy mistakes [#things-that-catch-people-out]

Each of these can break a first deploy:

* **Set `ADMIN_EMAILS` before you sign in for the first time.** It makes the first admin. If you sign in before setting it, your account can’t create tokens or confirm instruments
* **Point `BETTER_AUTH_URL` at this deployment’s own public origin.** Data Hub builds the Google callback URL from it, so a value copied from another environment sends people to that other host and sign-in fails. AI clients read the same value when they sign in over MCP, so a wrong one breaks them too
* **Google sign-in on Vercel preview deployments needs `OAUTH_PROXY_URL` and `OAUTH_PROXY_SECRET`.** Google accepts only redirect URLs registered in advance, and every preview gets a new URL. Previews therefore send the sign-in through one fixed deployment whose URL is registered. Production registers its own URL and leaves both variables unset
* **Create the Lambda’s token from the Lambda preset.** The Lambda reads an instrument’s type before choosing a processor, so without `instruments:read` every upload fails with a permission error. DishCam processing also reads the run’s file list, so it fails without `runs:read`. The **Lambda** preset includes both
* **Set `ENABLE_S3_FILES` to `true` or `false` for the AWS stack.** An empty value fails the deploy. Use `false` unless you want the Lambda to read files of 1 GiB or more from a mounted copy of the raw bucket instead of downloading them, which needs a VPC and costs extra; the runbook covers turning it on later
* **The bootstrap stack fails if the AWS account already has a GitHub identity provider** from another project. Reuse the existing one instead of creating a second
* **Set `INTEGRATION_SECRETS_KEY` before an admin saves Slack or Linear secrets.** Data Hub encrypts those secrets with it, and saving fails without it. Generate one with `openssl rand -hex 32`
* **An admin sets up the Slack channel and Linear in the web app.** They aren’t environment variables: an admin connects them under **Settings → Integrations** after the deploy, and feedback stays off until Linear is connected. The Slack app credentials for direct messages can be environment variables or saved there. See [Set up integrations](/docs/integrations)

## What finished looks like [#what-finished-looks-like]

Operators can install watchers and instruments start uploading. Hand them [Set up an instrument](/docs/set-up-an-instrument), and create their first tokens through [Issue and revoke tokens](/docs/manage-tokens). To turn on feedback reports and Slack messages, an admin then follows [Set up integrations](/docs/integrations).

From then on, deploys are automatic. Merging to `staging` or `production` deploys the web app, applies database migrations, and deploys the Lambda for that environment, so you run the steps above once per environment.

## The runbooks [#the-runbooks]

The deploy commands live next to the code in the data-hub repository. Start with [First-time deployment](https://github.com/Arcadia-Science/data-hub/blob/production/docs/developer/first-time-deployment.md):

* [First-time deployment](https://github.com/Arcadia-Science/data-hub/blob/production/docs/developer/first-time-deployment.md): the full sequence above, with every command
* [Continuous integration and deployment](https://github.com/Arcadia-Science/data-hub/blob/production/docs/developer/ci-and-deployment.md): how later deploys, migrations, and watcher releases happen
* [Local development](https://github.com/Arcadia-Science/data-hub/blob/production/docs/developer/local-development.md): run the app on a laptop, including a setup that needs no AWS or Google credentials
* [Architecture for contributors](https://github.com/Arcadia-Science/data-hub/blob/production/docs/developer/architecture.md): how the code is organized

For how the components fit together and how data moves between them, see [Architecture](/docs/architecture).

pages.markdown: # Set up an instrument (/docs/set-up-an-instrument) **For:** Lab operators and admins This walkthrough takes you from nothing to an uploading instrument: create an access token, install the watcher, register the instrument, get an admin to confirm it, then start watching. CLI flags, the full config schema, and Windows service setup each have their own page, linked where they come up. Data Hub is self-hosted. The web app, PostgreSQL database, and AWS stack (S3 plus the processing Lambda) must already be running. If they aren’t, an engineer needs the [Deploy Data Hub](/docs/self-hosting) guide first. ## Before you start [#before-you-start] You need: * **The watch folder**: the folder your instrument saves its output to. * **File patterns**: which files to upload, written as patterns such as `*.csv`, `*.xlsx`, or `*.tiff`. * **[uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/)** installed on the instrument PC (it manages Python for you). To make setup and maintenance easier, we recommend setting up remote access to the instrument PC via [Windows Remote Desktop](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows-server/remote/remote-desktop-services/remotepc/remote-desktop-allow-access). ## 1. Create an access token [#1-create-an-access-token] The watcher authenticates to Data Hub with a personal access token. Only admins can create tokens, so ask one if you aren’t an admin. In the Data Hub web app, go to **Settings → Access Tokens** and choose **Create token**. Give the token a **Name** that identifies the instrument PC, for example `Plate Reader PC`. Set **Expiration** to **No expiry**. An admin can still revoke the token at any time. Under **Scopes**, choose the **Watcher** preset. It grants only what a watcher needs: registering, reporting runs, and uploading files. Choose **Create token**, then copy the token. It starts with `dhub_` and is shown only once. Keep the token handy: you paste it into the setup wizard in step 3. For rotation, revocation, and the full scope list, see [Issue and revoke tokens](/docs/manage-tokens). ## 2. Install the watcher [#2-install-the-watcher] On the instrument PC, install the watcher with `uv`. The `windows-service` extra adds `pywin32` so you can follow [Run as a Windows service](/docs/windows-service), which is the default on a lab PC: ```sh uv tool install "data-hub-watcher[windows-service]" ``` On macOS or Linux, omit the extra: ```sh uv tool install data-hub-watcher ``` [Install and update the watcher](/docs/install-the-watcher) has the full install, check, and update steps. ## 3. Run the setup wizard [#3-run-the-setup-wizard] Start the wizard with `data-hub-watcher init`. It prompts you for one thing at a time: Choose the environment. For a live lab, this is production. Enter your Data Hub API URL, for example `https://datahub.your-domain.com/api/v1`. Paste the token from step 1 when it asks for the API key. The wizard checks the key, then lists the instruments already registered. Pick your instrument from the list, or choose **Register a new instrument** if it isn’t there. For a new instrument, enter an ID and a display name. The ID is a short, lowercase, hyphenated name like `bio-rad-cfx96`. **It can’t be changed later.** Enter the full path to the folder your instrument writes into. List which files to upload, such as `*.pcrd,*.csv`. The watcher ignores files that don’t match. Choose how files get grouped into runs. Pick the preset that matches how your instrument names its output, or write your own. The wizard previews a few matches so you can check the run IDs. For example, the default preset uses the filename prefix before the first underscore, so `RUN001_quant.csv` and `RUN001_melt.csv` both group into run `RUN001`. Set the stability period: how many seconds a file must stay unchanged before the watcher treats it as finished. The default is 5. Raise it for instruments that write large files slowly. Choose the upload mode. **Auto** uploads each file as soon as it’s stable. **Manual** waits until someone chooses **Upload** for the file in the web app. For run detection options, see [Configure run detection and uploads](/docs/configure-run-detection); [Watcher configuration](/docs/configuration-reference#run-detection) lists every preset. The wizard then registers the watcher, saves the config to `~/.data-hub/config.yaml` (`C:\Users\your_username\.data-hub\config.yaml` on Windows), and sends it to Data Hub. When it reports that setup is complete, an admin confirms the instrument. ## 4. Confirm the instrument’s registration [#confirm-the-instruments-registration] A pending instrument can’t upload to Data Hub until an admin confirms it from the web app. Until then its badge reads **Pending**, and its page shows a **Waiting for confirmation** card in place of the runs table. Members see one line saying the instrument is waiting for an admin. In the Data Hub web app, choose **Instruments → View all** in the sidebar. Open the **Pending** tab and find your instrument. It shows an amber **Pending** badge. Choose **Confirm…** on its row. A window shows what the watcher registered: the computer, the watch folder, the file patterns, how files become runs, and the upload mode. Check that it matches what you entered in the wizard. If it doesn’t, choose **Change settings first** to fix it. Choose an **Instrument type**, which is required, then choose **Confirm instrument**. The instrument moves to the **Active** tab. The instrument’s badge reads **Connecting** until the watcher service you start in step 5 checks in, and then **Online**. If the watcher hasn’t checked in 15 minutes after you confirm, the badge reads **Offline** with the notice “The watcher never checked in”. That’s expected if you haven’t started the service yet, and the badge turns **Online** at the first check-in. Open the instrument’s page and check the watch folder and file patterns shown under its name. They should match what you entered in the wizard. Files outside that folder, or with names that don’t match a pattern, won’t reach Data Hub. Admins can change an instrument’s type later: open the three-dot menu, choose **Edit details**, and pick a supported type. What each type produces is in [Instrument data preprocessing](/docs/instrument-preprocessing). Adding a new processor takes code changes; see [Adding a new instrument](https://github.com/Arcadia-Science/data-hub/blob/production/docs/developer/lambda.md#adding-a-new-instrument) in the developer docs. [Manage instruments](/docs/manage-instruments) covers confirming and editing instruments and reading an instrument’s page. ## 5. Start the watcher service [#start-the-watcher-service] First, preview what the watcher will do without starting it: ```sh data-hub-watcher watch --dry-run ``` The dry run checks the config, checks that Data Hub is reachable and the instrument is active, and lists the files it would upload. When it looks right, install and start the watcher as a Windows service. Run these from an **Administrator** terminal: ```sh data-hub-watcher service install data-hub-watcher service start ``` The service starts when the PC starts, keeps running after you sign out of Windows, and updates itself. [Run as a Windows service](/docs/windows-service) covers stopping and restarting it, and where it writes logs. On macOS or Linux, run the watcher in the foreground instead: ```sh data-hub-watcher watch ``` The watcher finds new files, groups them into runs, uploads them in auto mode, and checks in with Data Hub every 60 seconds. Runs appear in the web app as the watcher reports them, and their files follow as they upload. ## What you get once it’s running [#what-you-get-once-it-is-running] * Raw files upload to cloud storage * The instrument’s runs and files appear in the web app * The watcher service starts again whenever the PC restarts * The watcher’s activity, health, and settings appear on the instrument’s **Watcher** page, and the instrument’s badge shows whether new files can arrive * People who subscribe to the instrument can get notifications about new runs in the app and in Slack

pages.description: Use the web app to find runs, check that new files will arrive, read processed results, claim your runs, download files, comment, and reprocess or delete runs.
pages.markdown: # Browse runs (/docs/browse-runs) **For:** Everyone Once instruments are uploading, use the web app to find runs and work with them: read results, claim your runs, download files, and leave lab notes. Lab notebooks have their own page, [Lab notebooks](/docs/lab-notebooks). ## Orient yourself in the app [#find-a-run] The sidebar and the home page are the two starting points for daily work. **Home** lists recent runs across instruments, newest first, with counts for today and this week at the top. Filter by date range, who ran it, and instrument-specific metadata when it’s available, then page through the results. Below the runs, Home shows up to four of today’s comments; use the date picker to see comments from another range. The **Runs needing attention** card beside the counts shows how many runs, of any age, failed to upload, failed processing, or stalled. When it isn’t zero, choose it to list those runs. **Instruments** in the sidebar lists five instruments, and **View all** opens the full list. Each instrument’s page starts with its name and a status badge that says whether new files can arrive; see [Check that new files will arrive](#check-files-will-arrive). Under the name are the folder its watcher reads from and the file patterns it uploads, then a runs table with column filters that match the instrument type (for example wavelengths on a plate reader). **My runs** lists runs you’ve claimed, so you can return to your own work without filtering every run. Its **Runs needing attention** card counts only your runs. **Comments** lists every run comment by day. Open it from **View all comments** on Home. Each person’s profile page also shows the comments they wrote and the comments on runs they ran. ### Narrow a long run list [#narrow-a-long-run-list] Home and the instrument pages share the same four controls: * **Search runs**: filters the list by run name as you type * **Date range**: presets from Today through Last 4 weeks, plus a custom range. Home shows today’s runs until you pick another range, and **All time** shows every run * **Add filter**: filter by run status, or turn on **Show deleted runs** * **Column headers**: sort by **Run Started**, **Last Updated**, size, who ran it, or any instrument-specific column The **Lab Notebook** column header filters the list by lab notebook, or to runs in none; see [Find runs by lab notebook](/docs/lab-notebooks#find-runs). **Run Started** is when the instrument acquired the run. **Last Updated** changes when the run’s files change, or when someone edits, claims, or comments on it, or adds it to or removes it from a lab notebook. The default order is newest run first. The sort order is saved in the page link, so a link you share opens with the same order. ### What each run status means [#run-status] A run’s status tells you how far its files have got from the instrument to the web app: | Status | Meaning | | ----------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Failed | At least one file failed processing. The file’s row on the run page gives the reason. | | Stalled | At least one file has been processing for more than 20 minutes without finishing. Reprocess it to try again. | | Upload failed | The watcher gave up on at least one file, for example because its folder is no longer on the instrument PC. See [When an upload fails](#upload-failed). | | Waiting to upload | Files are on their way from the instrument PC: someone requested them, or the watcher uploads them on its own. | | Uploaded | The files are in storage. Processing hasn’t started, or this instrument type has no processor. | | Queued | You chose **Reprocess**, and the files are waiting for a free processing slot. They start as other files finish. | | Processing | The server is reading the files, extracting metadata, and building reports. | | Not uploaded | Some files are only on the instrument PC, and nothing will upload them until someone requests them. Common on instruments in manual upload mode. | | Completed | Processing finished. | | Empty | The run has no files. | A run with files in several states shows the first status in this table that applies. For example, a run with one failed file and nine completed files shows **Failed**, and a run with three processed files and 285 that nobody requested shows **Not uploaded**. **Waiting to upload** and **Not uploaded** replace the earlier **Pending upload**. A saved link or API call that filters by `pending` still works and matches both. ## Check that new files will arrive [#check-files-will-arrive] If a file you saved on the instrument PC hasn’t shown up, start with the badge beside the instrument’s name. It says whether new files can reach Data Hub. The same badge appears in the instruments table, on Home, and in search results. | Badge | What it means | | -------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | **Online** | New files upload automatically. For an instrument in manual upload mode, new files upload when someone requests them. | | **Restarting** | The instrument PC is restarting or the watcher is updating. Either takes a minute or two, and you don’t need to do anything. | | **Connecting** | The watcher was set up recently and hasn’t checked in yet. If it hasn’t checked in after 15 minutes, the badge turns **Offline**. | | **Offline** | New files won’t appear right now. A notice under the instrument’s name says why. | | **Pending** | An admin hasn’t confirmed this instrument yet. Admins see a card in place of the runs table; members see one line. | | **Retired** | The instrument no longer takes new runs. Its runs stay browsable. | Hover over the badge, or focus it with the keyboard, for a short explanation. [Concepts](/docs/concepts#instrument-status) has the full rules for each badge. Select the badge to open the instrument’s watcher page. The watcher is the program on the instrument PC that finds new files and uploads them. Anyone signed in can read its activity, health, and settings there, and only admins can change them. ### When the badge reads Offline [#when-offline] A red notice between the instrument’s name and its runs says what happened: | Notice | What happened | | ------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | **New files aren’t being picked up** | The watcher is running but can’t find its watch folder, which the notice names. An admin can choose **Change folder** to fix it. | | **The watcher isn’t checking in** | The watcher hasn’t checked in for 5 minutes, or didn’t come back within 15 minutes of a restart. The notice says when it last did. The PC may be off, or the watcher may have crashed. | | **The watcher never checked in** | The watcher was set up, but no check-in arrived within 15 minutes. Its service may not be running on the PC, or the PC can’t reach Data Hub. | | **Uploads from this instrument are paused** | Someone stopped the watcher on the PC. New files appear once it’s started again. | | **This instrument isn’t connected to a watcher** | The instrument never had a watcher, or its watcher was deregistered, which the notice dates and credits. Admins can choose **Connect a watcher**, which opens [Set up an instrument](/docs/set-up-an-instrument). | **See details** opens the watcher’s **Activity** tab. Members see only that link, or no link when there’s no watcher. To get it fixed, tell an admin what the notice says or send them the link. [Troubleshoot a watcher](/docs/troubleshoot-a-watcher#instrument-shows-offline) covers each reason. An instrument in manual upload mode, whatever its badge says, shows a blue note beside its file patterns: “Files upload when someone requests them.” That isn’t a problem. Files wait until someone chooses **Upload**; see [Request an upload](#request-upload). ## Search the workspace [#search] Press **⌘ K** (macOS) or **Ctrl K** (Windows/Linux) to open global search from any page. Results are grouped into runs, lab notebooks, files, instruments, users, and comments, so you can also look up a colleague’s work or the text of a lab note. Selecting a file opens its run with the files table filtered to that file. Lab notebooks match on their name, description, or notebook page link; see [Find runs by lab notebook](/docs/lab-notebooks#find-runs). ## Open a run and inspect results [#open-run-detail] Each run has a page at `/instruments/your_instrument_id/runs/your_run_id`. The arrows beside the run name step you to the next or previous run without going back to the list. The top of the page lists who ran it, the number of raw files, and their total size. Below that, the **Lab Notebooks** section lists the lab notebooks the run is in; see [Lab notebooks](/docs/lab-notebooks#add-runs). What you see after that depends on the instrument type and whether a processor ran: * Metadata tags for extracted fields, such as experiment type, wavelength, or temperature * Processed reports such as tables, images, PDFs, and videos, including interactive plate maps for plate readers and a video player for DishCam runs * A files table of everything in the run, labeled Raw or Processed, with each file’s size and status Select a metadata tag to open the instrument’s runs table filtered to that value. For example, selecting a wavelength tag lists every run on that instrument recorded at the same wavelength. Reports with many images, PDFs, or spectra show one item at a time. Search by filename to jump anywhere in the run, or use the arrows to step through it. The counter beside the arrows shows your position out of the total. Plate maps with more than 12 columns, such as 384-well plates, scroll sideways inside the plate. Per-type inputs and outputs are in [Instrument data preprocessing](/docs/instrument-preprocessing). ### Filter the files table [#filter-files] The files table has separate **Type** and **Status** filters. Use them to show, for example, only failed files or only processed CSVs. **Download all** and the run archive include only the files the filters show. ### Live file updates [#live-file-updates] While files are uploading, queued, or processing, the run page checks for updates every 5 seconds for up to 5 minutes. After that it stops and shows **Stopped checking for file updates**. Choose **Refresh** to check for another 5 minutes. Uploading or reprocessing files from the page also starts a new 5 minutes. ## Claim who ran it [#claim-who-ran-it] Choose **Claim** on the run page to put your name on the run. You can only claim or unclaim a run for yourself, so nobody else can put your name on a run. Your claim shows on the run and in the “ran by” filters. API tokens can’t claim runs; a signed-in person has to. ### Asked after a download [#claim-prompt] When you download a run archive or a file from a run nobody has claimed, Data Hub asks **Did you run this?** in a card near the bottom of the page. Choose **I ran this** to claim the run, or **Not me** so this browser doesn’t ask about the run again. Downloading several runs from a runs list asks once about all the unclaimed ones, and **I ran these** claims them all. An AI assistant connected to the [MCP server](/docs/mcp) is told when it downloads from an unclaimed run, so it can ask you and claim the run for you. ## Add runs to a lab notebook [#lab-notebook] A lab notebook gathers the runs behind one notebook page, such as a Notion or Google Docs page, from every instrument. On a run page, choose **Add to lab notebook** in the **Lab Notebooks** section. To add several runs at once, select them in a runs list and choose **Add to lab notebook** in the action bar. [Lab notebooks](/docs/lab-notebooks) covers adding runs, finding them, and each lab notebook’s page. ## Download files [#download-files] From the files table you can: * Preview a CSV, TSV, JSON, or other text file by selecting its row. The preview shows the first 1 MB of the file. Use the back and forward buttons to move between previewable files on the same page of the table. **Download** in that window saves the file * Select files and choose **Download** in the bar that appears above the files table. One file downloads directly. Two or more come as a single zip, which builds in the background like **Download all** * Choose **Download all** to build a zip of active files in the run, with any active file filters applied Large zips build in the background. When one isn’t ready yet, Data Hub tells you how long to wait before trying again. ## Act on several runs at once [#bulk-actions] Select the checkbox on one or more run rows to open an action bar at the bottom of the list. Run rows have no buttons of their own; every run action goes through this bar. * **I ran these**: claim every selected run in one step * **Remove my attribution**: unclaim them * **Upload**: ask the watcher to upload files that are still on the instrument PC. Data Hub refuses the request for a run whose instrument isn’t **Online** or **Restarting**, and a message says how many failed; see [Request an upload](#request-upload) * **Download**: download a zip of each selected run * **Reprocess**: run server-side processing again, including on runs whose files have stalled * **Add to lab notebook**: add every selected run to the same [lab notebook](/docs/lab-notebooks). Runs already in it are skipped * **Remove from lab notebook**: choose from the lab notebooks the selected runs are in, and remove every selected run from them * **Delete**: mark the selected runs deleted **Upload**, **Download**, **Reprocess**, **Delete**, and the lab notebook actions appear only when every selected run allows them. For example, **Reprocess** is hidden if one of the selected runs belongs to an instrument type with no processor, and the lab notebook actions are hidden if a selected run is deleted. **Remove from lab notebook** also needs at least one selected run to be in a lab notebook, and the lab notebook actions work on up to 100 runs at a time. The checkbox in the header row selects every run on the page, and **Clear** drops the selection. The selection stays when you move to another page of the same results. It clears when you change the search, a filter, or the sort, so the bar never acts on runs from a list you are no longer looking at. The files table on a run page works the same way: select files to get **Upload**, **Dismiss**, **Reprocess**, and **Download** for only those files. Its **Upload** follows the instrument’s badge, like the other [Upload buttons](#request-upload). Its selection also clears when you change the files search, a filter, or the sort. ## Comment on a run [#comment] The comment thread on a run page is for lab notes and follow-ups. A new comment can notify the people who claimed the run or already commented on it, and choosing a comment notification scrolls to that comment. Set preferences under **Settings → Notifications**; see [Configure notifications](/docs/configure-notifications). Only the author of a comment can edit it. Authors can delete their own comments, and admins can delete any comment. Comments posted by a script through an API token show the token’s name with a key icon instead of a person. ## Reprocess or delete a run [#reprocess-and-delete] Reprocessing runs server-side processing again. Use it after a file failed or stalled, or after an engineer fixes the code that reads a file type. The stored result doesn’t change until you reprocess. * On the run page, hover over a file and choose **Reprocess**. * To reprocess several files, select them in the files table and choose **Reprocess** in the bar. * To reprocess whole runs, select them in a run list and choose **Reprocess** in the bar. Reprocessing sends only the original instrument files. Files Data Hub generated, such as videos, previews, and CSVs, have no **Reprocess** button and are rebuilt from the originals. Reprocessed files go through a queue; see [How reprocessing is queued](#reprocess-queue). **Delete** marks the run deleted without removing its stored files. Anyone signed in can delete or restore a run. To find a deleted run, turn on **Show deleted runs** under **Add filter**, then open it and choose **Restore**. Files that were queued for reprocessing when the run was deleted stay queued but don’t start. If you restore the run, they start as processing slots free up. Deleting a run also cancels the uploads that were requested for its files, so the watcher stops trying to send them, and those files go back to **Not uploaded**. Restoring the run doesn’t bring the requests back, so choose **Upload** again if you still want the files; see [Request an upload](#request-upload). While a run is deleted, Data Hub refuses a watcher’s reports of it, so the watcher’s new files aren’t added. After you restore the run, restart the watcher to send them, or choose **Upload** on a file to have the watcher send that file without a restart. Watchers before 1.4.3 also send them when another file of the run finishes. See [A run was deleted on Data Hub](/docs/troubleshoot-a-watcher#a-run-was-deleted-on-data-hub). ### How reprocessing is queued [#reprocess-queue] Reprocessing starts at most 10 files at a time, counted across all runs and instruments. When you choose **Reprocess**, each file goes into a queue: * A file that can start right away shows **Processing**. * A file that has to wait shows **Queued**. It starts when another file finishes, and files that were queued earlier start first. * A run with queued files shows **Queued** in the runs list, unless another of its files has a status that comes earlier in the [status table](#run-status), such as **Failed**. * If Data Hub can’t send a file to the processor, or the processor ends with an error without saving a result, the file shows **Failed** with a message that says so, and the next queued file starts. Reprocess the failed file to try again. * To take the waiting files out of the queue, choose **Cancel queued** at the top of the run page. Each queued file shows **Failed** with a message that says the reprocess was cancelled, and you can reprocess it again. Files that have already started aren’t affected. Files that arrive from a watcher upload count toward the 10, but they start right away and never wait in the queue. A file that has been processing for more than 20 minutes without finishing stops counting, so one stuck file doesn’t hold up the queue. A large run takes several rounds. For example, reprocessing a run of 80 files starts 10 files, and the other 70 show **Queued** until slots open. You can leave the page, because the queue keeps running. A queued file has no **Reprocess** button. The engineer who deploys Data Hub can change the limit of 10 with the `PROCESSING_CONCURRENCY_LIMIT` environment variable; see the [web application environment variables](https://github.com/Arcadia-Science/data-hub/blob/production/docs/developer/getting-started.md#web-application). If a file that the queue started never finishes, for example because Data Hub restarted at the moment it started the file, it shows **Stalled** after 20 minutes. The queue then puts it back in line once. If it stalls a second time, it stays **Stalled** until you reprocess it. ## Get files that are still on the instrument PC [#files-on-the-pc] The watcher reports every file it finds, but some files stay on the instrument PC until someone asks for them, and some fail to upload. The footer under a run’s files table counts the files still on the instrument PC, the files that couldn’t upload, and the files uploaded. ### Request an upload [#request-upload] A file that the watcher found but nobody requested reads **Not uploaded**. To ask the watcher to send files, do one of these: * Choose **Upload** on one file * Choose **Upload all** at the top of the **Files** section, for every file in the run that reads **Not uploaded** or **Upload failed** A requested file reads **Uploading** until it arrives. The watcher picks up requests within a minute. On an instrument that uploads automatically, a new file reads **Waiting to upload** until the watcher sends it. This needs watcher 1.4.5 or later; with an older watcher the file reads **Not uploaded** for the minute or two before it arrives. The **Upload** and **Upload all** buttons on a run page follow the instrument’s badge. When one is turned off, the reason shows beside it: | Badge | Upload buttons | Beside them | | -------------- | ------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- | | **Online** | On | Nothing | | **Restarting** | On. Requests wait until the watcher is back | “The instrument PC is restarting. Uploads start once it’s back.” | | **Connecting** | Off | “The watcher hasn’t checked in yet.” | | **Offline** | Off | “Can’t upload while the watcher is offline.” | | **Pending** | Off | “This instrument is waiting for an admin to confirm it.” | | **Retired** | Off | “This instrument is retired.” | If the badge reads **Offline** and the run has files that are still on the instrument PC, a red notice sits above the **Files** section. It says how many files are still on the PC, which watcher isn’t running, and when it last checked in, and links to **See details**. A run with no waiting files never shows the notice, whatever the badge says. A request made while the instrument reads **Restarting** waits, and the watcher uploads the files once it’s back. If the watcher doesn’t check in for about 15 minutes, Data Hub cancels the request and the files read **Not uploaded** again. [Request uploads](/docs/manage-watchers#request-uploads) lists every case that cancels a request. The **Upload** button on a runs list doesn’t follow the badge. Select runs and choose it to ask for every waiting file in them. For an instrument that is **Offline**, **Connecting**, **Pending**, or **Retired**, Data Hub refuses that run’s request, and a message reports how many runs failed. Choose **Upload** from the run page instead to see why. On an instrument in [manual upload mode](/docs/concepts#upload-mode), every file waits until someone chooses **Upload** for it. **Dismiss** tells the watcher not to upload a file. See [Manage the watcher fleet](/docs/manage-watchers#approving-manual-uploads). ### When an upload fails [#upload-failed] The watcher gives up on a file when it can’t send it. The file then reads **Upload failed**, and hovering over the status shows why: * **The folder is no longer on the instrument PC.** Someone renamed or moved the run’s folder after the watcher found it. The watcher reports the folder under its new name as a new run, so look for a run with the same start time and a similar name. * **The file isn’t on the instrument PC.** The folder is there but the file was moved or deleted. * **The upload kept failing.** The watcher tried and the upload failed each time, for example because of a network problem. The message shows the last error. * **The path is outside the watch folder.** The watcher won’t upload a file outside the folder it watches. For a requested file, the watcher checks three times, about a minute apart, before it gives up. On an instrument that uploads automatically, it gives up as soon as an upload fails, and it tries again the next time it starts. A red notice above the **Files** section lists the files that couldn’t upload, one block per reason and folder. Each block says why and when the watcher gave up. The run reads **Upload failed** until every such file is uploaded or dismissed, and the watcher’s activity shows one **Couldn’t upload** entry per run and reason. Once the cause is fixed on the PC, choose **Upload again** in the block, or **Upload** on a single file, to try again. If the files are gone for good, choose **Dismiss these files**. Whoever requested the files gets one notification per run and reason, in the app and, if they connected Slack, as a direct message. See [Configure notifications](/docs/configure-notifications). Marking files **Upload failed** needs watcher 1.4.5 or later. An older watcher puts the file back to **Not uploaded** instead, without a reason; see [Roll out watcher releases](/docs/watcher-releases#what-each-version-adds). ## Use the same data outside the UI [#programmatic-access] You can also list and fetch the same runs and files over the [REST API](/docs/api) or the [Model Context Protocol (MCP) endpoint](/docs/mcp). REST needs a [personal access token](/docs/concepts#personal-access-token); scopes and creation are covered in [Issue and revoke tokens](/docs/manage-tokens). MCP clients sign in through the browser instead, and clients that support MCP Apps show the same interactive run report you see here.

pages.description: Gather the runs behind one notebook page from every instrument, find runs that aren’t in a lab notebook yet, and manage lab notebooks from the web app, scripts, and AI assistants.
pages.markdown:
# Lab notebooks (/docs/lab-notebooks)



**For:** Everyone

A lab notebook in Data Hub stands for one notebook page, such as the Notion or Google Docs page where an experiment is written up. Adding runs to it gathers them in one place, from every instrument, and lets whoever analyzes a run open the page that explains how the experiment was set up. A run can be in several lab notebooks.

## Add runs to a lab notebook [#add-runs]

On a run page, choose **Add to lab notebook** in the **Lab Notebooks** section. Then do one of these:

* Type a lab notebook’s name to pick one Data Hub already has
* Paste the notebook page’s link. If no lab notebook has that page yet, Data Hub creates one. Give it a name, which starts out filled in from the link, such as a Notion page’s title

In the same window, leave **Make me the owner** ticked to own a lab notebook you create this way. Tick **I ran this run** to claim the run at the same time.

The **Lab Notebooks** section of the run page lists each lab notebook the run is in, with who added it. Select a lab notebook’s name to open [its page in Data Hub](#notebook-page), or the arrow beside it to open the notebook page. Its **⋯** menu copies the notebook page’s link or removes the run from the lab notebook.

To add many runs at once, select them in a runs list and choose **Add to lab notebook** in the action bar; see [Act on several runs at once](/docs/browse-runs#bulk-actions).

### Rules for lab notebooks [#lab-notebook-rules]

* A run can be in up to 20 lab notebooks.
* Each notebook page has one lab notebook, with one name that every run in it shares.
* Two links count as the same page when they differ only in `http` or `https`, `www.`, a trailing slash, the part after `#`, or tracking parameters such as `utm_source`.
* Notion links count as the same page when they have the same page ID, so a link copied before the page was renamed still finds its lab notebook.
* Anyone signed in can create lab notebooks and add runs to them or remove runs from them.
* A deleted run stays in its lab notebooks. You can’t add it to a lab notebook or remove it from one until the run is restored.
* A deleted lab notebook keeps its runs, and restoring it brings them back. Pasting a deleted lab notebook’s link offers to restore it.

## Find runs by lab notebook [#find-runs]

Runs tables show each run’s first lab notebook in the **Lab Notebook** column, with **+1**, **+2**, and so on when there are more. The column header filters the list:

* **In any lab notebook** or **In no lab notebook**. Use **In no lab notebook** to find runs that still need one
* One lab notebook, to see only its runs. Each lab notebook in the menu shows how many of the listed runs it holds, and the menu’s search box narrows the list

Global search (**⌘ K** or **Ctrl K**) also finds lab notebooks by name, description, or link. Paste a notebook page’s URL to find its lab notebook, even when your copy of the link differs from the saved one.

## A lab notebook’s page [#notebook-page]

Each lab notebook has a page in Data Hub that lists its runs from every instrument. To open it, do one of these:

* Select a lab notebook’s name anywhere in Data Hub
* Choose it under **Lab Notebooks** in the sidebar, which lists the lab notebooks you opened last and the ones that most recently got a run
* Choose **View all** under **Lab Notebooks** to list every lab notebook, with its owner, run count, instruments, and newest run. Search that list by name, or paste a notebook page’s link to find its lab notebook

To create a lab notebook before it has any runs, choose **New lab notebook** on that list.

The page shows the lab notebook’s description and owner above its runs, which you can search, filter, and act on like any runs table. **Open lab notebook** opens the notebook page. To take runs out, select them and choose **Remove from this lab notebook**.

The **⋯** menu on the page has three actions:

* **Edit details**: change the lab notebook’s name, description, owner, or link. The name is shared by every run in it, and the link can’t point to a notebook page that another lab notebook already has
* **Copy page link**: copy the address of the Data Hub page. Paste it into the notebook page, so each page links to the other
* **Delete**: take the lab notebook off its runs and out of lists and search. The page stays, with **Restore**, which brings the lab notebook back with all of its runs

## From scripts and AI assistants [#lab-notebook-api]

Scripts manage lab notebooks through the [REST API](/docs/api)’s `/lab-notebooks` endpoints:

* Listing and reading lab notebooks needs the `runs:read` scope
* Creating, editing, deleting, and restoring lab notebooks, and adding or removing their runs, needs `lab-notebooks:write`
* A token that registered a watcher can add or remove only its own instrument’s runs, and can’t create, edit, delete, or restore lab notebooks

The run lists take `has_lab_notebook` to list runs in any lab notebook or in none, and `lab_notebook_id` to list one lab notebook’s runs. Each run in a response lists its `lab_notebooks`.

An AI assistant connected to the [MCP server](/docs/mcp) can do the same with the lab notebook tools in the [tools catalog](/docs/mcp/tools). Its `search_runs` tool filters by lab notebook with `hasLabNotebook` and `labNotebookId`.

pages.description: What Data Hub does to a raw file after upload, which instrument types have a processor, and what supporting a new instrument takes.
pages.markdown: # Instrument data preprocessing (/docs/instrument-preprocessing) **For:** Lab operators, admins, and engineers After a [watcher](/docs/concepts#watcher) uploads a raw file, Data Hub can run a **processor** on it. A processor is code that reads the vendor’s file, pulls out settings like wavelength or imaging mode, and builds something you can look at in the browser. Nine instrument types have one today. This page covers what each processor produces, why a file sometimes gets no processing, and what adding a new instrument involves. Supporting a new instrument is engineering work that an admin can’t do in settings. It needs a new Python module, a database migration, changes to both the web app and the Lambda (the AWS function that processes files), and a Lambda redeploy. See [Add support for a new instrument](#add-support-for-a-new-instrument). ## How a file reaches a processor [#how-preprocessing-works] 1. A file arrives in raw storage, which starts the Lambda. Storage starts it for every upload, whatever the instrument. 2. The Lambda checks whether any processor accepts the file’s type. If none does, it stops there, before it contacts the Data Hub API. 3. It looks up the instrument, then finds the processor for the instrument’s [type](#set-the-instrument-type). It stops here when the type has no processor, or when that processor doesn’t accept the file’s type. 4. The processor reads the file, extracts metadata, writes processed files when it has any, and updates the run through the API. 5. The file’s status moves from `processing` to `completed` or `failed`. ### Why an upload sometimes produces nothing [#why-an-upload-produces-nothing] Two things can make an upload produce nothing, and neither marks the file failed, because nothing went wrong: * **The processor doesn’t accept the file’s type**: each processor accepts only the file types listed in the table below. A TapeStation run starts processing only on its PDFs, so the peak-table CSVs it writes are stored but don’t start processing on their own. * **The instrument has no type set, or a type with no processor**: files upload and stay browsable, but you get no metadata and no reports. The file-type check also applies when you choose **Reprocess** in the web app. Reprocessing a file that the processor doesn’t accept marks it **Failed**, with a message that names the instrument type. Reprocessing does help when the instrument had no type, or a type with no processor, when the file arrived: set the type, then choose **Reprocess**. ### Set the instrument type [#set-the-instrument-type] Data Hub picks the processor by the instrument’s **type**, not its instrument ID. The ID (`azure-cielo-qpcr`) names one physical machine. The type (`qpcr`) names a vendor’s file format, and several instruments can share one. To set it, open the instrument page as an admin, choose **Edit details** from the three-dot menu, and choose an **Instrument type**. One type means one vendor’s output format. Names like `qpcr` and `fplc` sound general, but each belongs to a single vendor’s processor: `fplc` expects ÄKTA PDFs, and `qpcr` expects Azure Cielo exports. Giving a different vendor’s instrument an existing type sends its files to a processor that can’t read them. Supporting a second vendor means splitting the type in two, which is a code change. ## Supported instrument types [#supported-instruments-at-a-glance] | Type | Vendor and model | File types it processes on upload | You get | | -------------------- | --------------------------- | --------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------- | | `tape_station` | Agilent 4150 TapeStation | `.pdf` | Tape-type badge, PDF reports | | `fplc` | Cytiva ÄKTA FPLC | `.pdf` | PDF you can read on the run page, no metadata | | `gel_doc` | Azure 600 Gel Doc | `.tif`, `.tiff` | Contrast-enhanced PNG, imaging badges | | `qpcr` | Azure Cielo qPCR | `.csv`, `.pdf`, `.aze` | Dye-channel badges, melting curves, the instrument’s PDF report | | `epson_v700_scanner` | Epson V700 Scanner | `.tif`, `.tiff` | Plate preview JPG, colony measurements | | `hina_microscope` | Hina Microscope (Nikon ND2) | `.nd2` | Channel overlay JPG, a video of each timelapse, channel badges | | `plate_reader` | SpectraMax iD3 and iD5 | `.xls` | Well-data CSV, interactive plate maps | | `dishcam` | DishCam time-lapse camera | `.tif`, `.tiff`, `run.json` | A video of each photo stack, camera-setting badges | | `aunty` | Unchained Labs Aunty | `.xlsx` | A plate with a curve chart in each well, experiment badges | ## Agilent 4150 TapeStation [#agilent-4150-tapestation] Reads the tape type out of peak-table CSV filenames and shows TapeStation reports on the run page. * **Expected files**: CSVs named like `YYYY-MM-DD - HH-MM-SS-_peakTable.csv`, plus matching PDFs * **Metadata**: `Tape Type`, for example `gDNA` or `HSD1000`, when the filename matches that pattern * **Processed files**: none * **On the run page**: tape-type badge, a PDF viewer, and peak-table reports Only the PDF starts processing. A run with only CSVs stays unprocessed, and choosing **Reprocess** on one of its CSVs marks it **Failed**, because the TapeStation processor accepts only PDFs. ## Cytiva ÄKTA FPLC [#akta-fplc] Stores ÄKTA chromatography PDFs so you can read them in the browser. The processor reads nothing out of the PDF itself yet, so this type gets no badges or filters. * **Expected files**: `.pdf` reports from the ÄKTA * **Metadata**: none * **Processed files**: none * **On the run page**: files table, plus each PDF embedded under **Report Data** Leave a new FPLC as `generic` until an operator has checked that its PDFs are ÄKTA reports. ## Azure 600 Gel Doc [#azure-600-gel-doc] Rebuilds each gel TIFF as a viewable image and reads the imaging settings the instrument recorded. The processor stretches the contrast of each image, so the darkest 1% of pixels show as black and the brightest 1% show at full brightness. It does this per RGB channel, or once for a grayscale image. Then it lays every page of the TIFF side by side in one 300 dpi PNG. The stretch makes faint bands visible on screen and doesn’t change the raw file. * **Expected files**: TIFF from the Azure 600 * **Metadata**: `capture_type`, `imaging_mode` (true color, fluorescence, or chemiluminescence), `wavelengths`, `colors`, read from the TIFF `XPComment` tag * **Processed files**: contrast-enhanced PNG * **On the run page**: imaging badges, files table, image viewer for the PNGs Those metadata fields also drive the column filters on the instrument page. ## Azure Cielo qPCR [#azure-cielo-qpcr] Reads dye channel names, melting curves, and the instrument’s PDF report. * **Expected files**: * the Cq Values CSV, for dye channels * the melting curve CSV (a name ending in `_MeltingCurve.csv`) * the PDF report the instrument writes * `.AZE` project files * **Metadata**: `dye_channels`, the unique names in the Cq Values CSV’s `Fluorescence` column * **Processed files**: `{run_id}_melting_curve_derivatives.csv` and `{run_id}_melting_curve_plate.json` from the melting curve CSV. An `.AZE` file produces `{run_id}_aze_melting_curve_derivatives.csv`, `{run_id}_aze_melting_curve_plate.json`, and `{run_id}_aze_experiment.json`. * **On the run page**: dye-channel badges, the PDF report under **Report Data**, and a **Melting Curves** section The **Melting Curves** section shows the plate for one dye channel at a time. Select a well to see its melting curve and derivative, with a dashed line at the melting temperature. A run with more than one PDF gets previous and next buttons under **Report Data**. The other CSV files a qPCR run writes upload normally and show as completed, but contribute no metadata. ### `.AZE` project files [#aze-project-files] Data Hub reads melting curves from the Azure Cielo’s native `.AZE` project files as well as from the CSV export. Melting temperatures match the CSV export, but other values can differ. That’s because `.AZE` files store raw fluorescence, while the CSV export can be adjusted for baseline. A project with no melt data completes with no processed files. The watcher uploads `.AZE` files only when `*.AZE` is in the instrument’s file patterns. Patterns are case-sensitive, so match the case the instrument uses. See [Watcher configuration](/docs/configuration-reference#field-reference). An admin can add the pattern on the **Settings** tab of the instrument’s watcher page; see [Change a watcher’s settings](/docs/manage-watchers#change-a-watchers-config). You can also add it on the instrument PC with `data-hub-watcher config edit` and restart the watcher. ## Epson V700 Scanner [#epson-v700-scanner] Finds agar plates in a flatbed scan and measures the colonies on them. The processor looks for plates sitting in gold 3D-printed frames. For each plate it finds, it crops the plate and then detects colonies: 1. Trims the edge of the plate 2. Compares the plate against its background 3. Applies a difference-of-Gaussians filter, a standard way to pick out small spots 4. Applies a threshold 5. Measures whatever is left Measurements come out in physical units, so colony areas are comparable between scans. * **Expected files**: TIFF plate scans * **Metadata**: `dpi`, `color_mode`, `plate_count`, `plate_boxes`, plus `colony_detection` summaries when colonies were measured * **Processed files**: a web-sized JPG with plate outlines and colony boxes drawn on, and a `_colonies.csv` of per-colony area, centroid, eccentricity, and mean RGB * **On the run page**: scanner badges, files table, and reports for the processed CSV When no plates are found, you still get a resized JPG of the whole scan, and colony detection is skipped. An empty `plate_count` most likely means the frames weren’t recognized, not that the plates were blank. ## Hina Microscope [#hina-microscope] Turns each Nikon ND2 into a composite image you can view in the browser, and each timelapse into a video. For each time point, the processor turns every channel into one 2D frame. It takes the maximum projection over Z (the brightest value through the stack) and the first index over position. It reads one frame at a time, so large stacks process without loading the whole file. The processor stretches each frame’s contrast so the darkest 1% of pixels show as black and the brightest 1% at full brightness. Then it lays the channels over a brightfield background, each in its fluorophore color. * **Expected files**: ND2 * **Metadata**: `sizes`, `channels` (name, excitation and emission wavelength, color), and `dimensions`. Each timelapse file also records `frames`, `frame_interval_ms` (the measured time between frames), and `playback_fps` in its own file metadata. * **Processed files**: an RGB overlay JPG of the first time point for every file in the run, plus an MP4 for every file with more than one time point * **On the run page**: channel and size badges, files table, and a viewer with one item per file. A timelapse plays as a video, with its JPG shown before you press play. Any other file shows its JPG. A timelapse video plays at the capture rate or at 10 frames per second, whichever is faster, so slow captures stay watchable. A file that doesn’t record the time between frames plays at 10 frames per second. Each channel’s contrast comes from the first frame and stays the same for the whole video, so brightness doesn’t flicker and the first frame matches the JPG. Pixels that later grow brighter than the brightest 1% of the first frame show at full brightness. A signal that grows strongly during the capture can therefore look saturated. If the video can’t be made, the file shows **Failed** and the message says why. One cause is a timelapse that can’t finish within the [15-minute processing limit](#when-processing-fails). The JPG and the raw file are still available. A timelapse processed before Data Hub made videos gets its video when you choose **Reprocess** on the file or on the run. Timelapses take several minutes each. When you reprocess a run with more than 10 of them, 10 process at a time and the rest show **Queued**. Every file in a Hina run has the same channel layout, so whichever file finishes processing first writes the run’s metadata. Later files still get their JPG but skip the metadata write. If the layout changed partway through a run, reprocessing one file won’t correct the run’s metadata. An image too large to preview at full size gets a smaller preview instead. For example, a 6221 × 6221 pixel image is previewed at 3110 × 3110 pixels. The raw file is unchanged, and you can download it at full size. A file that showed **Failed** for this reason earlier gets its preview when you choose **Reprocess** on the file or on the run. Two kinds of image still show **Failed** instead of a preview: * An image from a color camera, which Data Hub can’t preview yet * An image far larger than the Hina Microscope has produced so far The message on the file says which. In both cases the raw file is stored and you can download it. ## SpectraMax iD3 and iD5 plate readers [#spectramax-id3-and-id5-plate-readers] Both models share one processor, which converts SoftMax Pro exports into the well data behind the interactive plate maps. * **Expected files**: SoftMax `.xls`, which is UTF-16 text with a `Plate:` header rather than a real Excel workbook * **Metadata**: `measurement_mode` (Absorbance, Fluorescence, or Luminescence), `measurement_type` (Endpoint, Kinetic, Spectrum, or Well Scan), and `wavelengths` as bare numbers with no unit suffix * **Processed files**: `{run_id}_raw_well_data.csv` * **On the run page**: wavelength, mode, and type badges, plus plate maps built from that CSV What the plate map shows depends on the read: * **Kinetic** reads get a time slider. Reads that skip the edge wells keep their time values, and runs that SoftMax Pro stopped early still process. * **Spectrum** reads (wavelength scans) get a wavelength slider. * **Luminescence** reads show no wavelength, because luminescence doesn’t use one. SoftMax Pro writes `#SAT` in a saturated well and `#Low` when the flash lamp missed a well. Those wells show as blank on the plate map, and the rest of the file processes normally. ## DishCam [#dishcam] Turns each DishCam photo stack into a video you can play on the run page. * **Expected files**: multi-page TIFF photo stacks, plus the `run.json` file the camera writes next to them * **Metadata**: camera settings from `run.json`: `fps`, `measured_fps`, `frames`, `duration_seconds`, `quality`, `format`, `started`, and `finished` * **Processed files**: an MP4 video and a JPEG still frame for each stack * **On the run page**: a video player at the top of the report, with play, pause, and a timeline you can drag. The still frame shows before you press play. The video plays at the capture rate or at 10 photos per second, whichever is faster, so slow captures stay watchable. The stored `fps` metadata still records the real capture rate. A stack processes once both the stack and its `run.json` are in storage, in either order. When a run gathers captures from several folders, each stack uses the `run.json` from its own folder. When two folders both have a `run.json`, the watcher renames later copies with a short tag, such as `run~3f9a1c2b.json`. Large stacks are read one photo at a time. If a stack can’t finish within the [15-minute processing limit](#when-processing-fails), it shows **Failed**, and the message says how far through the photos it got. You can still download the raw file. ## Unchained Labs Aunty [#unchained-labs-aunty] Reads Aunty exports, which measure protein melting temperature and particle size, and draws a plate of curves. * **Expected files**: the `.xlsx` export from the Aunty software. Thermal ramps, sizing runs, isothermal holds, and exports that contain only the results table without curves all process. * **Metadata**: `experiment_type` (`thermal_ramp`, `sizing`, or `isothermal`), `experiment_count`, and the first experiment’s settings: `analysis_mode`, `start_temp_c`, `end_temp_c`, `rate_c_per_min`, `temperature_c`, `analysis_version`, and `experiment_name` * **Processed files**: `{run_id}_aunty_curves.csv`, with every curve point for every well, and `{run_id}_aunty_plate.json`, which drives the plate view * **On the run page**: a plate with a small chart in each well. Select a well to open its full chart. On the instrument page, filter Aunty runs by experiment type, analysis mode, temperature, and ramp rate. ## Types with no processor [#instruments-without-a-matching-processor] Instruments typed `generic` or `instant_raman`, and instruments with no type set, upload without processing. Their files are stored, and you can browse, search, claim, comment on, and download them. They get no extracted metadata, badges, filters, or processed files. Leave a new instrument as `generic` until someone confirms which processor, if any, can read its files. Its files keep uploading in the meantime. ## When processing fails [#when-processing-fails] A file with status `failed` shows an error message on the run page. Open the run, then choose **Reprocess** on that file, or select runs in a run list and choose **Reprocess**. See [Reprocess or delete a run](/docs/browse-runs#reprocess-and-delete). Processing one file has a 15-minute limit. A file that hits the limit, or is too large to process at all, shows **Failed** with a message that explains why. The raw file stays in storage, and you can download it. A file that stays in processing for more than 20 minutes without finishing shows **Stalled**. That most likely means the processor stopped without reporting back. Reprocess it to try again. Reprocessing puts a file in a queue and starts at most 10 files at a time. A file that has to wait shows **Queued** until a slot opens. See [How reprocessing is queued](/docs/browse-runs#reprocess-queue). Reprocess files after an engineer fixes a processor, too. The fix changes the code, but results already stored stay the same until you reprocess. ## Add support for a new instrument [#add-support-for-a-new-instrument] **For:** Engineers Adding an instrument type is development work in the web app and the Lambda. Plan for a database migration and a Lambda image deploy. **Add the type.** Extend `instrumentTypeEnum` in `web/lib/db/schema.ts` and generate an `ALTER TYPE … ADD VALUE` migration. Reuse an existing type only when the new instrument writes the same vendor’s format. **Write the processor.** Add a module under `lambda/src/data_hub_lambda/` with a `process_file(instrument_id, run_id, filename)` function that reports progress through the Data Hub API. **Register it twice.** Add the type to `PROCESSORS` in `lambda/src/data_hub_lambda/processors.py`, with the file types it accepts, and to `PROCESSABLE_INSTRUMENT_TYPES` in `web/lib/instruments/processable-types.ts`. These two lists have to agree. The Lambda uses the first to pick a processor, and the web app uses the second to decide whether to offer **Reprocess**. **Add tests** for the processor and for the file types it accepts. **Deploy the Lambda image.** The raw bucket already starts the Lambda for every upload, so you don’t need a new S3 trigger. To try a processor on your own machine without S3 or API access, use the `data-hub-process` CLI. Its `handler` subcommand runs the whole handler against a local copy of S3. Full detail, including the archive builder and the Docker build, is in [the Lambda developer docs](https://github.com/Arcadia-Science/data-hub/blob/production/docs/developer/lambda.md#adding-a-new-instrument--processor).

pages.title: Configure notifications
pages.description: Choose in-app and Slack notifications for new runs, instruments that go offline, comments, failed uploads, service messages, and feedback, including per-instrument subscriptions and personal Slack direct messages.
pages.markdown: # Configure notifications (/docs/configure-notifications) **For:** Everyone Data Hub can notify you in the app and in Slack when: * New runs arrive * An instrument goes offline * Someone comments on a run you care about * Files you requested couldn’t upload * A script sends you a message * Feedback you sent is closed To choose, open **Settings → Notifications** while signed in. Everything on that page is a personal choice that affects only you. Only admins can change the connections the whole workspace shares, such as the [Slack channel for new runs](/docs/integrations#slack-channel) and the [Slack app behind direct messages](/docs/integrations#slack-app). They’re under **Settings → Integrations**. See [Set up integrations](/docs/integrations). You set in-app and Slack notifications separately, so you can turn on either one for a type without the other. ## In-app preferences [#in-app-preferences] | Setting | Effect | | ------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | **Mute new-run notifications** | Hides new-run notifications in the bell for every instrument. Offline alerts and your per-instrument choices stay as they are. | | **Instruments that go offline** | Notify when an instrument you subscribe to has been offline for 30 minutes, and again when it’s back online. See [When an instrument goes offline](#instrument-offline). | | **Comments on runs you ran** | Notify when someone comments on a run you’re attributed to. | | **Replies to your comments** | Notify when someone comments on a run you previously commented on. | | **Uploads that failed** | Notify when the watcher gives up on files you requested, for example because their folder is no longer on the instrument PC. You get one notification per run and reason. See [When an upload fails](/docs/browse-runs#upload-failed). | | **Service notifications** | Show messages that integrations and scripts send you through the API. | | **Updates on your feedback** | Notify when a [feedback report](/docs/send-feedback) you sent is resolved or declined. | | **New feedback** | Admins only. Notify when someone sends feedback about Data Hub. | ### Per-instrument subscriptions [#per-instrument-subscriptions] Under **Per-instrument**, turn on the instruments you want to hear about. A subscription covers the instrument’s new runs and its outages. **Mute new-run notifications** silences only the new runs, so your subscriptions still bring offline alerts while it’s on. You can also subscribe from the notifications switch on an instrument’s page, or from the instruments table’s notifications column when that column is shown. ### When an instrument goes offline [#instrument-offline] When an instrument you subscribe to shows **Offline** for 30 minutes in a row, Data Hub tells you once, with the reason from the [notice on its page](/docs/troubleshoot-a-watcher). When its badge is **Online** again, you get a second notification that says how long it was offline. Any reason for **Offline** counts: * The watch folder is missing * The watcher stopped checking in * The watcher never checked in after it was set up * Someone stopped the watcher * The instrument has no watcher Data Hub doesn’t send an alert in these cases: * A routine Windows restart or automatic update shows **Restarting** and doesn’t alert. A restart that doesn’t come back within 15 minutes turns **Offline**, and the 30 minutes start then. * You get no reminders while the instrument stays offline. A change of reason during the outage doesn’t send a second alert. * Retiring the instrument ends the outage without a message. ## The notification bell [#notification-bell] The bell icon in the app lists recent notifications: * New runs are grouped by day and instrument, and each group expands to show its runs. * Choosing a comment notification opens the run and scrolls to that comment. * A failed-upload notification says how many files couldn’t upload and why, and opens the run. * An offline or back-online notification names the instrument and opens its page. * Messages sent by a script through an API token show the token’s name with a key icon. ## Slack direct messages [#slack-direct-messages] Connect your Slack account on the same settings page to receive matching events as personal direct messages. After connecting, choose which types also go to Slack: * New instrument runs, for the instruments you subscribe to (the new-run mute applies only to the bell) * Instruments that go offline, for the instruments you subscribe to * Comments on runs you ran * Replies to your comments * Uploads that failed * Service notifications * Updates on your feedback * New feedback (admins only) Disconnect or reconnect from the same card. You have to connect with your organization’s Slack workspace, and Data Hub rejects any other workspace. If **Connect to Slack** is missing or doesn’t finish, an admin hasn’t set up the Slack app yet.
