See [Slack app for direct messages](/docs/integrations#slack-app).

pages.title: Send feedback and see what’s new
pages.description: Report a bug or request a feature about Data Hub from the app or an AI assistant, follow the report’s status, and read the in-app changelog.
pages.markdown: # Send feedback and see what’s new (/docs/send-feedback) **For:** Everyone Use **Feedback** to tell the team that runs Data Hub about a bug, a missing feature, or anything else about the app itself. Each report becomes an issue in your workspace’s Linear, and Data Hub tells you when that issue is closed. Feedback is for problems with Data Hub. A problem with one run’s data, such as a wrong plate map, belongs in a comment on that run, where the people who ran it will see it. ## Send a report [#send-a-report] Open the account menu at the bottom of the sidebar and choose **Feedback**. Choose a **Type**: **Bug**, **Feature request**, or **Other**. Enter a **Title** and a **Description**. Say what you expected and what happened instead. Optionally open **More details** and fill in **Trying to do**, **Tool**, and **Error message**. Choose **Send feedback**. Data Hub also records the page you were on, so you don’t need to paste a link. If you send a report with the same title within 24 hours, Data Hub returns the report you already sent instead of creating a second one. Once the first report has been closed, Data Hub creates a new one. The **Feedback** item appears only after an admin connects Data Hub to Linear. If you don’t see it, ask an admin to follow [Set up integrations](/docs/integrations#linear). ## What happens to a report [#what-happens-to-a-report] * Data Hub creates an issue in the Linear team your admins chose, with the label they picked for that type of report, if any. * The team works on the issue in Linear. * When the issue closes, Data Hub sends you a notification, and a Slack message if you turned that on. A report’s status follows its Linear issue: | Linear issue | Report status | | ---------------------------------- | ------------- | | Completed, such as **Done** | Resolved | | Canceled, or closed as a duplicate | Declined | | Anything else | Open | The notification names the Linear status too, such as **Resolved (Done)** or **Declined (Duplicate)**. Turn it on or off with **Updates on your feedback** under **Settings → Notifications**; see [Configure notifications](/docs/configure-notifications#in-app-preferences). You hear about a report once each time it closes. Moving the issue from one closed status to another doesn’t notify you again, but reopening and closing it does. ## Send feedback from an AI assistant [#from-an-ai-assistant] An AI assistant connected to Data Hub can send feedback for you, for example when a tool call fails. Assistants connect through [MCP](/docs/mcp), a standard way for AI assistants to use outside tools. The assistant shows you the draft first and sends it only after you agree. The assistant can also list the reports you sent and read one in full, by report ID or by Linear issue ID such as `ENG-1476`. The tools are listed under [MCP tools](/docs/mcp/tools). Every report needs a person behind it, so only signed-in users can send feedback. API tokens can’t, and scripts that call `POST /api/v1/feedback` have to use a signed-in session. ## Who sees which reports [#who-sees-which-reports] Members see only the reports they sent. They can list them through the API or an AI assistant, without the Linear assignee, priority, or activity. Admins review every report under **Settings → Feedback**: * **Open** and **Closed** are separate tabs. * Each row shows the Linear issue ID, status, label, priority, and assignee. * A report’s detail includes the Linear status changes and comments, and an **Open in Linear** link. Status changes happen in Linear. Data Hub has no control for changing a report’s status. Admins can also turn on **New feedback** under **Settings → Notifications** to hear when someone sends a report. ## See what’s new in Data Hub [#changelog] Choose **Changelog** in the account menu to see what has changed in Data Hub, newest first. It opens on top of the page you’re on. Each entry shows its title, and you select a title to read the entry. Some entries link to the page on this site that covers the change. Entries you haven’t seen before are marked **New** and start open. If none are new, or every entry is new, only the newest entry starts open. A dot on your account button means there’s an entry you haven’t seen yet. Opening the Changelog clears it. To share an entry, open it and choose **Copy link**. Anyone signed in to your Data Hub who opens the link sees the Changelog with that entry open. Someone who isn’t signed in has to sign in first and then open the link again. An AI assistant connected to Data Hub [gives the same links](/docs/mcp#questions-about-data-hub) when it tells you what changed.

pages.title: Install and update the watcher
pages.description: Install, reinstall, verify, and manually update the Data Hub watcher on an instrument PC across operating systems.
pages.markdown:
# Install and update the watcher (/docs/install-the-watcher)



**For:** Lab operators

Install the watcher on an instrument PC, check that it works, and update it by hand. These docs describe watcher 1.4.0 and later. Admins control automatic updates for every PC at once; see [Roll out watcher releases](/docs/watcher-releases).

## Prerequisites [#prerequisites]

* **[uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/)**: recommended. It installs Python for you, so you don’t need to install Python separately.
* **A personal access token** starting with `dhub_`. Admins create these at **Settings → Access Tokens**; members can’t create their own. See [Issue and revoke tokens](/docs/manage-tokens).
* **The watch folder and file patterns**: the folder the instrument saves to, and which files in it to upload.

## Install [#install]

Most lab instrument PCs run Windows, so install the `windows-service` extra by default. It adds `pywin32`, which the watcher needs for the [Run as a Windows service](/docs/windows-service) setup:

```sh
uv tool install "data-hub-watcher[windows-service]"
```

This installs the `data-hub-watcher` command in its own Python environment, managed by `uv`, so you can run it from any terminal.

On macOS or Linux, or on a PC where you’ll only run the watcher in a terminal window, leave out the extra:

```sh
uv tool install data-hub-watcher
```

## Configure [#configure]

```sh
data-hub-watcher init
```

The wizard asks for the environment, API key, instrument, watch folder, file patterns, run detection, stability period, and upload mode. New instruments start as `pending` until an admin confirms them; see [Set up an instrument](/docs/set-up-an-instrument).

The wizard saves the config to `~/.data-hub/config.yaml` and sends it to Data Hub. [Configure run detection and uploads](/docs/configure-run-detection) explains how to choose those settings, and [Watcher configuration](/docs/configuration-reference) lists every field.

## Verify [#verify]

```sh
data-hub-watcher watch --dry-run
```

The dry run checks the config, checks that Data Hub is reachable and the instrument is active, and lists the files it would upload, without starting to watch.

## Run [#run]

On a lab PC, run the watcher as a Windows service, so it starts when the PC starts, keeps running after you sign out, and updates itself. From an **Administrator** terminal:

```sh
data-hub-watcher service install
data-hub-watcher service start
```

[Run as a Windows service](/docs/windows-service) covers the commands to stop and restart it, where it writes logs, and what happens if it crashes.

For a one-off check, or on macOS or Linux, run the watcher in a terminal instead:

```sh
data-hub-watcher watch
```

The watcher watches the folder, waits for each file to stop changing, groups files into runs, uploads them in auto mode, and checks in with Data Hub every 60 seconds. Stop it with `Ctrl+C` in the terminal, or stop the service with `data-hub-watcher service stop`.

## Reinstall [#reinstall]

Reinstall the watcher if its install breaks, or if it’s missing the Windows service extra:

```sh
uv tool install --reinstall data-hub-watcher
# or with the Windows service extra:
uv tool install --reinstall "data-hub-watcher[windows-service]"
```

If the watcher runs as a Windows service, then run `data-hub-watcher service reinstall` from an Administrator terminal, so the service and the upgrade Scheduled Task use the new install.

## Change configuration later [#change-configuration-later]

```sh
data-hub-watcher config edit   # re-prompt each field
data-hub-watcher config open   # open the YAML in your editor
data-hub-watcher config show   # print the current config
```

The watcher sends the changes to Data Hub. A running watcher keeps its old settings until it restarts; see [Edits made on the PC](/docs/manage-watchers#edits-on-the-pc).

## Manual update (`self-update`) [#manual-update-self-update]

Use `self-update` to update right away, or on a PC that doesn’t run the watcher as a service. [Roll out watcher releases](/docs/watcher-releases) describes automatic updates.

```sh
data-hub-watcher self-update            # check + upgrade if needed
data-hub-watcher self-update --check    # report status only
data-hub-watcher self-update --force    # re-run even if versions match
```

The command asks Data Hub for the latest version and upgrades the way the watcher was installed:

| Install method                                         | Upgrade flow                                                                                                                                                                                |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Windows, with `uv tool install`                        | Hands the upgrade to the `DataHubWatcherUpgrade` Scheduled Task and returns once the task accepts it. The service restarts by itself. Follow `~/.data-hub/upgrade-worker.log` for progress. |
| macOS or Linux, with `uv tool install`                 | Runs `uv tool install --reinstall` for the latest version. **Restart the watcher** afterward.                                                                                               |
| `pip install` into a Python environment                | Runs `pip install -U` for the latest version. **Restart the watcher** afterward.                                                                                                            |
| A development checkout (editable install or `uv sync`) | Refused. Upgrade with `git pull && uv sync`.                                                                                                                                                |

<Callout type="warn">
  On Windows, when the watcher was installed with `uv tool install`, `data-hub-watcher service install` (or `service reinstall`) must have run once from an Administrator terminal, so the upgrade Scheduled Task exists.
</Callout>

### Pin a specific version [#pin-a-specific-version]

```sh
uv tool install "data-hub-watcher[windows-service]==1.4.5"
```

On macOS or Linux, leave out `[windows-service]`. Some features need a minimum watcher version, such as changing settings from the web app (1.4.0) or marking files **Upload failed** (1.4.5). Check [What each version adds](/docs/watcher-releases#what-each-version-adds) before you pin an older version.

Run `data-hub-watcher self-update --check` to see which version Data Hub offers. A pinned watcher still updates itself, at its next hourly check, once Data Hub offers a newer version than the pin. Admins choose that version for every PC, and roll it back, in [Roll out watcher releases](/docs/watcher-releases).

pages.title: Run as a Windows service
pages.description: Install and operate the Data Hub watcher as a Windows service so it starts on boot, survives logouts, and can auto-update in the background.
pages.markdown:
# Run as a Windows service (/docs/windows-service)



**For:** Lab operators

On a lab instrument PC, run the watcher as a Windows service. The service starts when the PC starts, keeps running after you sign out, restarts if it crashes, and installs [automatic updates](/docs/watcher-releases). Running `data-hub-watcher watch` in a terminal is for quick checks and for macOS or Linux.

## Install the service extra [#install-the-service-extra]

The service needs `pywin32`, which comes with the `windows-service` extra. The [default install](/docs/install-the-watcher#install) already includes it. If you installed without it, add it now:

```sh
uv tool install "data-hub-watcher[windows-service]"
```

Run [`data-hub-watcher init`](/docs/install-the-watcher#configure) first if you haven’t configured the watcher yet. The service uses the same `~/.data-hub/config.yaml` and per-environment `.env` file.

## Install and start [#install-and-start]

From an **Administrator** terminal:

```sh
data-hub-watcher service install
data-hub-watcher service start
```

`service install` sets the service to start shortly after Windows boots, once the network is up. It also tells Windows to restart the service if it crashes, and adds the `DataHubWatcherUpgrade` Scheduled Task that automatic updates use.

<Callout type="warn">
  Automatic updates on Windows need `service install` (or `service reinstall`) to have run at least once from an Administrator terminal. A PC whose service was installed before automatic updates existed needs one `service reinstall` to add the task.
</Callout>

## Lifecycle commands [#lifecycle-commands]

| Command                              | What it does                                  |
| ------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------- |
| `data-hub-watcher service install`   | Register the service                          |
| `data-hub-watcher service start`     | Start the service                             |
| `data-hub-watcher service stop`      | Stop the service                              |
| `data-hub-watcher service status`    | Show whether the service is running           |
| `data-hub-watcher service uninstall` | Remove the service                            |
| `data-hub-watcher service reinstall` | Stop, uninstall, install, and start in one go |

Run `service reinstall` after you update the watcher by hand, for example with `uv tool install -U` from an Administrator terminal. It carries on when the stop or the uninstall fails, so it works even if the service is already gone.

### How long a stop takes [#how-long-a-stop-takes]

Once the watcher is running, `service stop` finishes within about 25 seconds, even when Data Hub doesn’t answer. After the stop begins, the watcher starts no new file or upload part, and gives a part already on its way up to 15 seconds to arrive. In the last 10 seconds, it sends its `watcher_stopped` event and a final heartbeat, so it shows as **Stopped** when Data Hub answers.

A stop takes longer in two cases:

* **While the watcher is starting**: it sends its config and first heartbeat before it looks for a stop, and waits for Data Hub to answer each one, or for each to time out after 35 seconds. A stop during the first scan of a large folder ends at the next file, and the watcher scans the rest at its next start
* **While the watcher applies a settings change from Data Hub**: it waits up to 2 minutes for its uploads to finish

Watchers before 1.4.2 can take longer to stop when Data Hub doesn’t answer, and watchers before 1.4.3 scan the whole watch folder before they stop, which takes minutes on a large folder.

A file cut off by a stop isn’t lost. In auto mode, the watcher uploads it again the next time it starts. A `service stop` cancels requests made with **Upload**, so request those files again. A PC restart or an automatic update keeps them requested; see [When the PC restarts or shuts down](#when-the-pc-restarts-or-shuts-down).

To make the service load a different `.env` file from the default for its environment, such as `~/.data-hub/.env.production`, pass `--env-path` to `service install` or `service reinstall`.

## When the PC restarts or shuts down [#when-the-pc-restarts-or-shuts-down]

Restarting or shutting down the PC stops the service cleanly. The watcher sends a final heartbeat, so it shows as **Stopped** on its page and the instrument reads **Restarting**. The service starts again when the PC boots.

To tell a restart from a `service stop`, look for one of these:

* On the watcher’s **Activity** tab: “Service stopped because Windows is restarting or shutting down”
* In the raw `watcher_stopped` event: “Service stopped: Windows is shutting down”
* In `watcher.log` and the Windows Application log: `Data Hub Watcher stopping: Windows is shutting down`

An automatic update stops the service the same way. The watcher tells Data Hub the stop is for an update, so it shows as **Stopped** and the instrument reads **Restarting** while the new version installs.

### Requested uploads across a restart [#requested-uploads-across-a-restart]

Files someone requested with **Upload** stay requested across a restart or an automatic update, and the watcher uploads them once the service is running again. Hover over the watcher’s **Stopped** badge to see how long Data Hub will wait. If the watcher hasn’t checked in 15 minutes after its last heartbeat, Data Hub cancels the requests, the watcher shows **Unresponsive**, and the instrument reads **Offline**.

Thirty minutes after the instrument reads **Offline**, its subscribers are notified; see [When an instrument goes offline](/docs/configure-notifications#instrument-offline). A PC that is shut down every night therefore sends an alert each night.

Two stops cancel the requests at once: `service stop`, which leaves the instrument **Offline** with the notice “Uploads from this instrument are paused”, and an update you start by hand with `data-hub-watcher self-update`. [Request uploads](/docs/manage-watchers#request-uploads) lists every case that cancels a request.

### When the stop is cut short [#when-the-stop-is-cut-short]

At a restart, Windows gives a service 10 seconds to stop on Windows 10 version 1703 and later, and longer on older builds. The watcher keeps its own stop to about 8 seconds, which is enough for the final heartbeat when Data Hub answers. A file still uploading is cut off, and the watcher uploads it again after the restart; see [An upload was cut off by a restart or an update](/docs/troubleshoot-a-watcher#an-upload-was-cut-off-by-a-restart-or-an-update).

If Data Hub can’t be reached, or the stop is cut short for another reason, the final heartbeat doesn’t arrive. If the PC then stays down for more than 5 minutes, the watcher shows as **Unresponsive** until the service starts again. The `watcher_stopped` event that didn’t get sent is recorded when the service starts again, with the time of the stop (watcher 1.4.3 and later).

Windows 10 and 11 turn on Fast Startup by default. With it, **Shut down** in the Start menu doesn’t stop the service: Windows saves its state and the service carries on from it at the next start, so no final heartbeat is sent and no `watcher_stopped` event is recorded. **Restart** always stops the service, and so does a shutdown with Fast Startup turned off.

Watchers before 1.4.1 don’t hear about a Windows restart, so a restart ends them with no final heartbeat and no `watcher_stopped` event. Updating the watcher is enough to fix that, with no `service reinstall`. Watchers before 1.4.2 don’t tell Data Hub that a stop is for an automatic update, so Data Hub cancels requested uploads when they update.

## When the watcher is deregistered [#when-the-watcher-is-deregistered]

The service stops about three minutes after someone deregisters its watcher or retires its instrument, and stays stopped. It exits cleanly, so Windows doesn’t restart it as it would after a crash. Watchers before 1.4.3 keep running instead and get errors from Data Hub until someone stops them.

The error is in `watcher.log` and in the Application event log: `This watcher was deregistered on Data Hub, so its registration no longer exists. Run 'data-hub-watcher init' to register it again.` The service sends no `watcher_stopped` event and no final heartbeat, because Data Hub would refuse both.

Starting the service again, including at boot, checks the registration first. If the watcher is still deregistered, the start logs the same error and the service stops with an error. Windows then retries twice, after about one minute and again after about two, and leaves the service stopped. A service that already failed in the last 24 hours gets fewer retries.

To use the PC again, run `data-hub-watcher init` on the PC. If the instrument was retired, an admin has to reactivate it first, because `init` is refused for a retired instrument (see [Retire an instrument](/docs/retire-an-instrument#reactivate)). Then run `data-hub-watcher service start` from an Administrator terminal. See [Troubleshoot a watcher](/docs/troubleshoot-a-watcher#the-watcher-was-deregistered).

## Don’t run `watch` while the service runs [#do-not-run-watch-alongside-the-service]

Running `data-hub-watcher watch` in a terminal while the service is running isn’t supported, because both would write to the same log file and upload from the same watch folder. To debug in a terminal, stop the service first:

```powershell
data-hub-watcher service stop
data-hub-watcher --verbose watch
data-hub-watcher service start
```

## Where the service writes logs [#where-the-service-writes-logs]

The service and the CLI share one rotating log:

* `C:\ProgramData\DataHubWatcher\watcher.log`

A separate `service-bootstrap.log` in the same folder records crashes that happen before the service has fully started, such as a missing `pywin32`, a moved Python environment, or a broken install. To turn on debug logging without a reinstall, add `DATA_HUB_WATCHER_LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG` to the env file the service loads and restart the service (watcher 1.4.2 and later).

pages.title: Configure run detection and uploads
pages.description: Choose how the watcher groups files into runs, when files are ready to upload, and whether uploads are automatic or approved.
pages.markdown:
# Configure run detection and uploads (/docs/configure-run-detection)



**For:** Lab operators

Three settings decide which files become a run and when they leave the instrument PC: run detection, the stability period, and the upload mode. This page explains how to choose them. [Watcher configuration](/docs/configuration-reference) lists every field and its allowed values.

Admins can change these on the **Settings** tab of the instrument’s watcher page; see [Change a watcher’s settings](/docs/manage-watchers#change-a-watchers-config). On the PC, set them during `data-hub-watcher init`, with `data-hub-watcher config edit`, or by editing `~/.data-hub/config.yaml` and restarting the watcher.

## Group files into runs [#group-files-into-runs]

A **run** is the files from one acquisition, which the watcher reports together. **Run detection** gives each file a run ID, worked out from the file’s path inside the watch folder. The two common choices are these:

* **Prefix from the file name**: a pattern (a regular expression) picks out part of the name, for example everything before the first underscore, so `RUN001_data.csv` → `RUN001`
* **One folder per run**: each folder inside the watch folder is its own run, so `RUN001/data.csv` → `RUN001`

[Run detection](/docs/configuration-reference#run-detection) lists every preset and how to write your own pattern. Set `recursive: true` when files are in subfolders; otherwise the watcher watches only the top level of the watch folder.

When a run gathers files from several folders, two files can share a name, such as a `run.json` in each capture folder. The watcher keeps every copy and adds a short tag to the later names, such as `sample~3f9a1c2b.tif`.

If files appear on disk but never become runs, check for `pattern_mismatch` events on the watcher’s **Activity** tab and run `data-hub-watcher watch --dry-run`.

## Wait until writes finish [#wait-until-writes-finish]

The **stability period** is how many seconds a file must keep the same size and modification time before the watcher treats it as fully written. The default is 5 seconds, and it can be 1 to 300. Raise it for instruments that write large files slowly.

The watcher gives up on a file that keeps changing for longer than `max_stability_wait_seconds`, 300 seconds by default, and records a `stability_timeout` error event. Raise that limit for instruments whose writes take longer. It must be at least the stability period.

A file that the instrument keeps open after its last write can look finished while the watcher still can’t read it. The watcher tries the file again every minute until it can read it, then uploads it, and a request made with **Upload** stays requested in the meantime. The watcher’s **Activity** tab shows a **File not ready** event for each such file, and another each time the watcher starts or its settings change.

Watchers before 1.4.2 try such a file again only at their next start, and cancel a request for it after three tries.

## Choose auto or manual upload [#choose-auto-or-manual-upload]

| Mode       | Behavior                                                                                                                                                                        |
| ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **auto**   | Upload each file as soon as it’s found and stable. The watcher also uploads files someone requests with **Upload** on the run page, and retries uploads that a restart cut off. |
| **manual** | Report the run, but upload a file only after someone requests it. The watcher checks for requests once a minute.                                                                |

Use manual mode when someone must approve which files leave the instrument PC. Anyone signed in can approve files from the run page. An instrument in manual mode shows a note beside its file patterns saying files upload when someone requests them; see [Approve or dismiss files](/docs/manage-watchers#approving-manual-uploads).

## Existing files on first setup [#existing-files-on-first-setup]

`initial_scan` decides what happens to files already in the watch folder the first time the watcher connects to an environment:

* **`production`**: uploads them (`full`) by default
* **`staging` and `preview`**: record them and skip them (`new-only`) by default

Set `initial_scan` in the config when you need the other behavior; see [Initial scan](/docs/configuration-reference#initial-scan).

pages.title: Manage the watcher fleet
pages.description: Open an instrument’s watcher page, monitor watcher health, list every watcher, change a watcher’s settings, deregister watchers, and approve or request uploads.
pages.markdown: # Manage the watcher fleet (/docs/manage-watchers) **For:** Administrators Each instrument’s watcher has its own page, under the instrument, with the watcher’s activity, health, and settings. **Settings → Watchers** lists every watcher in one table, below the form for choosing which version watchers update to. Publishing a new version is covered in [Roll out watcher releases](/docs/watcher-releases). Members can open a watcher’s page too, but only to read it. Only admins see the settings form, **Restore**, **Deregister**, and **Settings → Watchers**. [Check that new files will arrive](/docs/browse-runs#check-files-will-arrive) describes what everyone else sees: the instrument’s status badge and its notices. ## Open a watcher’s page [#the-watcher-page] The watcher is part of its instrument, so its page is at `/instruments/your_instrument_id/watcher`. To open it: * Select the status badge beside the instrument’s name * Choose **Watcher** from the three-dot menu on the instrument page, or from a row’s menu on **Instruments** * Select **See details** in a notice on an instrument page or a run page * Select an instrument in the list under **Settings → Watchers** The heading reads **Watcher for** and the instrument’s name, with the watcher’s [status badge](/docs/concepts#watcher-status) beside it. Under it, a summary shows: * **Computer**: the name of the instrument PC * **Operating system** * **Version**: followed by **Up to date** when it matches the **Latest version** under **Settings → Watchers**, or **Update available** and the latest version when it’s lower * **Last heartbeat**: how long ago, with the exact time when you hover over it * **Upload mode**: **Automatic** or **Manual** One PC can run watchers for several instruments. When another active watcher reports the same computer name (ignoring capital letters, as Windows does), the summary names the other instruments and warns that restarting the computer takes them offline too. Deregistered watchers don’t count. Below the summary, links switch between **Activity**, **Health**, and **Settings**. They are separate addresses, so you can share a link to one: `/watcher` is **Activity**, `/watcher/health` is **Health**, and `/watcher/settings` is **Settings**. ### Past watchers [#past-watchers] An instrument has at most one active watcher, but it keeps every watcher it has had. When it has had more than one, a button at the top of the summary, **Viewing** and a computer name, opens a list of them, newest first. Each entry shows the computer, **Current** or its dates, and who deregistered it. A past watcher opens read-only. Its badge reads **Deregistered**, a notice explains that it is a past watcher and links back to the current one, and every tab shows that watcher’s own events, heartbeats, and settings history. The address ends in `?watcher=` and the watcher’s ID. A watcher ID from another instrument returns a not-found page. When an instrument has no current watcher, because its watcher was deregistered or the instrument was retired, `/watcher` opens on its most recent past watcher with that notice. Admins also see **Connect a new watcher**, which opens [Set up an instrument](/docs/set-up-an-instrument). An instrument that never had a watcher shows “No watcher has connected yet.” ### Old watcher links [#old-links] Watcher pages used to have their own addresses, and links to them still work: * `/watchers/your_watcher_id` opens the instrument’s watcher page, on the matching tab: `?tab=logs` opens **Activity**, `?tab=status` opens **Health**, and `?tab=configuration` opens **Settings**. A deregistered watcher opens as a past watcher * `/watchers` opens **Settings → Watchers** for admins, on its **Deregistered** tab if the link asked for it, and **Instruments** for members ## Monitor watcher health [#monitor-watcher-health] Each watcher sends a [heartbeat](/docs/concepts#heartbeat) to Data Hub every 60 seconds, reporting its version, instrument, watch folder, upload mode, upload counts, and how long it has been running. ### Status [#watcher-status-badge] The badge beside the page heading, and in the **Status** column of **Settings → Watchers**, shows the watcher’s state: **Online**, **Waiting: folder not found**, **Unresponsive**, **Stopped**, **Registered**, or **Deregistered**. [Watcher status](/docs/concepts#watcher-status) explains when each one shows. Hover over the badge for details, such as which folder a watcher in **Waiting: folder not found** is looking for. The instrument’s own badge (**Online**, **Restarting**, **Connecting**, or **Offline**) is a simpler summary of the same state, for the people who use the instrument; see [Instrument status](/docs/concepts#instrument-status). ### Activity [#activity] **Activity** is the watcher’s event log. The heading shows how many events fall in the date range, which starts at **Last 7 days**. Use the **Event type** filter and the date range picker to narrow it. The page shows the first 20 events, and **Show more** loads more. Each event is a row with a label, a plain message, and when it happened. Run IDs in a message link to the run. Select a row to expand it and see details such as the file’s size, the run, the number of upload parts, and the exact time. Admins also see the raw event as the watcher sent it, which is the most detailed record of what happened on the PC. Members see only the plain version. The labels are **Started**, **Stopped**, **File uploaded**, **Upload failed**, **Run reported**, **Settings synced**, **Error**, **Update started**, **Update finished**, **Update failed**, **Uploads cancelled**, and **Couldn’t upload**. An event of any other type gets a label made from its name. Some events get a more specific label: * **Missed heartbeat**: an error saying the watcher checked in again after missing some heartbeats * **File not ready**: a file the watcher can’t read yet and will try again. Choosing **Upload failed** in the **Event type** filter leaves these out, because those files haven’t failed The raw event keeps the type names the docs and the API use, such as `watcher_started`, `run_reported`, `file_uploaded`, `update_*`, and `error` with a `details.kind` field that says which error it was. Data Hub records two events itself: * `upload_requests_cancelled`, shown as **Uploads cancelled**, when someone deletes a run that has requested uploads * `uploads_failed`, shown as **Couldn’t upload**, when the watcher reports files it gave up on: one event per run and reason, such as “Couldn’t upload 129 files in run X: folder no longer on the instrument PC”. The files read **Upload failed**; see [When an upload fails](/docs/browse-runs#upload-failed). Watchers before 1.4.5 log a “Queued file missing” and a “Gave up uploading” error for each file instead A `file_uploaded` event reports `size_bytes`, `part_count`, `prep_seconds` (time spent hashing the file and requesting its upload link), and `upload_seconds` (time spent sending the file to storage). Divide `size_bytes` by `upload_seconds` to get the upload speed. For problems on the PC, see [Troubleshoot a watcher](/docs/troubleshoot-a-watcher). ### Health [#health] **Health** shows the last 7 days unless you pick another range, up to 31 days. It loads its heartbeat history only when you open it. It has three parts: * Four counts: **Files uploaded**, **Upload failures**, **Restarts** (with the reason, for example “All for automatic updates”), and **Missed heartbeats** (with how long each took to recover). A missed heartbeat is an error event that says the watcher checked in again after missing some * A bar chart of files uploaded per day * **Connectivity**: a grid with one row per day and one block per 30 minutes, in your time zone, which the caption names. Hover over a block to see what happened and when The connectivity grid uses these colors: * **Green**: checked in * **Gray**: restarted for an update * **Amber**: missed a heartbeat and recovered * **Red**: unresponsive. A block that holds a heartbeat but is followed by a long silence with nothing to explain it, such as an outage that’s still going on, is red too * **Light gray**: no data yet, or a half hour that didn’t happen because the clocks changed A watcher that shows amber blocks every few hours, or red blocks in the middle of the night, points at the PC or its network rather than at Data Hub. ## See every watcher at once [#all-watchers] **Settings → Watchers**, which only admins see, has the release form from [Roll out watcher releases](/docs/watcher-releases) at the top and the list of **All watchers** below it, one row per instrument’s watcher. The list’s heading shows how far a release has spread, for example “14 out of 16 on the latest version”. It’s green when every watcher runs the latest version or a newer one, and amber otherwise. The **Active** tab has one row for each watcher: * **Instrument**: opens the watcher’s page * **Computer**: sortable, with a stacked-layers icon when other active watchers share it. Hover over the icon, or focus it with the keyboard, to see how many watchers run on that computer and which instruments * **Version** * **Status**: the watcher’s [status badge](#watcher-status-badge) * **Settings**: **Change pending**, **Change rejected**, **Edited on PC, restart pending**, or a dash when there is nothing to report; see [Change a watcher’s settings](#change-a-watchers-config) * **Last heartbeat** * A three-dot menu with **Deregister** The **Deregistered** tab lists past watchers, with the **Instrument**, **Computer**, **Last version**, the date it was **Deregistered on**, and who it was **Deregistered by**. ## Change a watcher’s settings [#change-a-watchers-config] Admins can change a watcher’s settings from the web app, without going to the instrument PC. Open the watcher’s page and choose the **Settings** tab. It shows: * **Current settings**: what the watcher is running now, as it last reported. Admins get an **Edit** button here, which opens the form in a dialog with **Save change** and **Preview with recent files**. Saving closes the dialog. * **History**: every change, with who made it and when * **Raw config file (YAML)**, folded away at the bottom You can change: * **Watch folder**: any folder on the instrument PC * **File patterns** * **How files become runs**: a preset or your own pattern, and whether to include subfolders * **Upload mode**, **Parallel uploads**, **Stability period**, and **Max stability wait** The form checks each value as you type. **Preview with recent files** shows which of the instrument’s recent files the new patterns match and the run ID each would get. It only covers files Data Hub already knows about, so files on the PC that never matched a pattern don’t appear. After you save: 1. A **Change pending** notice appears at the top of the tab. 2. Within about a minute, the watcher learns from its next heartbeat that a change is waiting, and fetches it. 3. The watcher checks the change, including that the new folder exists and can be read. If a check fails, it keeps its current settings and a **Change rejected** notice gives the reason, both on the **Settings** tab and as an `error` event. 4. Otherwise it saves the new settings to `config.yaml`, waits up to two minutes for the uploads it’s sending, and starts watching again with the new settings. The change shows as **Applied**, and **Current settings** updates. A file that hadn’t finished uploading, such as a large file partway through, uploads again from the start after the change, unless the change moved the watch folder or switched to manual uploads. If the new settings match more files, the watcher reports files that are already on the PC as detected, but doesn’t upload them. To upload them, use **Upload** on the run page; see [Request uploads](#request-uploads). New files after the change follow the upload mode. If the watcher is offline, the change waits and is applied when the watcher next starts. If someone also edited `config.yaml` on the PC while it was offline, the newer of the two edits wins and the other stays in the history. The same form also opens from the notice on an instrument page that says Data Hub can’t find the watch folder: **Change folder** opens **Settings** with the form already open and the **Watch folder** field selected. See [Check that new files will arrive](/docs/browse-runs#check-files-will-arrive). ### Edits made on the PC [#edits-on-the-pc] An edit made on the PC while the watcher is running, such as with `data-hub-watcher config edit`, is saved to `config.yaml` and recorded in the history at once, as **Applied**. The watcher reads `config.yaml` only when it starts, though, so it keeps running its previous settings until it restarts. Until then the **Settings** tab shows **Edited on PC — restart pending**, and **Settings → Watchers** shows **Edited on PC, restart pending**. **Current settings** shows what the watcher is running, from the settings revision it reports in its heartbeat. ### History and restore [#config-history] The **History** card records every change, whether it came from Data Hub or from the config file on the PC (such as `data-hub-watcher config edit`). Each entry has its revision number, its state, who made it, or **From the instrument PC**, when, and a one-line summary of what changed. To go back to an earlier version, choose **Restore** on it. That saves its settings as a new change, and never edits the history. When two admins edit the same watcher at once, the second save is refused with a message to reload, so neither overwrites the other unseen. Members see the same cards, with the current settings, any notice, and the history, but no form and no **Restore**. A line with a lock icon says “Only admins can change watcher settings.” ### Change settings with the API or an AI assistant [#change-settings-with-the-api-or-an-ai-assistant] * **API**: `POST /api/v1/watchers/:watcherId/config-revisions` with `base_revision` and the full `settings`. Signed-in callers must be admins; tokens must list `watchers:admin` explicitly (legacy `*` and `watchers:write` tokens are refused). `GET /api/v1/watchers/:watcherId/config-revisions` lists the history. See the [generated API docs](/docs/api). * **MCP**: the `update_watcher_config` tool, for admins. It changes only the settings you name. The assistant shows you the change and asks you to confirm before it saves. ## Deregister a watcher [#deregister-a-watcher] Each instrument can have at most one active watcher. Deregister the old one when a PC is reimaged or replaced, or to clear “instrument already has an active watcher” on a new install. * **Web app**: open the watcher’s page, choose **Deregister** from its three-dot menu, or choose **Deregister** from the watcher’s row menu in **Settings → Watchers**. The dialog asks you to stop the watcher service on the PC first * **API**: `DELETE /api/v1/watchers/:watcherId` (requires `watchers:admin`) Deregistration is a soft delete: heartbeats, events, and runs stay with the instrument, under its past watchers and on the **Deregistered** tab of **Settings → Watchers**. The instrument’s badge reads **Offline** until a new watcher registers, and its page says when the watcher was deregistered and by whom. A watcher removed through the API with a token shows that token’s name as the one that removed it. A running watcher that’s deregistered stops by itself within about three minutes, and doesn’t start again: Windows doesn’t restart the service, and starting it is refused. To use the PC again, run `data-hub-watcher init` on it. Watchers before 1.4.3 keep running and getting errors until someone stops them on the PC. See [Troubleshoot a watcher](/docs/troubleshoot-a-watcher#the-watcher-was-deregistered). Retiring an instrument also deregisters its watcher automatically; see [Retire an instrument](/docs/retire-an-instrument). `init` is refused for a retired instrument, so reactivate it before anyone runs `data-hub-watcher init` on the PC again (see [Reactivate](/docs/retire-an-instrument#reactivate)). You don’t need to deregister a watcher only because its token was revoked. Re-running `data-hub-watcher init` with a new token takes over the existing registration; see [After revoking a token](/docs/manage-tokens#after-revoking-a-token). ## Request uploads [#request-uploads] **Upload** on a run page, or on selected runs in a run list, asks the watcher to send files that are still on the instrument PC. The watcher polls the server’s upload queue once a minute and uploads the files that were requested. * In **manual** upload mode, every file waits in this queue until someone requests it. * In **auto** upload mode, files upload on their own, and the queue holds files someone asks for again, such as ones whose upload failed. The **Upload** buttons on a run page follow the instrument’s badge. They work while it reads **Online** or **Restarting**, and are turned off for **Connecting**, **Offline**, **Pending**, and **Retired**, with the reason beside the button. Data Hub also refuses a request for such an instrument. See [Request an upload](/docs/browse-runs#request-upload). ### When Data Hub cancels a request [#when-requests-are-cancelled] Data Hub cancels pending upload requests, and the files go back to **Not uploaded**, in these cases: * **The watcher stops cleanly**, for example with `data-hub-watcher service stop` or a `self-update` you start by hand. It shows **Stopped**, and nothing is left to upload the files * **The watcher doesn’t come back after a PC restart, a shutdown, or an automatic update.** These stops are expected to be short, so the requests wait and the instrument reads **Restarting**. If no heartbeat arrives for about 15 minutes, Data Hub cancels them, the watcher shows **Unresponsive**, and the instrument reads **Offline**. See [When the PC restarts or shuts down](/docs/windows-service#when-the-pc-restarts-or-shuts-down) * **Someone deletes the run.** Data Hub records an `upload_requests_cancelled` event on the watcher with the run and the number of files; filter **Activity** by **Uploads cancelled** to find it. Restoring the run doesn’t bring the requests back, so request the uploads again. Other runs on the instrument keep their requests * **Someone deregisters the watcher** * **Someone changes the instrument’s watch folder**, from the web app or on the PC, so the watcher doesn’t look for files at paths that no longer apply * **A requested file keeps failing**, because it’s missing on disk or its upload fails. The watcher tries it on at most three checks before Data Hub cancels it, and requesting it again gives it three new tries. Before watcher 1.4.3, a request made right after a cancellation was cancelled at once Each cancellation shows on the watcher’s **Activity** tab under its own event type. Watchers before 1.4.1 don’t report a PC restart, and watchers before 1.4.2 don’t report an automatic update, so those stops cancel requests at once. ## Approve or dismiss files [#approving-manual-uploads] For instruments in [manual upload mode](/docs/concepts#upload-mode), the watcher reports runs but uploads a file only after someone approves it. The instrument’s page shows a note beside its file patterns: “Files upload when someone requests them.” Approve a file with **Upload**, or choose **Dismiss** to tell the watcher not to upload it. To act on several files at once, select them in the files table and use the bar that appears. **Dismiss** also works on a file whose upload failed, on any instrument. A dismissed file stays dismissed, even if the watcher reports it again. Dismissing differs from deleting: the file never reached Data Hub storage, so there’s nothing to restore. ### When a dismissed path gets a new file [#dismissed-path-new-file] The watcher reports each path only once, so a new file that the instrument later writes at a dismissed file’s path doesn’t appear on its own. It appears when the watcher reports that path again: after `data-hub-watcher state forget`, or when the watcher starts without its saved record of what it has reported, for example after a reinstall. Data Hub then treats it as a new file if its size or creation time differs from the dismissed file’s. On Linux, the modification time stands in for the creation time. Because Data Hub compares only size and time, two cases can surprise you: * A new file the same size as the dismissed one counts as the same file when it keeps the old creation time, so it stays dismissed. On Windows and macOS this happens when the instrument overwrites the file in place. On Windows it can also happen when the file is deleted and written again, or saved through a temporary copy, within about 15 seconds. * Copying a folder, for example with Explorer or `xcopy` on Windows or `cp` without `-p` on Linux, gives the copies new times. After you replace an instrument PC or restore its folder from a backup, a new watcher that scans the copied folder reports the files you dismissed as new files. Dismiss them again.

pages.title: Roll out watcher releases
pages.description: Publish watcher versions to PyPI, advertise them per environment, set a minimum version, force mandatory updates, roll the fleet back, and see what each version adds.
pages.markdown: # Roll out watcher releases (/docs/watcher-releases) **For:** Administrators Watchers update themselves to the version you choose for each environment under **Settings → Watchers**, which also lists every watcher with its version. These docs describe watcher 1.4.0 and later. [Install and update the watcher](/docs/install-the-watcher) covers installing the watcher on one PC and updating it by hand with `self-update`. ## How watchers update themselves [#how-fleet-upgrades-reach-a-pc] Every watcher checks for an update about once an hour, whether it runs as a Windows service or in a terminal. Each time, it does this: 1. Asks Data Hub for **Latest version** and compares it with its own version 2. Upgrades only if **Latest version** is newer and the watcher is idle: no uploads in the last 5 heartbeats, and no run reported within five times its stability period. **Mandatory update** skips the idle check 3. Installs the new version and restarts. A Windows service restarts through the Windows setting that restarts it after a crash 4. Records `update_started`, then `update_succeeded` or `update_failed`, which the watcher’s **Activity** tab shows as **Update started**, **Update finished**, or **Update failed** Automatic updates are off in the `preview` environment, so a pull request’s preview deployment can’t install code on lab PCs. ## Cut a new release [#cut-a-new-release] **For:** Engineers An engineer publishes a release by tagging a commit on `production`, and an admin then makes it the version watchers update to. Bump the version in `watcher/pyproject.toml` and merge through `staging` to `production`. Tag and push from `production`: ```sh git checkout production && git pull git tag watcher-v1.4.6 && git push origin watcher-v1.4.6 ``` Approve the `pypi` deployment under **Actions → Publish watcher** in GitHub. In **Settings → Watchers**, pick the new version under **Latest version**. The list comes from PyPI, so a release shows up as soon as PyPI publishes it. If PyPI can’t be reached, you can type the version instead. Each environment has its own setting, so set `staging` first and `production` once it looks good. Save **Latest version** only after the new version is on PyPI. If you save it earlier, every watcher tries to update, fails, and records `update_failed`. ## Release settings [#release-config-fields] | Field | Purpose | | ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | **Latest version** | The version watchers update to. Leave it blank to pause automatic updates. | | **Minimum supported version** | Optional. A watcher older than this has its heartbeats rejected with `426 Upgrade Required`, so it shows as unresponsive until it updates. It still checks for updates every hour, so it upgrades itself as long as **Latest version** is newer. Leave it blank for no minimum. | | **Mandatory update** | Moves every watcher to **Latest version** at its next hourly check, without waiting until it’s idle, and also moves newer watchers back. See [Mandatory updates](#mandatory-updates). Has no effect while **Latest version** is blank. | ## Watch the rollout [#watch-the-rollout] Below the release form, the **All watchers** heading shows “*N* out of *M* on the latest version”. It’s green when every active watcher runs that version or a newer one, and amber while some are behind. The **Version** column shows each watcher’s version, and a watcher’s own page says **Up to date**, or **Update available** with the latest version. See [Manage the watcher fleet](/docs/manage-watchers#all-watchers). ## Mandatory updates [#mandatory-updates] Turning on **Mandatory update** makes every watcher move to **Latest version** at its next hourly check, even if it’s busy uploading. Without it, a watcher only upgrades to a newer version, and only once it’s idle. A forced update in the middle of an acquisition can lose data, so keep **Mandatory update** for these cases: * A security fix * A change that stops older watchers from working with Data Hub * A rollback, or a bad version that does more harm running than a restart mid-upload would ## Roll back [#roll-back] Watchers never move to an older version on their own, so a rollback needs **Mandatory update**: If **Minimum supported version** is above the version you’re rolling back to, lower it first. Otherwise the rolled-back watchers can’t check in. Set **Latest version** to the older version for each affected environment, and turn on **Mandatory update**. Wait for the next hourly check, and watch the **Version** column in **All watchers**. The heading count treats a newer version as current, so it can read green before every watcher has moved back. Turn **Mandatory update** off once every watcher runs the older version. The newer version stays on PyPI, but Data Hub no longer offers it. ## What each version adds [#what-each-version-adds] Some Data Hub features need a minimum watcher version. To turn a feature on for every PC, set **Latest version** to at least the version that adds it. ### 1.4.5 [#v1-4-5] * A file the watcher gives up on reads **Upload failed**, with the reason. That covers a requested file that isn’t on the instrument PC, for example because its run folder was renamed or moved, and a file whose upload failed three times * Data Hub records one **Couldn’t upload** event per run and reason, instead of one error per file * In auto mode, a file whose upload fails reads **Upload failed** at once, and the watcher tries it again the next time it starts * Files an auto-mode watcher is about to upload read **Waiting to upload**. Files it reports without uploading, such as the ones already on the PC after a settings change that matches more files, read **Not uploaded** ### 1.4.3 [#v1-4-3] * When the watch folder disappears while the watcher runs, for example because a network drive drops, the watcher goes back to **Waiting: folder not found** and starts watching again once the folder is back. Files waiting to upload aren’t dropped, and a network share that stops answering no longer freezes the watcher * A stop during start-up, including during the scan of a large folder, ends cleanly with a `stopped` status and event, for `data-hub-watcher watch` and for the Windows service * A watcher whose registration was deleted on Data Hub stops after three heartbeats in a row get that answer, about 3 minutes, and says to run `data-hub-watcher init`. `watch` exits with code 3, the Windows service stays stopped, and starting the watcher again is refused with the same message. Any other error doesn’t stop it * Heartbeat counts aren’t lost when a heartbeat fails * Events that haven’t been sent are kept across a restart, a crash, or a Data Hub outage, and sent afterwards. Events that Data Hub refuses, or fails to take three times in a row, are dropped, and an `events_dropped` event says how many * A file of 100 MB or more that changes while it uploads is uploaded as it is then, instead of failing * A file requested again right after its request was cancelled gets three new tries * A watcher that finds a run deleted on Data Hub records one event for it and leaves the run alone until it restarts, or until Data Hub accepts an upload someone requested for one of the run’s files ### 1.4.2 [#v1-4-2] * Once the watcher is running, a stop finishes within about 25 seconds, even when Data Hub isn’t answering. The watcher sends its events before its final heartbeat, and starts no new file or upload part once a stop is requested * A watcher that stops to install an automatic update tells Data Hub why, so files someone requested with **Upload** stay requested while it comes back. The Windows service hands each update to its upgrade task only once * The Windows service writes a config or env file it can’t load to `watcher.log`, and reads `DATA_HUB_WATCHER_LOG_LEVEL` from its env file * A file the instrument keeps open after its last write uploads once the instrument lets go of it. The watcher tries it every minute, and a request for it from the run page stays requested ### 1.4.1 [#v1-4-1] * Restarting or shutting down a Windows PC stops the watcher service cleanly. The watcher sends a final heartbeat, so it shows as **Stopped**, and files someone requested with **Upload** stay requested and upload once the PC is back. Data Hub cancels those requests if the watcher isn’t back within about 15 minutes; see [When the PC restarts or shuts down](/docs/windows-service#when-the-pc-restarts-or-shuts-down) * In auto mode, the files of a run reported just before a restart, a power cut, or a crash upload after the next start. Older watchers can leave them on **Not uploaded**; [they can be uploaded from the run page](/docs/troubleshoot-a-watcher#a-file-stays-pending-after-the-watcher-restarted) * A run whose ID contains `#`, `?`, or another character with a special meaning in a web address gets its own files. Older watchers send them to another run or don’t upload them ### 1.4.0 [#v1-4-0] * Admins can [change the watcher’s settings from Data Hub](/docs/manage-watchers#change-a-watchers-config). The watcher picks up a saved change within about a minute and applies it, or rejects it and keeps its current settings when a check fails, such as a folder that doesn’t exist * After a change that matches more files, the watcher reports the files already on the PC but doesn’t upload them * A watcher whose folder is missing at start-up keeps running and shows **Waiting: folder not found**, so the folder can be fixed from Data Hub ### 1.3.0 and earlier [#before-1-4] These docs no longer describe watchers before 1.4.0. Update them to the latest version. * **1.3.0**: a large file uploads several parts at once, and several requested files upload side by side, within the [`instrument.upload_parallelism`](/docs/configuration-reference#field-reference) setting. The watcher asks again for a part’s upload link after a connection or server error, and the `file_uploaded` event records the file’s size and upload times * **1.2.2**: a run report that fails because Data Hub can’t be reached, or returns a server error, is retried until it goes through * **1.2.1**: **Upload** works on instruments that upload automatically, and an automatic upload cut off by a restart or an update is retried at the next start, on up to three starts * **1.2.0**: files of 100 MB or more upload in 64 MB parts, and files larger than 5 GB can upload * **1.1.0**: when a run gathers files from several folders, every file with the same name is kept, and later copies get a short tag in the name, such as `sample~3f9a1c2b.tif`. Adds the `data-hub-watcher state forget` command Files that a watcher before 1.1.0 skipped because of a duplicate name don’t upload on their own after the update. To upload them, stop the watcher, run `data-hub-watcher state forget --prefix your_folder_name/` on the instrument PC, where `your_folder_name/` is the folder in the watch folder that held the skipped files, and start the watcher again. ## When an update fails on a PC [#operator-side-failures] If `update_started` is followed by `update_failed`, or a watcher never updates, send the PC’s operator to [Troubleshoot a watcher](/docs/troubleshoot-a-watcher#auto-update-never-fires) and [Install and update the watcher](/docs/install-the-watcher#manual-update-self-update).

pages.title: Troubleshoot a watcher
pages.description: Fix watcher problems by symptom: will not start, files not detected, uploads stuck, auto-update quiet, and where to find logs.
pages.markdown: # Troubleshoot a watcher (/docs/troubleshoot-a-watcher) **For:** Lab operators and admins Find your symptom below. If none fits, start with the [logs](#where-are-the-logs). The instrument’s watcher page also shows the watcher’s events, heartbeats, and settings: select the status badge beside the instrument’s name, or choose **Watcher** from its three-dot menu. Anyone signed in can read it. ## An instrument shows Offline [#instrument-shows-offline] An instrument’s badge reads **Offline** when new files can’t reach Data Hub right now. A notice under the instrument’s name says why, and **See details** opens the watcher’s **Activity** tab. Find the notice below. | Notice | What it means | What to do | | ------------------------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | | **New files aren’t being picked up** | The watcher is running but can’t find its watch folder. | Create or reconnect the folder on the PC, or let an admin choose **Change folder**. See [The watcher shows “Waiting: folder not found”](#waiting-folder-not-found). | | **The watcher isn’t checking in** | No heartbeat for 5 minutes, or the watcher didn’t come back within 15 minutes of a restart or an update. The PC may be off, the watcher may have crashed, or the network may be blocking Data Hub. | On the PC, check that the watcher is running (`data-hub-watcher service status` on Windows) and that it can reach Data Hub; see [“Connection error” or “Request timed out”](#connection-error-or-request-timed-out). Its last events are on the **Activity** tab. | | **The watcher never checked in** | The watcher registered but sent no heartbeat within 15 minutes of registering, or of an admin confirming the instrument if that came later. The service may never have started, or the PC can’t reach Data Hub. | Start the watcher on the PC, as in [step 5 of Set up an instrument](/docs/set-up-an-instrument#start-the-watcher-service). If it won’t start, see [The watcher will not start](#the-watcher-will-not-start). If it is running, check that it can reach Data Hub; see [“Connection error” or “Request timed out”](#connection-error-or-request-timed-out). | | **Uploads from this instrument are paused** | Someone stopped the watcher, for example with `data-hub-watcher service stop` or Ctrl+C. | Start it again: `data-hub-watcher service start` on Windows, or `data-hub-watcher watch`. | | **This instrument isn’t connected to a watcher** | The instrument never had a watcher, or its watcher was deregistered, which the notice dates and credits. | Run `data-hub-watcher init` on the PC; see [The watcher stopped and says it was deregistered](#the-watcher-was-deregistered). Admins can follow **Connect a watcher**. | **Restarting** and **Connecting** aren’t problems: each turns **Offline** if it lasts more than 15 minutes. See [The instrument shows Restarting after a restart](#the-instrument-shows-restarting-after-a-restart). Files saved on the PC while an instrument is offline stay there, and the watcher picks them up once it runs again. People who subscribe to the instrument hear about it once the badge has read **Offline** for 30 minutes, in the app and in Slack if they turned that on, with the notice’s reason. They hear again when it’s back **Online**. See [When an instrument goes offline](/docs/configure-notifications#instrument-offline). ## Setup and registration [#setup-and-registration] ### “Instrument is still pending activation” [#instrument-is-still-pending-activation] The instrument was registered but an admin hasn’t confirmed it. Its badge reads **Pending**. Ask an admin to open **Instruments**, choose **Confirm…**, pick an instrument type, and choose **Confirm instrument**. See [Manage instruments](/docs/manage-instruments#confirm-a-pending-instrument). ### “Instrument already has an active watcher” [#instrument-already-has-an-active-watcher] Each instrument can have at most one active watcher, and an earlier install is still registered, for example on another PC or from before the PC was reimaged. The command prints the existing watcher’s ID. Deregister that watcher, then run `init` again: * **Web app**: open the instrument, select its status badge to open its watcher page, and choose **Deregister** from the ⋮ menu. You can also use the row menu in **Settings → Watchers**. Only admins see those menus. Watcher 1.4.3’s message names a menu that no longer exists; watcher 1.4.4 prints the address of the watcher’s page instead * **API**: `DELETE /api/v1/watchers/your_existing_watcher_id` with a token that has `watchers:admin` Deregistration is a soft delete: the history stays with the instrument as a past watcher, and on the **Deregistered** tab of **Settings → Watchers**. ### `init` rejects my API key [#init-rejects-my-api-key] The wizard refuses keys that don’t start with `dhub_`. It also removes invisible characters that the Windows clipboard can add, such as zero-width and non-breaking spaces. If a paste keeps failing, run `data-hub-watcher init --show-key` to see what the prompt received. ## The watcher won’t start [#the-watcher-will-not-start] * Run `data-hub-watcher config show` to check the config and environment * Run `data-hub-watcher watch --dry-run`, which prints the first check that fails * Check that an admin has confirmed the instrument; a **Pending** instrument can’t upload * On Windows, if the service won’t start, see [Windows service problems](#windows-service) ## The watcher stopped and says it was deregistered [#the-watcher-was-deregistered] Someone deleted the watcher’s registration on Data Hub. This happens when an admin deregisters the watcher in the web app, or retires its instrument (see [Deregister a watcher](/docs/manage-watchers#deregister-a-watcher)). After a deregistration, the instrument reads **Offline** and its notice says its watcher was deregistered. A retired instrument reads **Retired**, with no notice. Watcher 1.4.3 and later stop by themselves when this happens. The watcher logs one error: `This watcher was deregistered on Data Hub, so its registration no longer exists. Run 'data-hub-watcher init' to register it again.` You can find that error in `watcher.log` (see [Where are the logs?](#where-are-the-logs)). On Windows, it is also in the Application event log, and `service status` shows the service as stopped. The watcher waits for three heartbeats in a row that Data Hub answers with its “deregistered” reply. At the usual one-minute interval, that is about three minutes, so one wrong answer can’t stop the watcher. A different error, including Data Hub saying it has no watcher with that ID, doesn’t stop it. Once it has stopped, it uploads nothing and doesn’t come back on its own. Starting it again is refused with the same message. `watch` exits with code 3 when it stops this way, and when it refuses to start. To use the PC again: If the instrument was retired, ask an admin to [reactivate it](/docs/retire-an-instrument#reactivate) first. `init` is refused for a retired instrument. Run `data-hub-watcher init` on the PC to register a new watcher for the instrument. The PC keeps its upload history, so files that were already uploaded aren’t uploaded again. If `init` reports that the instrument already has an active watcher, see [Instrument already has an active watcher](#instrument-already-has-an-active-watcher). On Windows, run `data-hub-watcher service start` from an Administrator terminal. Watchers older than 1.4.3 don’t stop. They keep running and get errors from Data Hub until someone stops them. ## The watcher shows “Waiting: folder not found” [#waiting-folder-not-found] The watcher starts even when the watch folder is missing, for example when a network drive isn’t connected yet or the folder was renamed. The watcher keeps sending heartbeats but watches nothing. Its page shows **Waiting: folder not found**, and the instrument reads **Offline** with the notice “New files aren’t being picked up”. Hover over the watcher’s badge to see which folder it’s looking for; the notice names it too. The watcher checks for the folder again once a minute and starts watching as soon as it appears. To fix it: * Create or reconnect the folder on the PC, or * Point the watcher at the right folder from the web app: an admin chooses **Change folder** in the notice, which opens the watcher’s **Settings** tab with the **Watch folder** field selected; see [Change a watcher’s settings](/docs/manage-watchers#change-a-watchers-config) The watcher also goes back to this state when the folder disappears while it runs, for example when a network drive drops or the folder is deleted (watcher 1.4.3 and later). It notices within a minute, looks again a few seconds later so that a drop of a moment doesn’t count, stops watching, and shows **Waiting: folder not found**. It gives a file that was uploading at that moment up to 10 seconds to finish, cuts it off if it isn’t done, and uploads it again once the folder is back. When the folder returns, the watcher starts watching it again without a restart, and queues a `watcher_started` event that says it resumed. ## A config change shows “Change rejected” [#change-rejected] The watcher checked a change made in the web app and refused it, so it kept its previous settings. The reason shows in a **Change rejected** notice on the watcher’s **Settings** tab and as an `error` event with `details.kind` set to `config_revision_rejected`. For example, the folder doesn’t exist on the PC or the watcher can’t read it. Fix the cause, then save the change again or **Restore** an earlier version from the history. ## “Data Hub can’t read the watcher’s config file” [#config-file-unreadable] The watcher’s **Settings** tab shows this when the `config.yaml` the watcher sent breaks the rules the web app checks, for example a relative watch folder, more than 50 file patterns, or a run detection pattern with Python-only syntax such as `(?P…)`. The notice names each field that needs fixing, by its key in the file. Until it’s fixed, edits made on the PC aren’t recorded in the history, and if Data Hub has no earlier copy of the settings, there’s nothing to edit in the web app. Fix the file on the instrument PC, for example with `data-hub-watcher config edit`. ## A config change stays on “Change pending” [#change-pending] The watcher picks up a change after its next heartbeat, within about a minute. If the change stays pending, check that the watcher is **Online** on its page. An offline watcher applies the change when it next starts. ## The instrument shows Restarting after a restart [#the-instrument-shows-restarting-after-a-restart] When the PC restarts, or the watcher stops to install an automatic update, the instrument’s badge reads **Restarting** for up to 15 minutes, not **Offline**. Nothing is wrong. The watcher checks in once a minute, so it can take up to a minute after the service starts to show as **Online**. Refresh the page after a minute. A new watcher reads **Connecting** until its first check-in, and **Offline**, with the notice “The watcher never checked in”, if none arrives within 15 minutes. If the badge turns **Offline** with the notice “The watcher isn’t checking in”, the watcher didn’t come back. Check that the process is running and see [“Connection error” or “Request timed out”](#connection-error-or-request-timed-out). Older watchers don’t say they are restarting, so they read **Offline** from the moment the PC goes down; see [When the PC restarts or shuts down](/docs/windows-service#when-the-pc-restarts-or-shuts-down). ## Heartbeats fail with `426 Upgrade Required` [#heartbeats-fail-with-426-upgrade-required] The watcher is older than the **Minimum supported version** an admin set under **Settings → Watchers**, so Data Hub refuses its heartbeats and it shows as **Unresponsive**. Its instrument reads **Offline**. It keeps checking for updates every hour and upgrades itself if **Latest version** is newer. To upgrade now, run `data-hub-watcher self-update`. See [Roll out watcher releases](/docs/watcher-releases#release-config-fields). ## “Connection error” or “Request timed out” [#connection-error-or-request-timed-out] The watcher can’t reach the Data Hub API. Check these: * The instrument PC is connected to the network * The config has the right environment (`staging`, `production`, or `preview`); run `data-hub-watcher config show` * The PC can reach the API URL for that environment, for example by opening it in a browser on the PC ### A run is missing after a connection problem [#a-run-is-missing-after-a-connection-problem] The watcher retries a run report that failed because it couldn’t reach Data Hub, or because Data Hub returned a server error. The first retry comes after 5 seconds. The wait then doubles up to 5 minutes between tries, and the watcher keeps trying every 5 minutes until the report goes through. It needs no new file and no restart, so the run appears on its own once the problem clears. The watcher records one `run_report_failed` event when a run’s report first fails. It doesn’t record another for the same run while it keeps retrying, even if more files in the run finish in the meantime. A failure that isn’t a connection problem or a server error, such as `401 Unauthorized`, is not retried, because it would fail the same way. Each one is recorded, except the refusals of a run that was deleted on Data Hub, which watcher 1.4.3 and later record once per run (see [A run was deleted on Data Hub](#a-run-was-deleted-on-data-hub)). Fix the cause, then restart the watcher. ## A run was deleted on Data Hub [#a-run-was-deleted-on-data-hub] A run report or an upload request that fails with `409 Conflict` and a message that starts “This run was deleted on Data Hub” means someone deleted the run. Data Hub refuses a watcher’s report of a deleted run, and its requests to upload the run’s files, and the files in a refused report aren’t added to the run. Watcher 1.4.3 and later record one event for the run, a `run_report_failed` event or an `upload_failed` event, whichever the watcher meets first, and stop reporting the run and uploading its files until the watcher restarts. A restart tries once more, and records one more event if the run is still deleted. After you restore the run, restart the watcher to send its files. A file that someone requests with **Upload** on the run page doesn’t wait for the restart: the watcher asks Data Hub for each requested file, and once Data Hub accepts one, the watcher reports and uploads the run’s new files again. Earlier watchers record one event for each file, and do it again each time they start. After you restore the run, they send its files when another file of the run finishes or the watcher restarts. To stop the errors without restoring the run, move the run’s files out of the watch folder. ## Files aren’t being detected [#files-are-not-being-detected] * Check the watch folder and file patterns. The instrument’s page in the web app shows both, or run `data-hub-watcher config show` on the PC. Admins can change them from the web app; see [Change a watcher’s settings](/docs/manage-watchers#change-a-watchers-config) * Check that the instrument saves its files into that folder, not a shared network drive or another folder * Check the file patterns. They’re case-sensitive, so `*.csv` doesn’t match `data.CSV` * If files are in subfolders, turn on subfolders in run detection (`recursive: true`); see [Configure run detection and uploads](/docs/configure-run-detection) * Run `data-hub-watcher watch --dry-run` to preview matches * Look for `pattern_mismatch` events on the watcher’s **Activity** tab ## Files are detected but not uploading [#files-are-detected-but-not-uploading] * In **manual** mode, files wait for approval in the upload queue; see [Manage the watcher fleet](/docs/manage-watchers#approving-manual-uploads) * On the run page, the **Upload** buttons are turned off while the instrument is **Connecting**, **Offline**, **Pending**, or **Retired**, with the reason beside them. Fix the watcher first; see [An instrument shows Offline](#instrument-shows-offline). While the instrument is **Restarting** they stay on, and the request waits for the watcher * Files read **Not uploaded** until someone requests them, or **Waiting to upload** while an auto-mode watcher (1.4.5 and later) is about to send them * A file that reads **Upload failed** is one the watcher gave up on. Hover over its status for the reason; see [A file reads Upload failed](#a-file-reads-upload-failed) * Check the log for `upload_failed` * A `state_write_failed` event in the watcher’s event log means the PC’s disk is full or the watcher’s state file can’t be written. Free up space; the watcher retries on its own and uploads the files once it can write again * A revoked or expired token shows up as `401 Unauthorized`. Create a new token and re-run `init`; see [Issue and revoke tokens](/docs/manage-tokens#after-revoking-a-token) ### A file reads Upload failed [#a-file-reads-upload-failed] The watcher marks a file **Upload failed** when it gives up on it, and its activity shows one **Couldn’t upload** entry per run and reason. Hover over the file’s status for the reason: * **The folder is no longer on the instrument PC.** The run folder was renamed or moved after the watcher found it. The watcher reports the folder under its new name as a new run, so check for a run with the same start time and a similar name. If its files are already uploaded, dismiss the old ones. * **The file isn’t on the instrument PC.** The file was moved or deleted. Put it back and choose **Upload**, or choose **Dismiss**. * **The upload kept failing.** For example, because of a network or storage problem. The message shows the last error. Choose **Upload** to try again once it’s fixed. * **The path is outside the watch folder.** Check the watcher’s **Watch folder** setting. Watchers before 1.4.5 put the file back to **Not uploaded** without a reason, and log a “Queued file missing” and a “Gave up uploading” error for each file instead. See [When an upload fails](/docs/browse-runs#upload-failed). ### An upload was cut off by a restart or an update [#an-upload-was-cut-off-by-a-restart-or-an-update] The watcher retries an automatic upload that didn’t finish, such as one cut off by a restart or an update, the next time it starts, on up to three starts. Until it succeeds, the file reads **Upload failed** with the reason. Choose **Upload** on the run page to try again sooner. Watchers before 1.4.5 don’t mark the file.
