Instead they record `upload_retries_exhausted` when the upload still failed after three starts, or `pending_upload_missing` when the file was no longer on disk at start. ### A file stays on Not uploaded after the watcher restarted [#a-file-stays-pending-after-the-watcher-restarted] Watchers before 1.4.1 could lose track of a file in an automatic upload when the watcher stopped without shutting down cleanly, such as after a reboot, a power cut, or a crash, right after it reported the run. The run is in Data Hub, but the file reads **Not uploaded** and nothing uploads it, because after the restart the watcher treats the file as already handled. Watcher 1.4.1 and later record a run and its files on the PC together, so a restart like that doesn’t leave a file behind. Updating doesn’t pick up files that an older watcher already lost this way. Ask for them from the run page: Open the run, select the files that read **Not uploaded**, and choose **Upload**. To ask for the files of several runs at once, select the runs in the run list and choose **Upload**. See [Request an upload](/docs/browse-runs#request-upload). The watcher picks up the request within a minute and uploads the files that are still on the instrument PC. ## Automatic updates never happen [#auto-update-never-fires] Check these, in order: * The watcher runs as a Windows service, or on a schedule. A watcher started by hand in a terminal may not run long enough to reach its hourly update check * The environment isn’t `preview`, where automatic updates are always off * The watcher isn’t waiting until it’s idle. Run `data-hub-watcher self-update` to update now, or ask an admin to turn on **Mandatory update** * **Last heartbeat** on the watcher’s page is recent. A watcher that has stopped checking in also stops checking for updates [Install and update the watcher](/docs/install-the-watcher#manual-update-self-update) and [Roll out watcher releases](/docs/watcher-releases) cover failed updates, such as `update_started` followed by `update_failed`, development installs, and a missing Scheduled Task. ## Windows service problems [#windows-service] ### The service exits immediately [#the-service-exits-immediately] A config file that doesn’t load stops the service: one that’s missing, can’t be read, isn’t saved as UTF-8, has broken YAML, or has a value the watcher doesn’t accept. `watcher.log` has an error that starts with `Cannot load config`, followed by the reason. The error also gives the command that checks the file, in the form `data-hub-watcher --config "C:\path\to\config.yaml" config validate`. Run it as written, because without `--config` it checks the config file of the person who runs it, not the one the service uses. Fix what it reports and start the service again. An env file that isn’t saved as UTF-8 stops the service the same way, with an error that starts with `Cannot load env file`. Windows PowerShell 5.1 writes UTF-16 for `>` and `>>`, so `echo X=Y >> .env.production` breaks a UTF-8 env file. Watchers before 1.4.2 wrote only a traceback to the Application event log for either problem. If it stops before writing to `watcher.log`: * Check `C:\ProgramData\DataHubWatcher\service-bootstrap.log` for a crash before the service fully started, such as a missing `pywin32`, a moved Python environment, or a broken install * Query the Windows Application event log: ```powershell Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{LogName='Application'; StartTime=(Get-Date).AddHours(-1)} | Where-Object { $_.ProviderName -match 'Python|DataHubWatcher' -or $_.Message -match 'DataHubWatcher' } | Format-List TimeCreated, ProviderName, Id, LevelDisplayName, Message ``` * Run the service in a terminal to see the full error: ```powershell & "C:\path\to\venv\Scripts\python.exe" -m win32serviceutil debug DataHubWatcher ``` ### `self-update` says “Upgrade dispatched” but nothing happens [#self-update-says-upgrade-dispatched-but-nothing-happens] On Windows, when the watcher was installed with `uv tool install`, the upgrade runs separately as the SYSTEM account and takes 30 to 60 seconds. To follow it: ```powershell Get-Service data-hub-watcher Get-Content ~/.data-hub/upgrade-worker.log -Tail 20 -Wait ``` ### Turn on debug logging for the service [#turn-on-debug-logging-for-the-service] Add `DATA_HUB_WATCHER_LOG_LEVEL=DEBUG` to the env file the service loads, such as `~/.data-hub/.env.production`, and restart the service. No reinstall needed. This works with watcher 1.4.2 and later; earlier versions ignore the setting in the env file. ## Where are the logs? [#where-are-the-logs] The watcher keeps the current log and up to five older ones, 10 MB each. `watch` in a terminal and the Windows service write to the same file: | Platform | Log file | | ------------- | ------------------------------------------- | | Windows | `C:\ProgramData\DataHubWatcher\watcher.log` | | macOS / Linux | `~/.data-hub/watcher.log` | To print debug messages in the terminal, add `--verbose`: `data-hub-watcher --verbose watch`. On Windows, the output of an update goes to `~/.data-hub/upgrade-worker.log`. ## API clients get `401 Unauthorized` [#api-clients-get-401-unauthorized] The bearer token is missing, mistyped, revoked, or expired. Check **Settings → Access Tokens**, and ask an admin for a new token if needed. See [Issue and revoke tokens](/docs/manage-tokens). A script that calls the watcher or processing routes with a browser session, instead of a token, also gets `401`. Those routes accept only personal access tokens; see [How a token acts](/docs/manage-tokens#how-a-token-acts). ## MCP clients get `401 Unauthorized` [#mcp-clients-get-401-unauthorized] MCP doesn’t accept personal access tokens, so a client configured with `Authorization: Bearer dhub_…` gets a 401 on every call. Remove the header, leave only the URL, and let the client run its sign-in flow. Setup per client is in [MCP overview](/docs/mcp#connect-a-client). A connected client that starts failing has most likely lost its sign-in, so sign in again from the client. If reads work and one tool fails with a missing-scope message, the client holds `read` but not `write`; reconnect and approve both. ## Ask an agent to diagnose it [#ask-an-agent-to-diagnose-it] An AI assistant connected over MCP can look into a watcher problem for you with the `troubleshoot_instrument` prompt; see [MCP prompts](/docs/mcp/prompts).

pages.title: Administration overview
pages.description: Where admins manage instruments, watchers, tokens, members, and watcher releases.
pages.markdown:
# Administration overview (/docs/administration)



**For:** Administrators

Admins can:

* Confirm new instruments
* Check that each instrument’s watcher is running
* Issue and revoke tokens
* Choose who else is an admin
* Roll out new watcher versions
* Connect Linear and Slack
* Delete any run comment
* Review the feedback people send about Data Hub

These pages under **Settings** are for admins only, and members don’t see them in the settings menu:

* **Feedback**: every feedback report people have sent
* **Integrations**: the connections to Linear and Slack
* **Watchers**: the form for rolling out watcher versions, and a list of every watcher
* **Members**: who is an admin

Each instrument also has its own watcher page, under the instrument, and members can read it.

[Security and permissions](/docs/security) explains roles and scopes. Lab operators set up instruments by following [Set up an instrument](/docs/set-up-an-instrument).

## What you manage [#what-you-manage]

  <Card title="Manage instruments" href="/docs/manage-instruments" description="Review and confirm pending instruments, and read an instrument’s status." />

  <Card title="Issue and revoke tokens" href="/docs/manage-tokens" description="Create and revoke the personal access tokens that watchers and API clients use." />

  <Card title="Manage members" href="/docs/manage-members" description="Promote members to admin, and demote admins." />

pages.title: Manage instruments
pages.description: Review and confirm pending instruments, read an instrument’s status badge, watch folder, and file patterns, and edit its name and type.
pages.markdown: # Manage instruments (/docs/manage-instruments) **For:** Administrators When a lab operator registers an instrument from the watcher, it appears as `pending` and can’t upload until you confirm it. [Set up an instrument](/docs/set-up-an-instrument) covers the operator’s side. [Retire an instrument](/docs/retire-an-instrument) covers retiring and reactivating. ## Instrument states [#instrument-states] The **Instruments** page has tabs for active, pending, and retired instruments. | Status | UI label | Meaning | | ---------- | -------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | | `pending` | Pending | Registered but not confirmed. Watchers can’t upload. | | `active` | Active | Confirmed and accepting uploads. | | `inactive` | Retired | Taken out of service. No new uploads, and past runs stay browsable. | Each instrument also has a status badge that says whether its new files can arrive. See [Read an instrument’s page](#view-instrument-health). ## Confirm a pending instrument [#confirm-a-pending-instrument] Confirming opens a review of what the watcher was set up to do, so you can check it before files start to flow. Open the Data Hub web app and go to **Instruments**. Open the **Pending** tab (or find the amber **Pending** badge), and choose **Confirm…** on the instrument’s row. You can also open the pending instrument’s page, which has a **Waiting for confirmation** card with the same button. Read the review. It shows the instrument’s ID, which can’t be changed later, and what the watcher registered: * **Registered from**: the computer, and the name of the token the watcher registered with * **Watch folder**: the folder the watcher reads from * **File patterns**: which files the watcher uploads * **How files become runs**: a plain name for the preset, with one example from a recent or sample file name * **Upload mode**: **Automatic** or **Manual** Choose an **Instrument type**. It’s required, because it decides how files are processed and which details appear on run pages. Choose **Confirm instrument**. The instrument becomes active and its type is saved in one step. If something in the review looks wrong, choose **Change settings first**. It opens the watcher’s **Settings** tab, which works for a pending instrument, so you can fix the folder or patterns before you confirm. See [Change a watcher’s settings](/docs/manage-watchers#change-a-watchers-config). After you confirm, the operator starts the watcher service on the PC (step 5 of [Set up an instrument](/docs/set-up-an-instrument#start-the-watcher-service)). The badge goes from **Connecting** to **Online** once the watcher checks in. If the watcher hasn’t checked in 15 minutes after you confirm, the badge turns **Offline**, and its notice says the watcher never checked in. Members who open a pending instrument’s page see one line instead of the card: “This instrument is waiting for an admin to confirm it. Runs will appear here after that.” A signed-in user has to be an admin to confirm an instrument. Through the API, confirming is `PATCH /api/v1/instruments/your_instrument_id` with `status` and `instrument_type` in the same request. A script that uses a token needs the `instruments:write` scope instead of the admin role. See the [generated API docs](/docs/api). ## Read an instrument’s page [#view-instrument-health] The top of each instrument page shows what you need to tell whether its files will reach Data Hub: * **Status badge**: next to the instrument name, it reads **Online**, **Restarting**, **Connecting**, **Offline**, **Pending**, or **Retired**. Hover over it for a short explanation. Select it to open the watcher’s page, the only place that shows the watcher’s hostname and version. * **Watch folder**: the folder the watcher reads from. Hover over it for a reminder that files saved anywhere else don’t appear, and select it to copy the path. * **File patterns**: the patterns the watcher uploads, such as `*.csv`. * **Manual upload note**: an instrument in manual upload mode shows “Files upload when someone requests them” beside the patterns, whatever the badge says. The badge follows the instrument’s one watcher, which checks in once a minute. After a restart, a watcher can take up to a minute to show as online. The rules are in [Instrument status](/docs/concepts#instrument-status). When the badge reads **Offline**, a notice between the header and the runs table says why. The actions it offers depend on the reason: * **The watch folder is missing**: **See details** opens the watcher’s **Activity** tab. Admins also get **Change folder**, which opens the watcher’s settings form with the **Watch folder** field selected. * **The watcher isn’t checking in, or someone stopped it**: **See details** opens the watcher’s **Activity** tab. * **The instrument has no watcher, or its watcher was deregistered**: there’s no current watcher to look at. Admins get **Connect a watcher**, which opens [Set up an instrument](/docs/set-up-an-instrument), and members get no action. [Check that new files will arrive](/docs/browse-runs#check-files-will-arrive) describes the notices from the scientist’s side, with a table of every notice. Files saved anywhere other than the watch folder, such as a shared network drive, don’t appear in Data Hub. Neither do files whose names don’t match a pattern. Admins can change the folder and patterns on the watcher’s **Settings** tab; see [Change a watcher’s settings](/docs/manage-watchers#change-a-watchers-config). You can also change them on the PC with `data-hub-watcher config edit`; see [Watcher configuration](/docs/configuration-reference). Data Hub judges a watcher’s health from its heartbeats, the check-ins it sends once a minute. See [Manage the watcher fleet](/docs/manage-watchers). ## Edit an instrument [#edit-an-instrument] The three-dot menu on an instrument page and the row menu on the **Instruments** table hold the admin actions: * **Edit details**: change the **Display name** and the **Instrument type** * **Watcher**: open the instrument’s watcher page, where its settings are * **Retire** or **Reactivate**: see [Retire an instrument](/docs/retire-an-instrument) Members see no menu on the instrument page. They reach the watcher page through the status badge. The instrument type decides which processor reads the instrument’s files, including DishCam and Aunty. See [Instrument data preprocessing](/docs/instrument-preprocessing). The instrument ID never changes, because Data Hub uses it in the storage path of every file.

pages.title: Retire an instrument
pages.description: Retire an instrument so it stops accepting uploads and watchers, while keeping historical runs and files.
pages.markdown: # Retire an instrument (/docs/retire-an-instrument) **For:** Administrators Retire an instrument when it’s taken out of service for good or for a long time. Retiring sets its status to `inactive`, shown as **Retired**, and stops new uploads. The instrument leaves the sidebar and the home page’s list of instruments. Nothing is deleted from storage, and you can reactivate it later. ## What retirement does [#what-retirement-does] When you retire an instrument: * Its status becomes `inactive`, shown as **Retired**. Data Hub records who retired it and when, and the instrument page shows both. * It stops accepting new runs and watchers. * Its badge reads **Retired**, and the **Upload** buttons on its run pages are turned off. * All existing runs and files stay browsable. * Its watcher is deregistered in the same request, so it stops checking in. The watcher stays on the instrument’s watcher page as a past watcher. An instrument’s ID never changes. To stop using an instrument that has already produced data, retire it instead of trying to rename or delete it. ## Retire from the web app [#retire-from-the-web-app] Open the instrument’s page. Open the three-dot menu, which only admins see, and choose **Retire**. The row menu on **Instruments** has the same item. Read the window that opens, then choose **Retire instrument**. The window says how many runs are kept and that nothing is deleted from storage. When the instrument has a watcher, it also says the watcher will be deregistered so it stops checking in. The instrument moves to the **Retired** tab on **Instruments**. ## Reactivate [#reactivate] From a retired instrument’s page, open the three-dot menu and choose **Reactivate**. The row menu on the **Retired** tab has the same item. The status returns to `active`, and the instrument appears in the sidebar and on the home page again. After you reactivate, an operator has to register a watcher again by running `data-hub-watcher init` on the instrument PC. The watcher that was deregistered at retirement stays disconnected. Until a new one registers, the badge reads **Offline** and a notice says the instrument isn’t connected to a watcher. Admins can choose **Connect a watcher** to open [Set up an instrument](/docs/set-up-an-instrument). ## Via the API [#via-the-api] ```sh # Retire curl -X PATCH https://datahub.example.com/api/v1/instruments/bio-rad-cfx96 \ -H "Authorization: Bearer dhub_your_token_here" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"status":"inactive"}' # Reactivate curl -X PATCH https://datahub.example.com/api/v1/instruments/bio-rad-cfx96 \ -H "Authorization: Bearer dhub_your_token_here" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{"status":"active"}' ``` Signed-in users need the admin role. Scripts that use a token need the `instruments:write` scope.

pages.title: Issue and revoke tokens
pages.description: Create, use, and revoke personal access tokens that authenticate the watcher and other Data Hub API clients, and see what a token can and can’t do.
pages.markdown: # Issue and revoke tokens (/docs/manage-tokens) **For:** Administrators Personal access tokens authenticate the watcher, the processing Lambda, and scripts that call the Data Hub API. Only admins can create and revoke tokens. Members can view the list at **Settings → Access Tokens** but can’t create or delete tokens. For roles and scopes, see [Security and permissions](/docs/security). ## How a token acts [#how-a-token-acts] A token acts under its own name, which the web app shows with a key icon, not as the admin who created it. Tokens can’t claim runs or send or review feedback, because those need a signed-in person. The routes that the watcher and the Lambda call accept only tokens, so a browser session gets `401 Unauthorized` there. See [How tokens act](/docs/security#how-tokens-act) for the full rules. ## Create a token [#create-a-token] ### In the web app [#in-the-web-app] Sign in as an admin. Go to **Settings → Access Tokens**. Choose **Create token**. Enter a **Name** that identifies the client (for example, `FPLC watcher, Lab 201`). People see this name wherever the token acts, so make it recognizable. Choose an **Expiration**: 30 days, 90 days (the default), 1 year, or no expiry. Under **Scopes**, choose a preset, or choose **Customize scopes** to select individual scopes. Choose **Create token**. Data Hub shows the token only once, so copy it now. It starts with `dhub_`, followed by 64 hexadecimal characters (0–9 and a–f). ### Scope presets [#scope-presets] A preset selects the minimum scopes a common client needs: * **Read-only**: view instruments, runs, files, watchers, and archive jobs; change nothing * **Watcher**: what a watcher needs to register, report runs, and upload files * **Lambda**: what the processing Lambda needs to read instruments and runs, and write run and file results The **Lambda** preset includes `runs:read`, which DishCam processing needs to pair each photo stack with its `run.json`. A Lambda token created from an older preset gets `403 FORBIDDEN` on DishCam files. Create a new token from the current preset and update the Lambda’s `DATA_HUB_API_KEY`; the [Lambda developer docs](https://github.com/Arcadia-Science/data-hub/blob/production/docs/developer/lambda.md#supported-instrument-types) describe the swap. A token’s scopes are fixed when you create it. To change them, revoke the token and create a new one. ### Via the API [#via-the-api] Only admins can create and delete tokens through the API, and only from a signed-in browser session (a session cookie). Tokens can’t manage other tokens. ```sh curl -X POST https://datahub.example.com/api/v1/tokens \ -H "Cookie: session_cookie_here" \ -H "Content-Type: application/json" \ -d '{ "name": "FPLC watcher", "scopes": ["instruments:read", "instruments:write", "watchers:read", "watchers:report", "runs:create", "runs:update", "runs:upload", "files:update"], "expires_at": "2027-01-01T00:00:00Z" }' ``` `scopes` is required and must list at least one specific scope. Data Hub rejects the wildcard `*` and the older coarse scopes `runs:write`, `files:write`, and `watchers:write`. `expires_at` is optional; without it, the token never expires. Data Hub rejects a request that includes `user_id`, because tokens don’t belong to a person. The response includes the token once, in the `token` field. ## Use a token [#use-a-token] ### With the watcher [#with-the-watcher] Paste the token when `data-hub-watcher init` asks for it. You can also set it first: ```sh export DATA_HUB_API_KEY=dhub_your_token_here data-hub-watcher init ``` ### With the REST API [#with-the-rest-api] ```sh curl https://datahub.example.com/api/v1/instruments \ -H "Authorization: Bearer dhub_your_token_here" ``` See the [API overview](/docs/api) for more. MCP clients sign in with OAuth instead of a token. See [MCP overview](/docs/mcp). ## View tokens [#view-tokens] **Settings → Access Tokens** lists every active token with these columns: * **Name** * **Created by**: the admin who made the token. For tokens created before October 6, 2026, this shows the person the token used to act as. * **Token**: the prefix only, because Data Hub never stores the full token * **Scopes** * **Last used** * **Expires** * **Created** ## Revoke a token [#revoke-a-token] Go to **Settings → Access Tokens**. Choose the delete icon on the token’s row, then confirm. The token stops working immediately. Clients using it start receiving `401 Unauthorized`. To revoke a token through the API, send a `DELETE` from a signed-in admin session: ```sh curl -X DELETE https://datahub.example.com/api/v1/tokens/your_token_id \ -H "Cookie: session_cookie_here" ``` A revoked token leaves the list, but Data Hub keeps its record. Wherever the token acted, its name stays visible and is marked **(revoked)**. ## After revoking a token [#after-revoking-a-token] If a running watcher used that token: Create a new token with the **Watcher** preset. On the instrument PC, run `data-hub-watcher init` again and enter the new token. The new token takes over the existing watcher registration, so you don’t need to deregister the old one first. Restart the watcher (`data-hub-watcher watch` or the Windows service). ## When someone leaves [#when-someone-leaves] Tokens keep working after the admin who created them leaves or their account is deleted, because tokens act as themselves. When someone leaves, check the **Created by** column and revoke any of their tokens that nobody else should keep using. ## Token hygiene [#token-hygiene] * **Name tokens clearly**: name each one after the PC or client it belongs to, for example “FPLC watcher, Lab 201” * **Set expirations**: give temporary setups a token that expires * **Give each token the fewest scopes it needs**: don’t hand out a broad token for a single read-only integration; see [Token scopes](/docs/security#token-scopes) * **Revoke unused and exposed tokens immediately**: revoke a token when you stop using its watcher or the token may have been exposed. Revoking takes effect at once, and clients using the token start getting `401 Unauthorized`; see [After revoking a token](#after-revoking-a-token). * **Revoke a departing person’s tokens**: tokens keep working when the person who created them leaves, so check the **Created by** column under **Settings → Access Tokens** Data Hub stores only a SHA-256 hash of each token, never the token itself.

pages.title: Manage members
pages.description: Promote members to admin, and demote admins, from Settings → Members.
pages.markdown: # Manage members (/docs/manage-members) **For:** Administrators Members sign in with Google. Admins decide who else has the admin role. [Security and permissions](/docs/security#roles) lists what members and admins can each do. ## Open the members list [#open-the-members-list] Go to **Settings → Members**. The settings menu hides this page from members, and a member who opens its URL sees an **Admins Only** message. The table lists everyone who has signed in, with their name, email, role, and an **Admin** switch. ## Promote or demote [#promote-or-demote] Turn **Admin** on or off on a row to give or remove admin access, then confirm. Data Hub checks the role again on every admin action, so the change applies from that person’s next one. The admin-only buttons and sidebar entries they see can take up to 5 minutes to change, because they come from their [cached session](/docs/security#session-lifetime). You can’t demote yourself. That rule stops the last admin from removing their own admin role. Ask another admin to demote you if you need to. ## Choose the first admins [#first-admin-bootstrap] The first admins come from the `ADMIN_EMAILS` environment variable, a comma-separated list of email addresses that ignores case. Data Hub makes each listed person an admin every time they sign in. After that, any admin can promote others from this page. People appear on this page after they first sign in to your deployment, and Data Hub has no invitations. Any Google account that your Google OAuth client accepts can sign in. That client, which your team created when it set up Data Hub, decides who appears here. See [Who can sign in](/docs/security#who-can-sign-in).

pages.title: Set up integrations
pages.description: Connect Data Hub to Linear for feedback reports, and to Slack for personal direct messages and a shared new-run channel, from Settings → Integrations.
pages.markdown: # Set up integrations (/docs/integrations) **For:** Administrators and engineers **Settings → Integrations** holds the connections the whole workspace shares. Only admins see it. The page has three parts: * **Linear**: where feedback reports go, and where their status comes from * **Slack app**: the credentials behind personal Slack direct messages and **Connect to Slack** * **Slack channel**: a webhook that posts a message to a shared channel whenever a new run arrives Each person’s own notification choices are separate, under **Settings → Notifications**. See [Configure notifications](/docs/configure-notifications). ## How secrets are stored [#integration-secrets-key] Data Hub encrypts the secrets you paste on this page before saving them: the Linear client secret and signing secret, and the Slack bot token and client secret. It never shows a saved secret again. To change one, paste a new value and save. Encryption needs the `INTEGRATION_SECRETS_KEY` environment variable on the web app. It’s 64 hexadecimal characters. Generate one with `openssl rand -hex 32`, set it in Vercel, and redeploy. Until it’s set, saving a secret fails, and the Slack app card says so. If the key changes after secrets were saved, Data Hub can’t read them anymore. The affected field says **Can’t read saved value**. Put the old key back, or paste the value again and save. ## Linear for feedback reports [#linear] Feedback that people send from Data Hub becomes an issue in your Linear workspace, and the report’s status follows that issue. Until an admin saves a Linear team here, the **Feedback** item stays out of the account menu. Sending feedback through the API or an AI assistant returns an error saying feedback isn’t set up. [Send feedback](/docs/send-feedback) covers what reporters see. The Linear card walks you through four steps. ### 1. Connect your Linear app [#linear-connect] Data Hub signs in to Linear as an app, so you create one app in Linear for it. In Linear, go to **Settings → API → OAuth applications** and create a new application. Name it **Data Hub**. Linear shows this name on every issue it files. Linear asks for a callback URL. Data Hub doesn’t use one, so paste the URL shown in the step, which is your deployment’s address. Turn on **Client credentials**, then save. Copy the client ID and client secret into the Linear card in Data Hub, and choose **Connect**. Data Hub checks the credentials with Linear before it saves them. If client credentials are turned off for the app, the card says so; turn them on in the app’s settings in Linear and choose **Connect** again. If the credentials belong to a different Linear workspace than the one already connected, Data Hub asks before switching. Switching clears the team, project, labels, and signing secret. Issues already in Linear stay there. ### 2. Choose where reports go [#linear-destination] Choose the **Team** that receives reports. Only public teams are listed, because Linear doesn’t show private teams to apps. Optionally choose a **Project**. Optionally choose a label for each kind of report: **Bug**, **Feature request**, and **Other**. Labels can come from the team or from the whole workspace. Linear adds the matching label to each new issue. Choose **Save and turn on feedback**. Everyone sees **Feedback** in their account menu from then on. Changing the team later clears the project and labels. Status updates also stop until the Linear webhook from step 3 points at the new team. ### 3. Get status updates from Linear [#linear-status-updates] A webhook tells Data Hub when an issue changes, so it can update the report and tell the person who sent it when the issue closes. In Linear, go to **Settings → API** and choose **New webhook**. Paste the **Webhook URL** shown in the step. It ends in `/api/v1/integrations/linear/webhook`. For **Team**, choose the team from step 2. Under events, turn on **Issues** only. Save the webhook, then copy its signing secret into **Signing secret** in Data Hub and save. Data Hub uses the signing secret to check that each update comes from Linear. The step shows **Waiting for an update from Linear** until the first one arrives. Any change to an issue in the team sends one, including the test report in the next step. ### 4. Send a test report [#linear-test-report] Choose **Send test report**. Data Hub files a report as you and links to the new Linear issue. Move that issue to **Done** in Linear. The step confirms that the issue closed and that you got a Data Hub notification. You can also skip the test. ### After setup [#linear-after-setup] Once setup is finished, the Linear card shows a summary: * The connected workspace * Where reports go * Whether status updates are working, and when the last one arrived * What reporters see for each Linear status, as in this table | When the Linear issue moves to | The reporter sees | | --------------------------------------- | ----------------- | | **Done**, or any other completed status | Resolved | | **Canceled** | Declined | | **Duplicate** | Declined | | Any other status | Open | Data Hub notifies the reporter once, when the issue first closes. Moving an issue from one closed status to another, such as **Done** to **Released**, doesn’t notify again. Reopening an issue and closing it again does. If Data Hub keeps rejecting updates from Linear, **Status updates** shows **Not working**. Look for a wrong signing secret, or for Linear turning the webhook off after repeated failures. Paste the signing secret again from the webhook’s page in Linear, and check that the webhook is still turned on. **Disconnect Linear** turns feedback off. Issues already in Linear stay there. ## Slack app for direct messages [#slack-app] Personal Slack direct messages and the **Connect to Slack** button use one shared Slack app. Create the app once in the [Slack API portal](https://api.slack.com/apps), then give Data Hub its credentials. You can reuse an existing Slack app, including the one behind the channel webhook. ### Create the app [#create-the-slack-app] In the Slack API portal, choose **Create New App → From scratch**, or open an existing app. Under **OAuth & Permissions**, add these scopes: **Bot Token Scopes:** | Scope | Purpose | | ------------ | -------------------------------------------- | | `chat:write` | Send direct messages with `chat.postMessage` | **User Token Scopes:** | Scope | Purpose | | --------- | ----------------------------------- | | `openid` | Sign in with Slack (OpenID Connect) | | `profile` | Display name in the identity token | Under **Redirect URLs**, add one callback URL per environment. The path is always `/api/v1/settings/slack/callback`: | Environment | Example URL | | ----------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Local | `http://localhost:3000/api/v1/settings/slack/callback` | | Staging | `https://staging.datahub.example.com/api/v1/settings/slack/callback` | | Production | `https://datahub.example.com/api/v1/settings/slack/callback` | After someone connects Slack, Slack sends them back to a callback URL. Data Hub uses `SLACK_REDIRECT_URI` as that URL. When it isn’t set, Data Hub uses the address of the site the person is on, followed by this path. Either way, the URL has to match one of the URLs you listed exactly. Under **Install App**, choose **Install to Workspace** (or **Reinstall** after changing scopes). ### Give Data Hub the credentials [#slack-app-credentials] Enter the credentials in the **Slack app** card under **Settings → Integrations**, or set them as environment variables on the web app. A value saved in the card takes effect right away, with no redeploy, and is used instead of the matching environment variable. | Card field | Environment variable | Where to find it | Required | | ------------------------ | --------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------- | | **Bot token** | `SLACK_BOT_TOKEN` | **Install App** → Bot User OAuth Token (`xoxb-…`) | Yes | | **Client ID** | `SLACK_CLIENT_ID` | **Basic Information** → App Credentials | Yes | | **Client secret** | `SLACK_CLIENT_SECRET` | **Basic Information** → App Credentials | Yes | | **Allowed workspace ID** | `SLACK_TEAM_ID` | Workspace URL segment `T…` in `app.slack.com/client/T…` | No, but recommended so connections stay on your workspace | Each field shows where its value comes from: **Saved here**, **Using** followed by the variable name, or **Not set**. **Remove saved value** makes the environment variable the source again. If Data Hub can’t read a saved value, for example because `INTEGRATION_SECRETS_KEY` changed, it uses the environment variable in the meantime. Two settings exist only as environment variables, and changing them needs a redeploy: | Variable | Purpose | Required | | -------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------- | | `SLACK_STATE_SECRET` | Signs the short-lived value Data Hub checks while a person connects Slack. Generate one with `openssl rand -base64 32` | No (falls back to `AUTH_SECRET`) | | `SLACK_REDIRECT_URI` | Full callback URL, when it differs from the site’s address plus the callback path | No | Members can then connect under **Settings → Notifications**. Deployment guides are linked from [Deploy Data Hub](/docs/self-hosting). ## Slack channel for new runs [#slack-channel] The **Slack channel** card holds a Slack incoming webhook. Data Hub posts one message to that channel each time a new run is reported. This is separate from personal direct messages, which each person turns on for themselves. In your Slack app, open **Incoming Webhooks**, turn them on, and add a webhook for the channel you want. Copy the webhook URL. It starts with `https://hooks.slack.com/services/`. Paste it into the **Slack channel** card and save. The card shows **Configured** and who last changed it. To change channels, paste a new webhook URL. To stop the messages, remove the webhook. This setting has no environment variable.

# API overview (/docs/api)



**For:** Developers and integrators

The Data Hub web app serves the REST API at `/api/v1/`. The watcher, the Lambda, and the web app all call it. Data Hub is self-hosted, so the base URL is your deployment’s host plus `/api/v1`. Examples use `https://datahub.example.com`; replace it with your host.

The generated pages in this **API** section of the sidebar describe each endpoint’s request and response. Each deployment also publishes an OpenAPI 3.1 document at `/api/v1/openapi.json`.

## Authentication [#authentication]

The REST API accepts two kinds of credentials, and [Security and permissions](/docs/security) describes the full model:

* **Session cookies**: the web app uses these after someone signs in with Google. Scopes apply only to tokens, so a signed-in session passes every scope check.
* **Bearer tokens**: the watcher, the Lambda, and scripts send `Authorization: Bearer dhub_…`

```sh
curl https://datahub.example.com/api/v1/instruments \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer dhub_your_token_here"
```

Every token request needs a [scope](/docs/security#token-scopes), and a missing scope returns `403 FORBIDDEN`. Some actions that change data also need the admin role; see [Admin-gated operations](/docs/security#admin-gated-operations).

Some routes accept only one of the two kinds of credentials:

* The routes the watcher and the Lambda call accept only tokens, and return `401 UNAUTHORIZED` to a session. These cover watcher registration and heartbeats, upload links, file updates, run creation and updates, and instrument creation.
* Claiming runs, sending feedback, reviewing feedback, and managing tokens need a signed-in person, so tokens can’t call them.

Admins create tokens in the web app; see [Issue and revoke tokens](/docs/manage-tokens).

## First request [#first-request]

List instruments:

```sh
curl https://datahub.example.com/api/v1/instruments \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer dhub_your_token_here"
```

Fetch the OpenAPI document, which needs no credentials:

```sh
curl https://datahub.example.com/api/v1/openapi.json
```

The document covers the routes that integrations use:

* instruments
* runs
* comments
* lab notebooks
* files
* watchers
* archive jobs
* search
* `POST /notifications/dispatch`

It leaves out the routes that only the web app uses: `/tokens`, `/users`, `/feedback`, `/settings/*`, and the notification inbox. The MCP server has its own docs; see [MCP](#mcp).

## Instruments and their watcher [#instrument-connection]

An instrument has at most one active watcher, so `GET /instruments` and `GET /instruments/:id` describe it with one object instead of counts:

* `watcher`: the instrument’s active watcher, or `null` when it has none. It includes `id`, `status`, `status_reason`, `last_heartbeat_at`, `file_patterns`, `upload_mode`, and `config_state`. With the `watchers:read` scope, it also includes five fields that say where the watcher runs: `hostname`, `os_info`, `version`, `watch_directory`, and `shared_computer_with`. A token that has `instruments:read` but not `watchers:read` gets the watcher without those five fields. The fields are missing from the object, not set to `null`. A signed-in browser session passes every scope check, so it always gets them.
* `connection`: whether new files can reach Data Hub. `state` is `online`, `restarting`, `connecting`, or `offline`. `reason` says why the instrument is offline (`folder_missing`, `unresponsive`, `never_checked_in`, `stopped`, `no_watcher`, or `deregistered`), and is `null` otherwise. The rules are the same ones behind the badge in the web app; see [Instrument status](/docs/concepts#instrument-status). `connection` ignores the instrument’s own `status`, so a `pending` instrument can be `online`. The web app shows **Pending** or **Retired** first, and `connection.state` only after that.
* `past_watcher_count`: how many deregistered watchers the instrument has had.

`GET /instruments/:id` still returns `watcher_count`, but it’s deprecated. It keeps its old value for now. A later release will remove it, and the changelog will announce the date first. Read `watcher` instead, which is `null` when there’s no watcher.

`GET /search` returns the same instrument results as the `global_search` MCP tool. An instrument result now includes `connection`, which replaces the deprecated `watcherStatus` and `lastWatcherHeartbeatAt`. Those two fields keep their old values for now.

## Actions taken by a token [#actions-taken-by-a-token]

A token acts under its own name, not as a person, so responses name the token when it did something:

* A comment posted by a token has `user: null` and a `token` object with the token’s `id` and `name`. A comment posted by a person has `token: null`.
* A run deleted by a token has `deleted_by_token` set, alongside `deleted_at`.
* A file deleted by a token has `deleted_by_token` set, alongside `deleted_at`, and `deleted_by` null. A file deleted by a person has `deleted_by` set to their user ID and `deleted_by_token` null.
* A lab notebook created, last edited, or deleted by a token has `created_by_token`, `updated_by_token`, or `deleted_by_token` set, and the matching person field null. A run added to a lab notebook by a token has `linked_by_token` set and `linked_by` null.

Read both fields when you display who did something. See [How a token acts](/docs/manage-tokens#how-a-token-acts).

## Deleted files [#deleted-files]

Deleting a file hides it from its run. The file stays in storage, records who deleted it, and can be restored. A deleted file is left out of the run’s downloads and of the `files` that `GET /instruments/:id/runs/:runId` returns. Pass `include_deleted=true` to that route to list deleted files too, each with `deleted_at` and who deleted it. A deleted file keeps its ID, so you can still download it by ID.

* `DELETE /files/:id` deletes one file, and `POST /files/:id/restore` brings it back. Pass `include_linked=true` to take along the files linked to it. For a raw file, those are the processed files made from it and the `run.json` saved with its capture, which a delete takes only when every raw file in that folder is being deleted. A restore also brings back the raw file a processed file was made from.
* `POST /instruments/:id/runs/:runId/files/delete` and `.../files/restore` take `file_ids` (1 to 100) and `include_linked`, and answer with a result for each file in the order you sent them. A file that can’t be changed, for example because it’s still processing or another file now has its name, gets a `409` result and doesn’t stop the others.
* `GET /instruments/:id/runs/:runId/files/linked?file_ids=1,2` lists the files that a delete would take along, so you can show them first. Add `for=restore` to list the deleted files a restore would bring back.

All of them need the `files:delete` scope. A file that’s queued or processing can’t be deleted until it finishes, and the files of a deleted run can’t be deleted or restored.

## Send notifications [#send-notifications]

`POST /notifications/dispatch` sends a short message to chosen people, with an optional link to a run. It needs a token with the `notifications:create` scope. Each person’s **Service notifications** setting decides whether the message appears in the notification bell, as a Slack direct message, or both. The message shows the token’s name as its sender. The generated [dispatch notifications](/docs/api/notifications/dispatchNotifications) page lists the request fields.

## Pagination and filtering [#pagination-and-filtering]

Run search (`GET /instrument-runs` and `GET /instruments/:id/runs`) and the lab notebook list (`GET /lab-notebooks`) return results in pages. They accept:

* `page`: the page number, starting at 1
* `per_page`: page size, 1 to 100 for runs and 1 to 200 for lab notebooks

Responses include pagination fields such as `page`, `per_page`, `total`, and `total_pages`.

Run report items use `offset` and `limit` (up to 200) instead. Their responses return `offset`, `limit`, and `total`.

Run search can also filter by:

* instrument
* date range
* who ran it (`ran_by`)
* lab notebook
* instrument-specific metadata

Each generated endpoint page in this **API** section lists the exact query parameters.

## Error responses [#error-responses]

Errors come back inside an `error` object:

```json
{
  "error": {
    "code": "NOT_FOUND",
    "message": "Instrument not found.",
    "details": null
  }
}
```

The common codes are:

* `VALIDATION_ERROR` (400)
* `UNAUTHORIZED` (401)
* `FORBIDDEN` (403)
* `NOT_FOUND` (404)
* `CONFLICT` (409)

A missing scope returns `code: "FORBIDDEN"` with a message that names the scope.

Feedback routes have two more codes. `LINEAR_UNAVAILABLE` (502) means Data Hub couldn’t reach Linear, where reports are stored. `FEEDBACK_NOT_CONFIGURED` (503) means no admin has connected Linear yet; see [Set up integrations](/docs/integrations#linear).

## MCP [#mcp]

The MCP server answers `GET` and `POST` requests at `/mcp/v1` over Streamable HTTP, outside `/api/v1`. Clients sign in with OAuth instead of a personal access token. They need the `read` scope to connect and the `write` scope to call any tool that changes data. See [MCP overview](/docs/mcp).

pages.title: MCP overview
pages.description: Connect an AI client to Data Hub over the Model Context Protocol, including OAuth sign-in, the read and write scopes, and per-client setup.
pages.markdown: # MCP overview (/docs/mcp) **For:** Everyone Data Hub runs a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server at `/mcp/v1`. MCP is an open standard that lets AI assistants such as Claude use outside tools. An assistant connected to Data Hub can look up instruments, runs, files, and watcher health. When the assistant first connects, it opens your browser so you can sign in. The [tools](/docs/mcp/tools), [prompts](/docs/mcp/prompts), and [resources](/docs/mcp/resources) catalogs are generated from the live server, so they match what your client finds when it connects. ## Authentication [#authentication] The MCP server signs you in with OAuth. You give your client only the endpoint URL, for example `https://datahub.example.com/mcp/v1`. The first connection opens your browser: Sign in to Data Hub with Google, unless you already have a session open. Read the **Authorize application** screen. It names the client, the host it redirects to, and the access it’s asking for. Choose **Allow**. Your client stores the access token it receives and renews it without asking again. **Allow** grants everything on the screen at once, with no checkbox for each permission. If any line looks wrong, choose **Deny**. ### Scopes [#scopes] MCP uses two scopes of its own, instead of the REST API’s token scopes such as `runs:read`: * **`read`**: needed to connect at all, and covers every read-only tool, resource, and prompt * **`write`**: also needed by tools that change something, including claiming runs, commenting, managing lab notebooks, requesting uploads, reprocessing, and deleting and restoring runs and files Most clients ask for both, because the server offers both. A client granted only `read` still connects and still reads. The first tool that changes something fails with a message naming the missing scope. Each entry in the [tools catalog](/docs/mcp/tools) lists the scope that the matching REST route needs, which tells you what data the tool touches. Over MCP, Data Hub checks only `read` and `write`. The client acts as you, with your role. Admin-only actions, such as deleting someone else’s comment, work over MCP only when you’re an admin. Claiming runs and sending feedback work because a signed-in person is behind the client, even though API tokens can’t do either. ## Connect a client [#connect-a-client] Examples use `https://datahub.example.com`; replace it with your deployment’s host. ### Claude Code [#claude-code] Register the server with [`claude mcp add`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp-quickstart). Run this in your terminal, not inside a `claude` session: ```bash claude mcp add --transport http --scope user data-hub https://datahub.example.com/mcp/v1 ``` Run `claude mcp list` to confirm that the server was added. Then start a session with `claude` and run `/mcp` to sign in. ### Claude Desktop [#claude-desktop] Add Data Hub through **Settings → Connectors → Add custom connector**, because the `claude_desktop_config.json` file handles only local servers. Paste `https://datahub.example.com/mcp/v1` as the URL, choose **Add**, then choose **Connect** to sign in. Leave the OAuth client fields under **Advanced settings** empty, because Data Hub registers clients when they connect. Claude connects to your server from Anthropic’s cloud, not from your own computer, so your deployment must be reachable from the public internet. You can’t add a deployment running on `localhost` this way; use Claude Code or Cursor for local work. ### Cursor [#cursor] Add the server to `.cursor/mcp.json` in your project, or to `~/.cursor/mcp.json` for every project: ```json { "mcpServers": { "data-hub": { "url": "https://datahub.example.com/mcp/v1" } } } ``` Open **Settings → Tools & MCP**. The server appears with a **Needs authentication** label; choose it to sign in through your browser. The tools appear once you approve access. ### Other clients [#other-clients] Any client that supports Streamable HTTP and the MCP authorization spec needs one setting: the URL `https://datahub.example.com/mcp/v1`. For local development, use `http://localhost:3000/mcp/v1` instead. Clients that support MCP but not OAuth can connect through [`mcp-remote`](https://www.npmjs.com/package/mcp-remote), which runs the browser sign-in for them. ## Questions about Data Hub [#questions-about-data-hub] The assistant can answer questions about Data Hub itself, such as how to install a watcher, what a run status means, or what changed last week. It searches the documentation or the [changelog](/docs/send-feedback#changelog), reads what fits, and links it in its answer. Three tools do this, and all need only the `read` scope: * `search_docs` returns up to five matching sections of the docs, each with a short excerpt and a link * `read_doc` returns one docs page, or one section of a page, as Markdown * `search_changelog` lists changelog entries by date, or finds them by topic, and returns each one in full with a link that opens it in the Changelog Ask it what changed this week, what’s new since a date, or when something changed. Dates are calendar days, and both the first and the last day count. The answers come from the docs and changelog that ship with your deployment, so they match the version you run. That includes a staging deployment that’s ahead of the published site. A change appears in the changelog once it has reached your deployment. Clients that let you attach resources by hand can also attach any docs page by its `datahub://docs/` address, for example `datahub://docs/manage-tokens`. The assistant reads the guides and the changelog. It doesn’t read the generated [API](/docs/api) endpoint pages or the [tools](/docs/mcp/tools), [prompts](/docs/mcp/prompts), and [resources](/docs/mcp/resources) catalogs, because the client already receives the catalog when it connects. When the docs don’t cover a question, the assistant says so and offers to [send feedback](#feedback) about the gap. ## Delete and restore files [#delete-and-restore-files] `delete_files` deletes up to 100 files of one run, and `restore_files` brings deleted files back. Both answer with a result for each file, so one that can’t be changed doesn’t stop the others. They change only the files you name, unless the assistant passes `includeLinked: true` to take along the files linked to them: for a raw file, the processed files made from it, and the `run.json` saved with its capture when every raw file in that folder is being deleted. The assistant is told to check with you before it does. A deleted file stays in storage and records who deleted it. `list_run_files` leaves deleted files out unless you pass `includeDeleted: true`, and then shows when each was deleted and by whom. `get_file` still finds a deleted file by its ID. A file that’s still being processed can’t be deleted until it finishes. `dismiss_file` is deprecated. It deletes one file by its ID, and it will be removed. Use `delete_files` instead. ## Interactive run reports [#interactive-run-reports] Clients that support MCP Apps, an extension of the Model Context Protocol, show the same interactive run report as the web app when the assistant calls `get_run_report`. The report includes image carousels, plate maps, and the Aunty plate with its well charts. Clients without MCP Apps support get the same data as text and describe it instead. ## Feedback [#feedback] The assistant can send [feedback about Data Hub](/docs/send-feedback) for you, for example after a tool call fails. It shows you the draft first and sends it only after you agree. Sending feedback needs only the `read` scope. The assistant can also list the reports you sent and read one in full, by report ID or by Linear issue ID such as `ENG-1476`. Until an admin [connects Linear](/docs/integrations#linear), the feedback tools return an error saying feedback isn’t set up. For a problem with one run’s data, ask the assistant to post a run comment instead. ## Instruments and their watcher [#instrument-connection] **For:** Developers and integrators `list_instruments` and `get_instrument` describe an instrument’s watcher with these fields: * `watcher`: the instrument’s one active watcher, or `null` when it has none * `connection`: whether new files can reach Data Hub. Its `state` is `online`, `restarting`, `connecting`, or `offline`, with a `reason` when it’s offline. * `pastWatcherCount`: how many deregistered watchers the instrument has had The fields match the REST API’s, in camelCase; see [Instruments and their watcher](/docs/api#instrument-connection). MCP signs you in with OAuth, not with a token that has chosen scopes. So `watcher` always includes where the watcher runs, as `list_watchers` and `get_watcher` do. Some older fields still come back with the values they had, but they’re deprecated. The [tools catalog](/docs/mcp/tools) marks each one and names the field to use instead. ## Machine-readable catalog [#machine-readable-catalog] **For:** Developers and integrators The catalog pages are built from a JSON document that you can fetch yourself: ```bash curl https://datahub.example.com/mcp/v1/schema.json ``` It lists every tool, prompt, and resource, with JSON Schema for arguments and for each tool’s response. The document needs no sign-in.

pages.description: Short definitions of the Data Hub vocabulary: instruments, watchers, runs, statuses, processing, and access.
pages.markdown:
# Concepts (/docs/concepts)



**For:** Everyone

Short definitions of the words these docs use, grouped by what they describe: the equipment, the data, the rules that turn files into runs, and who can do what.

## Instruments and watchers [#equipment-and-fleet]

### Instrument [#instrument]

A piece of lab equipment registered in Data Hub. Each instrument has an **instrument ID** made of lowercase words joined by hyphens, such as `akta-fplc` or `plate-sealer-a`, and a display name for people to read. The ID can’t change, because Data Hub uses it in the storage path of every file and to identify the instrument everywhere else.

An instrument has three states. The **Instruments** page groups them into a tab per state, and a status badge beside each name shows whether new files can reach Data Hub:

| State      | Shown as                                                                                 | Meaning                                                                      |
| ---------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `pending`  | **Pending** tab, with a **Pending** badge                                                | Registered but not yet confirmed by an admin. A watcher can’t upload for it. |
| `active`   | **Active** tab, with an **Online**, **Restarting**, **Connecting**, or **Offline** badge | Confirmed and accepting uploads.                                             |
| `inactive` | **Retired** tab, with a **Retired** badge                                                | Deactivated. No longer accepting uploads, but its runs stay browsable.       |

See [Set up an instrument](/docs/set-up-an-instrument), [Manage instruments](/docs/manage-instruments), and [Retire an instrument](/docs/retire-an-instrument).

### Instrument type [#instrument-type]

Separate from the instrument ID. The type tells Data Hub which [processor](#preprocessor) reads files from this instrument, so it decides what metadata, badges, and reports you get.

Admins set it from the instrument page: open the three-dot menu, choose **Edit details**, and pick a supported type. An instrument with no matching type still stores and serves raw files. It gets no extracted metadata and no processed files. See [Instrument data preprocessing](/docs/instrument-preprocessing).

### Instrument status [#instrument-status]

The badge beside an instrument’s name, in the instruments table, on Home, and in search results. It answers one question: will new files from this instrument show up? It’s meant for the people who use the instrument, so it leaves out the watcher’s details.

Hover over the badge, or focus it with the keyboard, for a one-sentence explanation. On an instrument’s page and in the instruments table, select the badge to open the instrument’s [watcher page](/docs/manage-watchers#the-watcher-page). In search results the whole row is the link, so the badge there is only a label.

| Badge          | When it shows                                                                                                                                                                   | What it means                                                                                             |
| -------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Pending**    | The instrument isn’t confirmed yet. This wins over everything below, even when its watcher is checking in.                                                                      | Waiting for an admin to confirm this instrument.                                                          |
| **Retired**    | The instrument is retired. This wins over the watcher’s state.                                                                                                                  | This instrument no longer takes new runs. Its runs stay browsable.                                        |
| **Connecting** | The watcher registered but hasn’t sent its first heartbeat, and 15 minutes haven’t passed since it registered or since an admin confirmed the instrument, whichever came later. | The watcher was set up recently and hasn’t checked in yet.                                                |
| **Restarting** | The watcher stopped for a Windows restart or an automatic update less than 15 minutes ago.                                                                                      | The instrument PC is restarting or the watcher is updating. Either takes a minute or two.                 |
| **Online**     | The watcher is watching and its last heartbeat is less than 5 minutes old.                                                                                                      | New files upload automatically, or when someone requests them if the instrument is in manual upload mode. |
| **Offline**    | Anything else: the instrument has no watcher, or its watcher was deregistered; the watcher is silent, never checked in, stopped by someone, or can’t find its watch folder.     | New files won’t appear right now. A notice on the instrument page says why.                               |

Only the watcher’s own state decides **Online**, **Restarting**, **Connecting**, and **Offline**. A pending change to the watcher’s settings never changes the badge. An instrument that is **Offline** shows a notice with the reason; see [Check that new files will arrive](/docs/browse-runs#check-files-will-arrive). If it stays **Offline** for 30 minutes, people who subscribe to it are notified; see [When an instrument goes offline](/docs/configure-notifications#instrument-offline).

### Watcher [#watcher]

The `data-hub-watcher` command-line program that runs on an instrument PC. It watches a folder, groups new files into runs, uploads them to cloud storage, and checks in with Data Hub every minute. Each instrument can have at most one active watcher at a time.

Each watcher registers with Data Hub and gets a registration ID for each [environment](#environment) it connects to. Each instrument’s watcher has its own page, under the instrument, with its activity, health, and settings. Deregistering a watcher is a [soft delete](#soft-delete): the instrument keeps it as a past watcher, and its history stays visible for auditing. See [Manage the watcher fleet](/docs/manage-watchers).

### Watcher status [#watcher-status]

The state a watcher’s page shows, and **Settings → Watchers** shows for admins, worked out from the watcher’s most recent [heartbeat](#heartbeat):

| Status                        | Meaning                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| ----------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Online**                    | A heartbeat arrived in the last 5 minutes.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| **Unresponsive**              | No heartbeat for more than 5 minutes: the process crashed, the PC is off, or the network is blocking Data Hub. A watcher that stopped for a Windows restart, a shutdown, or an automatic update gets 15 minutes instead. So does a new watcher that never sent a heartbeat, counted from when it registered or its instrument was confirmed; hovering over its badge says it never checked in. |
| **Stopped**                   | The watcher shut down cleanly and said so in its last heartbeat. A stop you chose, such as `data-hub-watcher service stop`, shows **Stopped** until the watcher starts again. A stop for a Windows restart, a shutdown, or an automatic update shows **Stopped** for 15 minutes, then **Unresponsive** if the watcher hasn’t returned.                                                         |
| **Waiting: folder not found** | The watcher is running and checking in, but its watch folder is missing, so it isn’t watching anything. It starts watching again once the folder is back. Watchers before 1.4.3 notice a missing folder only when they start.                                                                                                                                                                  |
| **Registered**                | The watcher registered but hasn’t sent its first heartbeat. It turns **Unresponsive** 15 minutes after it registered, or after an admin confirmed its instrument if that came later. It stays **Registered** while its instrument is pending, because the watcher doesn’t start until the instrument is confirmed.                                                                             |
| **Deregistered**              | A past watcher. Someone deregistered it, or retired its instrument. Its page is read-only.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |

Hover over a **Stopped** badge to see when it turns **Unresponsive** if the watcher doesn’t return. Watchers before 1.4.1 don’t tell Data Hub about a Windows restart, and watchers before 1.4.2 don’t mark a stop for an automatic update, so Data Hub doesn’t expect those watchers back.

An unresponsive watcher keeps its registration and history, so you can read its last events to work out what happened. See [Troubleshoot a watcher](/docs/troubleshoot-a-watcher).

Instruments show a simpler summary of this status, the [instrument status](#instrument-status) badge. An instrument has one active watcher, so the badge follows that watcher; an instrument with no active watcher reads **Offline**.

### Heartbeat [#heartbeat]

The check-in a watcher sends to Data Hub every 60 seconds. It reports the watcher’s version, instrument ID, watch folder, upload mode, upload counts, and how long it has been running. Data Hub uses it for **Last heartbeat** on the watcher’s page, the status badges, and the connectivity grid on the **Health** tab.

The same loop runs the hourly update check. The watcher checks for requested uploads separately, also once a minute, so a slow upload can’t delay a heartbeat. If a heartbeat fails to send, watcher 1.4.3 and later add its counts to the next one.

### Events [#events]

A watcher’s log of what it did and what went wrong, such as `watcher_started`, `run_reported`, `file_uploaded`, `update_succeeded`, and `error`. The watcher sends its events with each heartbeat. The watcher’s **Activity** tab shows them with a plain label and message, so you can see what happened on the PC without going to it. Data Hub records some events itself, such as `upload_requests_cancelled` when someone deletes a run that had requested uploads.

With watcher 1.4.3 and later, events that couldn’t be sent are kept on the PC and sent later with their original time, and an `events_dropped` event counts any that were lost. See [Activity](/docs/manage-watchers#activity) and [Troubleshoot a watcher](/docs/troubleshoot-a-watcher).

### Environment [#environment]

Which Data Hub deployment a watcher talks to: `staging`, `production`, or `preview`. A `preview` is a Vercel preview deployment, and you give the watcher its API URL by hand. Each environment has its own database, so one PC keeps a separate registration and local records for each environment and can switch between them.

## Data [#data]

### Run [#run]

The files from one acquisition, grouped together. The watcher gives each file a **run ID** using its [run detection](#run-detection) rule, then reports the run to Data Hub. The first file creates the run, and later files with the same run ID join it. Spaces at the start or end of a run ID are ignored, so `RUN001` with a space after it is the same run as `RUN001`.

### Run status [#run-status]

How far a run’s files have got from the instrument to the web app. From the most urgent down, a run shows **Failed**, **Stalled**, **Upload failed**, **Waiting to upload**, **Uploaded**, **Queued**, **Processing**, **Not uploaded**, **Completed**, or **Empty**. When a run’s files are in different states, the run shows the first of these that applies.

Filter by status under **Add filter** on any run list. [What each run status means](/docs/browse-runs#run-status) explains each one.

### File and file category [#file-and-file-category]

Every file in a run has a category, shown as a label in the run’s files table:

* **Raw**: what the instrument wrote, uploaded unchanged
* **Processed**: what a [processor](#preprocessor) made from a raw file, such as a CSV of well values, a contrast-adjusted PNG, or a preview JPG

Both categories download the same way, and file filters on the run page work on this label. See [Download files](/docs/browse-runs#download-files).

### Processor [#preprocessor]

The server-side code that reads a raw file, extracts metadata, and writes processed files. It runs in an AWS Lambda when a file arrives in raw storage, or when you choose **Reprocess**. Reprocessing starts at most 10 files at a time and queues the rest; see [How reprocessing is queued](/docs/browse-runs#reprocess-queue). Which processor runs depends on the [instrument type](#instrument-type), and not every type has one. Per-type inputs and outputs are in [Instrument data preprocessing](/docs/instrument-preprocessing).

### Run archive [#run-archive]

The zip that **Download all** builds for a run. It covers the run’s active files and respects any file filter you have applied. Large archives build in the background as an archive job, so the first request can return a wait time rather than a file.

### Attribution [#attribution]

The record of who ran a run. Choose **Claim** on a run to put your name on it. You can only claim runs for yourself, and API tokens can’t claim runs. Claims fill **My runs** and the “ran by” filters, and claiming a run subscribes you to its comments. See [Claim who ran it](/docs/browse-runs#claim-who-ran-it).

### Lab notebook [#lab-notebook]

A Data Hub record that stands for one notebook page, such as a Notion or Google Docs page. It has a name, an optional description and owner, and the runs added to it from any instrument. A run can be in several lab notebooks, and anyone signed in can create lab notebooks and add or remove runs. See [Lab notebooks](/docs/lab-notebooks).

## Turning files into runs [#turning-files-into-runs]

### Run detection [#run-detection]

The rule that gives each file a run ID. There are two kinds:

* **Prefix**: a pattern (a regular expression) picks the run ID out of the file name. The default `^([^_]+)` takes everything before the first underscore, so `RUN001_data.csv` → `RUN001`
* **Directory**: each folder inside the watch folder is its own run, so `RUN001/data.csv` → `RUN001`

The full set of presets, and how to write your own pattern, is in the [Configuration reference](/docs/configuration-reference#run-detection).

### Stability period [#stability-period]

How many seconds a file must stay unchanged, with the same size and modification time, before the watcher treats it as fully written and ready to upload. The default is 5 seconds; raise it for instruments that write large files slowly. [Wait until writes finish](/docs/configure-run-detection#wait-until-writes-finish) covers files that keep changing or that the instrument keeps open.

### Upload mode [#upload-mode]

How files get from the instrument to cloud storage:

* **auto**: files upload as soon as they’re found and stable. The watcher also uploads files someone requests from the run page
* **manual**: the watcher reports runs but uploads a file only after someone requests it in the web app. It checks for requests once a minute. Use this when someone must approve which files leave the instrument PC

### Initial scan [#initial-scan]

What the watcher does with files already in the watch folder the first time it connects to an environment. In `production` it uploads them (`full`). In `staging` and `preview` it records them and skips them (`new-only`), so test environments don’t fill up with old files. See the [Configuration reference](/docs/configuration-reference#initial-scan).

### Dismiss [#dismiss]

Dismissing a file that the watcher found but didn’t upload, or one whose upload failed, tells the watcher not to upload it. A dismissed file stays dismissed, even if the watcher reports it again. Dismissing differs from deleting: the file never reached Data Hub storage, so there’s nothing to restore.

[Approve or dismiss files](/docs/manage-watchers#approving-manual-uploads) explains how, and when a new file at the same path shows up again.

### Soft delete [#soft-delete]

Data Hub marks things deleted instead of erasing them, so their history stays for auditing. Deleting a run hides it from run lists without removing its stored files, and **Show deleted runs** brings it back into view. It also cancels any uploads that were requested for the run’s files, and restoring the run doesn’t bring them back. Deregistering a watcher keeps its events and heartbeats. Anyone signed in can restore a deleted run from the run page.

## People and access [#people-and-access]

### Role [#role]

Data Hub has two roles, **Member** and **Admin**. Members sign in, browse instruments and runs, claim and comment on runs, send feedback, and read the token list. Admins can also confirm and update instruments, create and revoke tokens, promote or demote other users, delete any comment, review feedback, and manage integrations. Full permission tables are in [Security and permissions](/docs/security#roles).

### Personal access token [#personal-access-token]

A secret starting with `dhub_` that the watcher and scripts send to sign in to the Data Hub API. Each token has permission [scopes](#scope), and only admins create and revoke tokens. Data Hub shows the full token once, when it’s created.

A token acts as itself, under its own name. Comments it posts and runs it deletes show the token’s name with a key icon, not a person. Because a token isn’t a person, it can’t claim runs or send feedback. See [Issue and revoke tokens](/docs/manage-tokens).

### Scope [#scope]

A permission a token has, such as `runs:read`. Data Hub refuses a token’s request with `403 FORBIDDEN` when the token lacks the scope that request needs. People signed in to the web app have every scope, so scopes only limit tokens. The scope table is in [Security and permissions](/docs/security#token-scopes).

### Feedback report [#feedback-report]

A bug report or feature request about Data Hub itself, sent from the account menu or by an AI assistant. Each report is stored as an issue in your workspace’s Linear, and its status (Open, Resolved, or Declined) follows that issue. See [Send feedback and see what’s new](/docs/send-feedback).
