# Architecture (/docs/architecture)



**For:** Engineers and operators

Data Hub has four components that work together through S3, a REST API, and a shared Python library. This page explains how they fit together. The [first-time deployment guide](https://github.com/Arcadia-Science/data-hub/blob/production/docs/developer/first-time-deployment.md) in the data-hub developer docs explains how to deploy them.

## System overview [#system-overview]

<Mermaid
  chart="flowchart LR
    W[Watcher] -->|raw files| S3[S3 raw]
    S3 -->|trigger| L[Lambda]
    W -->|heartbeats, runs| API[API]
    L -->|processed data| Sproc[S3 processed]
    L -->|results| API
    L -->|run-zip multipart| Sarc[S3 archives]
    API -->|presigned URLs| S3
    API -->|presigned URLs| Sarc
    API -->|build archive| L
    API --> DB[(PostgreSQL)]
    API --> UI[Web app]
    MCP[MCP clients] -->|tools, resources| API"
/>

## Components [#components]

| Component      | Package            | Description                                                                                    |
| -------------- | ------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Web app        | `data-hub-web`     | Next.js web app, REST API, and MCP server. Deployed on Vercel.                                 |
| Lambda         | `data-hub-lambda`  | AWS Lambda function that runs instrument-specific processing when a file is uploaded to S3.    |
| Watcher        | `data-hub-watcher` | CLI on lab instrument PCs. Finds new files, uploads them to S3, and reports status to the API. |
| Shared library | `data-hub-shared`  | Shared Python library: S3 utilities, instrument enums, and test infrastructure.                |

## Data flow [#data-flow]

### Automatic upload (auto mode) [#automatic-upload-auto-mode]

1. A lab instrument writes output files to a watch folder.
2. The **watcher** finds new files through file system events and waits until each one stops changing.
3. It groups files into runs and reports each run to the **API**.
4. It uploads raw files to **S3** at the key `{instrument_id}/{run_id}/{filename}`.
5. The S3 upload starts the **Lambda**.
6. The Lambda passes the file to the instrument’s processor, which reads it. When the deployment turns the option on, some processors read large files from a read-only mount of the raw bucket instead of downloading them. This covers processors that read a file in pieces, for files of 1 GiB or more or too large for the Lambda’s disk.
7. The Lambda creates or updates the run and its files through the **API**, which sends a **Slack** notification once for each new run.
8. People view the run in the **web app**.

### Manual upload (manual mode) [#manual-upload-manual-mode]

Steps 1–3 are the same, but the watcher doesn’t upload right away:

4. The server adds files to an upload queue.
5. Once a minute, the watcher checks the queue and uploads the files someone requested.
6. Steps 5–8 from auto mode follow.

Auto-mode watchers check the same queue, so **Upload** on a run page works for them too.

## Key design decisions [#key-design-decisions]

* **S3 is the integration boundary.** The watcher and the Lambda never talk to each other. The watcher writes files to S3, and the Lambda reads them from there.
* **API-driven coordination.** The watcher registers with the API, syncs its YAML config, and sends heartbeats. Watcher health in the web app and the upload queue both depend on those calls.
* **Pre-signed URLs from the API.** The web app creates pre-signed S3 upload and download URLs. File contents then move directly to and from S3 without passing through the API. On Vercel, the app assumes an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role through OpenID Connect (OIDC), so it needs no long-lived AWS keys.
* **Lambda-built run archives.** **Download all** hands the work to the Lambda, which zips the files into a separate archives bucket with an S3 multipart upload. The web app then redirects the browser to a short-lived pre-signed URL. File contents never pass through Vercel.
* **Shared library for contracts.** Instrument IDs, S3 utilities, and environment config live in `data-hub-shared`, so the Lambda and the watcher stay consistent.
* **MCP for AI access.** The web app serves an MCP endpoint at `/mcp/v1` that offers tools, resources, and prompts to AI clients. Clients sign in with OAuth through the same Better Auth instance that signs people in to the web app. An agent therefore acts as the person who approved it. See [MCP overview](/docs/mcp).

## Branch and environment strategy [#branch-and-environment-strategy]

| Branch       | Purpose                                         |
| ------------ | ----------------------------------------------- |
| `staging`    | Pre-production. Pull requests merge here first. |
| `production` | Live. Changes are promoted from `staging`.      |

Feature branches target `staging` through pull requests (PRs). Continuous integration (CI) runs on every PR and on merges to both branches. Merges to `staging` and `production` deploy each component to its environment automatically. Staging and production are separate deployments with separate databases.

# Watcher configuration (/docs/configuration-reference)



**For:** Lab operators

This page is the complete reference for the watcher’s configuration. It covers the `config.yaml` schema, where the watcher’s files live, and the environment variables that affect it. It also covers the behavior those fields control: run detection, upload modes, and the initial scan.

## File locations [#file-locations]

The watcher keeps all its files under `~/.data-hub/`:

| Path                                   | Contents                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| -------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `~/.data-hub/config.yaml`              | The main config, described below. Use `--config` or `DATA_HUB_CONFIG_PATH` to read a different file.                                                                                                     |
| `~/.data-hub/.env.<environment>`       | The API key for an environment (for example `.env.staging`, `.env.production`, `.env.preview`). The watcher still loads the older `~/.data-hub/.env`, but the file for the environment takes precedence. |
| `~/.data-hub/watcher-<environment>.db` | The watcher’s SQLite state for one environment: uploaded files, runs, detected files, and the baseline.                                                                                                  |
| `~/.data-hub/watcher.log`              | Rotating log (10 MB × 5 backups). On Windows: `C:\ProgramData\DataHubWatcher\watcher.log`.                                                                                                               |
| `~/.data-hub/upgrade-worker.log`       | Transcript of Windows upgrades that run through `uv tool`.                                                                                                                                               |

## Environment variables [#environment-variables]

| Variable                     | Purpose                                                                                                                 |
| ---------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `DATA_HUB_API_KEY`           | Supplies the API key, so `init` doesn’t ask for it. The watcher saves it into the `.env` file for the environment.      |
| `DATA_HUB_CONFIG_PATH`       | Reads the config from a different path, like `--config`.                                                                |
| `DATA_HUB_WATCHER_LOG_LEVEL` | Set to `DEBUG` in the service’s `.env` file to turn on debug logging without a reinstall. Needs watcher 1.4.2 or later. |

## `config.yaml` [#configyaml]

```yaml
version: 1
environment: production          # "staging", "production", or "preview"
api_base_urls:                   # one API base URL per environment
  production: https://datahub.example.org/api/v1
watcher_ids:                     # one registration id per environment
  production: your_watcher_id    # assigned by the API when the watcher registers
initial_scan: null               # null (default), "full", or "new-only"
instrument:
  id: akta-fplc                  # kebab-case instrument ID
  watch_directory: /path/to/data
  file_patterns:
    - "*.csv"
    - "*.xlsx"
  enabled: true
  upload_mode: auto              # "auto" or "manual"
  stability_period_seconds: 5    # 1–300
  max_stability_wait_seconds: 300  # 1–86400; must be >= stability_period_seconds
  upload_parallelism: 4          # 1–32
  run_detection:
    pattern: '^([^/]+)/'         # regex with one capture group (run ID)
    recursive: true
```

### Field reference [#field-reference]

An admin can also change the fields marked **Web** from the web app, and the watcher saves those changes to this file. See [Change a watcher’s settings](/docs/manage-watchers#change-a-watchers-config).

| Field                                   | Type          | Web | Description                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| --------------------------------------- | ------------- | --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `version`                               | int           |     | Config schema version. Currently `1`.                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| `environment`                           | enum          |     | `staging`, `production`, or `preview`.                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| `api_base_urls`                         | map           |     | One API base URL per environment, keyed by environment name. Set at `init`, or by `config set-environment --api-base-url`. A config with a single top-level `api_base_url` is moved into this map on load.                                 |
| `watcher_ids`                           | map           |     | One watcher registration ID per environment. The API assigns them.                                                                                                                                                                         |
| `initial_scan`                          | enum \| null  |     | `null` (the environment’s default), `full`, or `new-only`. See [Initial scan](#initial-scan).                                                                                                                                              |
| `instrument.id`                         | string        |     | Kebab-case instrument ID. It never changes, and it starts every storage key.                                                                                                                                                               |
| `instrument.watch_directory`            | string        | Web | Absolute path of the watch folder, where the instrument writes its files.                                                                                                                                                                  |
| `instrument.file_patterns`              | string\[]     | Web | Glob patterns matched against each file’s name, case-sensitive. The watcher uploads only matching files. 1–50 patterns.                                                                                                                    |
| `instrument.enabled`                    | bool          |     | Whether the watcher processes this instrument.                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| `instrument.upload_mode`                | enum          | Web | `auto` or `manual`. See [Upload modes](#upload-modes).                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| `instrument.stability_period_seconds`   | int (1–300)   | Web | Seconds a file must stay unchanged before the watcher treats it as finished. Default `5`.                                                                                                                                                  |
| `instrument.max_stability_wait_seconds` | int (1–86400) | Web | Seconds a file that’s still changing may stay pending before the watcher gives up on it and records a `stability_timeout` event. Must be at least `stability_period_seconds`. Default `300` (5 minutes).                                   |
| `instrument.upload_parallelism`         | int (1–32)    | Web | The most uploads the watcher runs at the same time. Each part of a large file counts as one upload, so a single file can use several connections. Default `4`. Raise it on PCs with a fast network link; lower it on a slow or shared one. |
| `instrument.run_detection.pattern`      | regex         | Web | Regular expression with one capture group, applied to each file’s path relative to `watch_directory`.                                                                                                                                      |
| `instrument.run_detection.recursive`    | bool          | Web | `true` also watches subfolders; `false` watches only the top level. Default `true`.                                                                                                                                                        |

<Callout type="info">
  A config written by an older watcher has a single top-level `watcher_id` and `api_base_url`. When the watcher loads that config, it moves both values into `watcher_ids` and `api_base_urls` under the active environment. It removes the old fields the next time it saves the config, so you don’t need to edit anything.
</Callout>

## Run detection [#run-detection]

The watcher applies the `pattern` regular expression (regex) with `re.search` to each file’s path relative to `watch_directory`, with backslashes changed to `/`. Capture group 1 is the run ID, and the pattern must have exactly one capture group. In YAML, put patterns in single quotes so backslash sequences like `\d` don’t need escaping.

The web app also checks patterns in JavaScript, so it refuses syntax that only Python supports, such as named groups (`(?P<name>…)`). Use a plain capture group instead.

The `init` wizard offers these presets, or you can enter your own regex:

| Preset                 | Pattern                        | Recursive | Run ID is…                                                        |
| ---------------------- | ------------------------------ | --------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Filename prefix        | `^([^_]+)`                     | no        | everything before the first `_`: `RUN001_data.csv` → `RUN001`     |
| Top subdirectory       | `^([^/]+)/`                    | yes       | the top-level folder: `RUN001/data.csv` → `RUN001`                |
| Deepest subdirectory   | `([^/]+)/[^/]+$`               | yes       | the immediate parent folder: `plate-a/well-b/data.csv` → `well-b` |
| Timestamp subdirectory | `(?:^\|/)(\d{8}_\d{6}_\d{3})/` | yes       | a `YYYYMMDD_HHMMSS_fff` folder anywhere in the path               |
| Filename stem          | `^(?:.+/)?([^/]+?)\.[^/.]+$`   | no        | the filename without its extension (each file is its own run)     |

## Upload modes [#upload-modes]

* **`auto`**: files upload to cloud storage as soon as the watcher detects their run. The watcher also uploads files requested from the run page. It retries an upload that didn’t finish the next time it starts, for up to three starts.
* **`manual`**: the watcher reports runs without uploading. The server decides which files to upload through a queue that the watcher checks once a minute. Use it when someone must approve uploads. See [Manage the watcher fleet → Approving manual uploads](/docs/manage-watchers#approving-manual-uploads).

Files of 100 MB or more upload in 64 MB parts, and the parts of one file upload at the same time. The watcher can upload files larger than 5 GB. Several queued files can also upload at the same time. Together, parts and files stay within `instrument.upload_parallelism` uploads at once, so a large file doesn’t depend on a single connection.

## Initial scan [#initial-scan]

The first time the watcher enters an environment, through `init` or `config set-environment`, `initial_scan` decides what happens to files already in the watch folder. The default depends on the environment:

* `production` → `full`: the watcher uploads the existing files, because production is the deployment your lab uses for its real data.
* `staging` and `preview` → `new-only`: the watcher records the files already on disk as a baseline and skips them. It uploads only files created afterwards.

So a new `init` on `staging` or `preview` doesn’t upload a PC’s history. Set `initial_scan: full` to upload it anyway, for example to fill staging on purpose. Set `initial_scan: new-only` on production to skip its backlog.

Upgrading an existing watcher doesn’t change any of this. The watcher’s state database for that environment already lists files it uploaded or detected, so the watcher doesn’t record a new baseline.

## Switching environments [#switching-environments]

One PC can move between `staging`, `production`, and `preview`. These are separate deployments with separate databases, so each keeps its own registration in `watcher_ids` and its own credentials in `~/.data-hub/.env.<environment>`.

```sh
# Switch to staging (reuses a stored registration, or registers one).
data-hub-watcher config set-environment staging

# Point at a preview deployment (the base URL is required).
data-hub-watcher config set-environment preview \
  --api-base-url https://data-hub-git-my-branch.vercel.app/api/v1
```

A switch does these things:

* checks that it can reach the target API with the key
* reuses the watcher ID stored for that environment, or registers a new one
* sends the config to the new environment
* records a `watcher_stopped` event in the old environment, with a message that names the environment it switched to

A running `watch` process or service keeps using the old environment until you restart it. On Windows, run `service stop && service start`; elsewhere, restart `watch`.

# Watcher CLI (/docs/cli-reference)



**For:** Lab operators

This page lists the flags and subcommands for `data-hub-watcher`, generated from the Click CLI in the watcher package. For step-by-step guides, see [Install and update the watcher](/docs/install-the-watcher), [Run as a Windows service](/docs/windows-service), and [Roll out watcher releases](/docs/watcher-releases).

## Command reference [#command-reference]

This catalog comes from the installed CLI’s help text and lists every command, argument, and option.

## Global flags

These options apply to every `data-hub-watcher` command (watcher 1.4.5).

**Flags**

- `--config PATH` `path` env: `DATA_HUB_CONFIG_PATH` — Override config file path.
- `--verbose` `boolean` — Enable debug logging.
- `--version` `boolean` — Show the version and exit.

## `data-hub-watcher config`

View and manage the watcher config file.

### `data-hub-watcher config edit`

Re-prompt each config field with current values as defaults.

### `data-hub-watcher config open`

Open the config file in your editor, then re-validate.

**Flags**

- `--editor` `text` — Editor command (e.g. --editor code).

### `data-hub-watcher config path`

Print the resolved config file path.

### `data-hub-watcher config set-environment`

Switch the watcher to a different API environment.

**Arguments**

- `ENVIRONMENT` (required) `choice (staging | production | preview)`

**Flags**

- `--api-base-url` `text` — API base URL for the target environment. Required the first time you switch to an environment; reused from config on later switches.
- `--api-key` `text` — API key for the target environment.
- `--show-key` `boolean` — Echo the API key as typed (useful on Windows terminals).
- `--no-register` `boolean` — Fail instead of registering a new watcher if none is stored for the target env.

### `data-hub-watcher config show`

Pretty-print the current config.

### `data-hub-watcher config validate`

Validate the config file (offline, no network calls).

## `data-hub-watcher init`

Interactive setup wizard + API registration.

**Flags**

- `--show-key` `boolean` — Echo the API key as it is typed/pasted. Useful on Windows terminals where hidden input is unreliable for paste.

## `data-hub-watcher self-update`

Check the server for a newer watcher release and upgrade in place. Designed for unattended use — schedule via Windows Task Scheduler (e.g. weekly) so lab PCs converge on the latest published version without operator intervention.

**Flags**

- `--check` `boolean` — Print the server-reported target version without performing the upgrade.
- `--force` `boolean` — Run the upgrade subprocess even if the local version already matches the target.

## `data-hub-watcher service`

Windows service management.

### `data-hub-watcher service install`

Install the watcher as a Windows service.

**Flags**

- `--env-path FILE` `file` — Path to the .env file. Defaults to ~/.data-hub/.env.<environment>.

### `data-hub-watcher service reinstall`

Stop, uninstall, install, and start the watcher Windows service. Useful after upgrading the watcher wheel from an Administrator shell so the SCM picks up the new ``data_hub_watcher.service`` entrypoint without needing four separate ``service`` invocations.

**Flags**

- `--env-path FILE` `file` — Path to the .env file. Defaults to ~/.data-hub/.env.<environment>.

### `data-hub-watcher service start`

Start the watcher Windows service.

### `data-hub-watcher service status`

Show the watcher Windows service status.

### `data-hub-watcher service stop`

Stop the watcher Windows service.

### `data-hub-watcher service uninstall`

Uninstall the watcher Windows service.

## `data-hub-watcher state`

Inspect or reset the local upload history.

### `data-hub-watcher state forget`

Forget upload history under a folder so those files are reported again. Clears every state database a watcher on this PC can open: the one `watch` uses and the one the Windows service uses. Stop the watcher first. It only scans the disk when it starts, so a running watcher will not pick the forgotten files back up.

**Flags**

- `--prefix` (required) `text` — Folder under the watch directory to forget, e.g. alice/.
- `--yes` `boolean` — Skip the confirmation prompt.

## `data-hub-watcher upload`

Upload files to Data Hub (manual trigger). One-shot mode: pass both --file and --run-id to upload a single file. Queue mode:    omit both to process the server-side upload queue.

**Flags**

- `--file PATH` `path` — Specific file to upload.
- `--run-id` `text` — Associate upload with a specific run.
- `--dry-run` `boolean` — Log what would be uploaded without uploading.

## `data-hub-watcher watch`

Start watching for new files. If the watcher's registration was deleted on Data Hub, a running watcher stops and exits with code 3, and one that is started refuses to start and exits with code 3 as well. Either way it says to run 'data-hub-watcher init' to register again.

**Flags**

- `--dry-run` `boolean` — Validate and log but don't start monitoring.

## Interactive setup notes [#interactive-setup-notes]

`init` and `config edit` ask for values in the terminal. Those prompts aren’t CLI flags, so they don’t appear in the catalog.

API keys must start with `dhub_`. The watcher removes zero-width and non-breaking space characters, which some Windows clipboards add to a pasted key. See [Install and update the watcher → Configure](/docs/install-the-watcher#configure).

## Upload examples [#upload-examples]

Upload files once, without running the watcher:

```sh
data-hub-watcher upload --file /path/to/file.csv --run-id RUN001
data-hub-watcher upload
data-hub-watcher upload --dry-run
```

Pass both `--file` and `--run-id` to upload one file. Leave out both to work through the server’s upload queue, the way a manual-mode watcher does.

## Switching environments [#switching-environments]

`config set-environment` can take `--api-base-url`, `--api-key`, `--show-key`, and `--no-register`, and so can `config edit` when the environment changes. Switching to a preview deployment needs `--api-base-url` the first time. See [Watcher configuration → Switching environments](/docs/configuration-reference#switching-environments).

## Windows service notes [#windows-service-notes]

`service` commands need Windows and the `windows-service` install extra. Use `--env-path` on `service install` and `service reinstall` when the service should load a `.env` file other than the default one. [Run as a Windows service](/docs/windows-service) has the full details.

## Self-update examples [#self-update-examples]

```sh
data-hub-watcher self-update
data-hub-watcher self-update --check
data-hub-watcher self-update --force
```

How the upgrade works depends on how you installed the watcher. See [Install and update the watcher → Manual update](/docs/install-the-watcher#manual-update-self-update).

pages.markdown:
# Security and permissions (/docs/security)



**For:** Administrators and developers

This page explains who can do what in Data Hub: the two roles, the scopes that limit what each token can do, and how to handle tokens safely. To create or revoke a token, see [Issue and revoke tokens](/docs/manage-tokens).

## Authentication [#authentication]

The API accepts three kinds of credentials:

* **Session cookies**: the web app uses these after someone signs in with Google through [Better Auth](https://www.better-auth.com). Scopes apply only to tokens, so a signed-in session passes every scope check.
* **Bearer tokens**: personal access tokens (`dhub_…`) that the watcher, the Lambda, and scripts send as `Authorization: Bearer dhub_your_token_here`. A token acts as itself, under its own name; see [How tokens act](#how-tokens-act).
* **OAuth access tokens**: Data Hub gives these to MCP clients after you sign in and approve a consent screen. See [MCP access](#mcp-access).

Data Hub stores only a SHA-256 hash of each token. It shows the token itself once, when it’s created.

### Who can sign in [#who-can-sign-in]

Any Google account that finishes signing in becomes a member of your deployment. Data Hub doesn’t check anything itself: it has no invitations, no email allowlist, and no email-domain check. The first successful sign-in creates the member record.

You limit who can sign in on the Google side instead, in the OAuth client your team creates when it deploys Data Hub. A consent screen set to **Internal** accepts only accounts in your Google Workspace organization. A consent screen set to **External** accepts any Google account, including personal ones. Engineers make that choice when they [create the OAuth client](https://github.com/Arcadia-Science/data-hub/blob/production/docs/developer/first-time-deployment.md#create-a-google-oauth-client).

Data Hub accepts 10 Google sign-in attempts per minute from one IP address and rejects the rest.

Every new member starts with the member role, never admin. [Choose the first admins](/docs/manage-members#first-admin-bootstrap) explains how the first admins get the role.

### Session lifetime [#session-lifetime]

Signing in stores a session in the database and sets a signed cookie. The session expires 7 days after its last refresh. The web app refreshes it at most once a day, so a session in daily use doesn’t expire on its own.

The cookie also holds a signed copy of the session for 5 minutes, so most page loads don’t need the database. Requests read the copy instead of the database row. A change made directly in the database, such as deleting a session, takes effect when the copy expires, not on the next request.

Removing someone’s access on the Google side, for example by removing them from your Workspace organization, blocks their next sign-in. Any session they already have open keeps working until it expires. To cut them off sooner, delete that user’s rows from the `session` table. Signing out from the sidebar ends the session immediately.

## Roles [#roles]

Data Hub has two roles: member and admin.

A **member** can:

* sign in to the web app
* view instruments, runs, files, and the token list
* claim runs
* comment, and edit or delete their own comments
* create, edit, delete, and restore lab notebooks, and add runs to them or remove runs from them
* delete and restore runs
* send feedback and see the reports they sent

Members can’t create or revoke tokens, confirm or update instruments, or manage other users.

An **admin** can do everything a member can, and also:

* confirm and update instruments
* change watcher configs
* create and revoke tokens
* promote and demote other users
* delete any run comment
* review every feedback report
* manage **Settings → Integrations**
* set watcher release versions

The first admin comes from the `ADMIN_EMAILS` environment variable, a comma-separated list that ignores case. Data Hub promotes the people on that list every time they sign in. After that, any admin can promote others from **Settings → Members**. Admins can’t demote themselves, which keeps the last admin from removing their own role.

### Admin-gated operations [#admin-gated-operations]

Some actions that change data need the admin role, as well as a scope or instead of one:

* `PATCH /api/v1/instruments/:id`: a signed-in person must be an admin. Tokens still need only `instruments:write`, so the watcher and the Lambda aren’t affected.
* `POST /api/v1/tokens` and `DELETE /api/v1/tokens/:id`: admins only, from a signed-in session. Tokens can’t manage other tokens.
* `GET /api/v1/users` and `PATCH /api/v1/users/:userId`: admins only, from a signed-in session. **Settings → Members** uses these routes.
* `/api/v1/settings/integrations/*`: admins only, from a signed-in session. **Settings → Integrations** uses these routes.
* `POST /api/v1/watchers/:watcherId/config-revisions`: a signed-in person must be an admin. A token must list `watchers:admin` explicitly, so older `*` and `watchers:write` tokens get `403`. The MCP `update_watcher_config` tool is admin-only.
* `DELETE` on a run comment: admins can delete any comment. Everyone else, tokens included, can delete only their own.
* `GET /api/v1/feedback`: admins get every report, and members get only the reports they sent.

### Remote watcher config [#remote-watcher-config]

An admin, or a token that lists `watchers:admin` explicitly, can change a watcher’s watch folder to any folder the watcher’s account can read on the instrument PC. The watcher then uploads matching files from that folder. Grant admin and `watchers:admin` only to people and automation you trust with that access.

Data Hub records every change and who made it, in the **History** on the watcher’s **Settings** tab. Data Hub can’t change the watcher’s environment, API URL, token, or instrument ID.

## How tokens act [#how-tokens-act]

A personal access token acts as itself, not as the admin who created it. Data Hub records everything a token does under the token’s name. The web app shows that name with a key icon on:

* comments
* deleted runs
* retired instruments
* removed watchers
* notifications sent through the API

A revoked token keeps its record, so its name stays visible and is marked **(revoked)**.

Claiming runs, sending feedback, and reviewing feedback need a signed-in person, because a token isn’t a person. Tokens can’t do them, whatever their scopes. AI assistants can, because they sign in as the person who approved them; see [MCP access](#mcp-access).

The routes that the watcher and the Lambda call work the other way round. They accept only tokens and return `401 Unauthorized` to a browser session, so a signed-in member can’t act as a watcher. These routes cover:

* watcher registration and heartbeats
* upload links
* file updates
* run creation and updates
* instrument creation

A token that registered a watcher can change runs and files only on instruments whose current watcher it registered. On any other instrument, it gets `403 Forbidden` when it tries to:

* change runs, uploads, files, comments, lab notebook memberships, or download archives
* send a notification about a run

That token also can’t rename, retype, retire, or confirm any instrument, or remove or reconfigure any watcher, its own included, because the watcher itself never does those things. A few more rules apply:

* A token whose watchers were all deregistered can’t change any instrument’s runs or files until it registers a watcher again.
* The Lambda’s token registered no watcher, so it works on every instrument.
* These limits cover changes only. Reads follow the token’s scopes, and the **Watcher** preset has no scope that reads runs or files.
* Once an older token has registered a watcher, its `*` or coarse `:write` scope doesn’t let it read runs or files either; see [Tokens with older scopes](#older-scopes).

Tokens keep working when the admin who created them leaves. Revoke a departing person’s tokens yourself; see [When someone leaves](/docs/manage-tokens#when-someone-leaves).

## Token scopes [#token-scopes]

Every personal access token has a list of permission **scopes**. Data Hub rejects a token request with `403 FORBIDDEN` when the token doesn’t have the scope the route needs. Give each token only the scopes it needs.

| Scope                  | Grants                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| ---------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `instruments:read`     | Read instruments, the status on the web app’s home page, and each instrument’s watcher state and file patterns. Where the watcher runs (hostname, operating system, version, watch folder, and other instruments on the same computer) needs `watchers:read` too |
| `instruments:write`    | Create instruments and edit their configuration                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| `runs:read`            | Read and search runs, their files, comments, attributions, and lab notebooks                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| `runs:create`          | Create run records                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| `runs:update`          | Update run metadata                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| `runs:delete`          | Soft delete and restore runs                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| `runs:reprocess`       | Run the processing workflow for a run again                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| `runs:upload`          | Request pre-signed S3 URLs to upload files to a run                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| `runs:comment`         | Post run comments as this token, and edit or delete the ones it posted                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| `lab-notebooks:write`  | Create, edit, delete, and restore lab notebooks, and add runs to them or remove runs from them. Tokens made before this scope was renamed from `runs:link` keep it                                                                                               |
| `files:read`           | Read file metadata and download files and run archives                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| `files:create`         | Register file records against a run. Each record must point at its own file in that run’s folder in S3                                                                                                                                                           |
| `files:update`         | Update file metadata and upload state                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| `files:delete`         | Delete and restore files in a run                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| `files:reprocess`      | Run the processing workflow for a file again                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| `watchers:read`        | Read watcher status, heartbeats, and upload queues, and where each instrument’s watcher runs (hostname, operating system, version, watch folder)                                                                                                                 |
| `watchers:report`      | Register, send heartbeats and events, and push watcher config                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| `watchers:admin`       | Delete watchers and change their config, including which folder on the instrument PC they upload from. Changing config needs this scope listed explicitly; older `*` and `watchers:write` tokens can’t                                                           |
| `archive-jobs:read`    | Read run-archive job status                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| `archive-jobs:write`   | Update run-archive job status (Lambda callback)                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| `notifications:create` | Send notifications to people, optionally about a run                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| `*`                    | Matches every scope, or only the **Watcher** preset’s scopes on a token that has registered a watcher. Kept only for older tokens; rejected on new tokens                                                                                                        |

Two presets select the scopes a common client needs:

* **Watcher**: `instruments:read`, `instruments:write`, `watchers:read`, `watchers:report`, `runs:create`, `runs:update`, `runs:upload`, and `files:update`
* **Lambda**: `instruments:read`, `runs:read`, `runs:create`, `runs:update`, `files:create`, `files:update`, and `archive-jobs:write`

A read-only analysis token needs the `:read` scopes for the data you want to query.

### Tokens with older scopes [#older-scopes]

New tokens must list specific scopes. `POST /api/v1/tokens` rejects the wildcard `*` and the older coarse scopes `runs:write`, `files:write`, and `watchers:write`.

Tokens that already have those scopes keep working until you replace them, with one exception. On a token that has registered a watcher, deregistered watchers included, they count only for what a watcher needs:

* `*` gives the **Watcher** preset’s scopes
* `runs:write` gives `runs:create`, `runs:update`, and `runs:upload`
* `files:write` gives `files:update`
* `watchers:write` gives `watchers:report`

Scopes the token lists itself still count.

The `runs:attribute` and `feedback:admin` scopes no longer exist, because claiming runs and reviewing feedback need a signed-in person. Data Hub removed them from existing tokens on October 6, 2026.

## Integration secrets [#integration-secrets]

Data Hub encrypts the Linear and Slack secrets that admins save under **Settings → Integrations**, using the key in the `INTEGRATION_SECRETS_KEY` environment variable. The app never shows a secret again after it’s saved. See [Set up integrations](/docs/integrations#integration-secrets-key).

## MCP access [#mcp-access]

The MCP server at `/mcp/v1` accepts OAuth access tokens, not personal access tokens. To connect, you sign in to Data Hub and approve a consent screen that names the AI client and the access it wants. The client then receives an access token that works only for that deployment’s MCP endpoint.

Data Hub rejects a token issued to a client with no person behind it, so every MCP action is recorded against a person. MCP uses two scopes of its own, instead of the token scopes above:

* `read`: needed to connect, and covers every read-only tool, resource, and prompt
* `write`: also needed by any tool that changes data, such as claiming a run or deleting one

A grant belongs to one client and one person, and it has that person’s own permissions. Clients register themselves when they connect. Registering creates an OAuth client record but grants nothing on its own. Google sign-in still decides who gets through, and the consent screen still decides what they hand over.

The web app has no screen for reviewing or revoking MCP grants yet. Removing someone from your Google Workspace organization blocks new grants. To cut off a client that already has a token, delete the matching rows from the `oauthAccessToken` and `oauthRefreshToken` tables.

To set up a client, see [MCP overview](/docs/mcp).

## Token hygiene [#token-hygiene]

Name each token clearly, set expirations, and give each token only the scopes it needs. Revoke a token as soon as you stop using it or it may have been exposed. The full checklist is in [Token hygiene](/docs/manage-tokens#token-hygiene).

## Pages that load without signing in [#public-pages-gated-bodies]

Some web pages load without a session, so that apps that show link previews can read the page’s metadata, such as its title. These are the home page, instrument pages, run pages, and settings pages. Without a session, the page shows a sign-in prompt instead of real data.

Three separate safeguards keep the app out of search engines:

* `robots` metadata
* `robots.txt`
* an `X-Robots-Tag` header

Every `/api/v1/*` route always needs a session cookie or a bearer token.
